en: Preface to the Newly Carved Interlinear Commentary on the *Śīla-sūtra-śāstra* Observe that the great void is vast and expansive;
having transcended all faults at the ford of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), the true mind is a luminous mirror, inherently endowed with all virtues within the realm of eternal bliss.
This is what is called the *śīla* (precepts) of the fundamental nature of the Dharma-Buddha, wherein all myriad virtues [are complete].
How perfectly complete it is! How sublime indeed! Nevertheless, when the winds of objects blow with violent force, the ocean of the mind surges;
following conditions, it flows and changes, and by pursuing sensory dust, it becomes bound by attachment. Thus, one is made to wear horns and shed fur, enduring bitter suffering with no end in sight.
To harbor this bright jewel yet wander aimlessly through the six realms, exhausted by hardship and toil—this is truly a matter for lamentation. I...
When the Great Hero appeared in Zhugan (India), his distant origins were vast and obscure. He realized the Way within the realm of quiescent light and cast its reflection upon the land of the mind.
Thus, at the site of the terrace of nirvana, he first formulated the Bodhisattva precepts;

these accord with the essence of the Dharma-nature in severing evil and cultivating good, and follow the function of True Suchness in responding boundlessly to circumstances. Essence and function share a single source, manifesting—
Subtly and secretly penetrating—this is called the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (Tri-śaraṇa-śīla). All myriad practices are fully contained therein.
Alas, how magnificent! Yet, human natures are not uniform; their endowments and constitutions differ. How can one possibly be capable of the great conduct of a Bodhisattva?
The Greatly Awakened Compassionate Father thus divided the three aggregates of precepts and first bestowed them upon the assembly of śrāvakas as the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint).
Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Receiving the bodhisattva’s precepts of dignified conduct (*vinaya*) is called 'leaving home' and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*)."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva’s morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) is that which corresponds to the various Vinayas of the various schools.

Since the time those five dreams manifested portents and the white tuft [between the Buddha's brows] withdrew its radiance, the Venerable Upagupta compiled the treasury of precepts, calling it the *Mūla-mahāvinaya-piṭaka*.
From generation to generation, the sages have transmitted it to one another, never having diverged onto different paths. This continued until...
The path of the *Upāsaka-śīla* was not transmitted by the Three Sages; the heterodox teachings of Mahādeva arose and contended over five points.

Although there were divergent attachments among the two groups, the five groups, the eighteen schools, and the five hundred schools, the practice and realization remained non-dual, and the bridge to liberation followed a single principle.

Thus, the omen of breaking the golden staff and pulling the white cotton cloth is preserved herein. Long ago, during the Zhou dynasty, stars flew... (Note: The final phrase "周星飛" appears to be a fragmentary reference to a historical or astrological event, likely alluding to a specific period or phenomenon associated with the Zhou dynasty.)
For over a thousand years, the True Way remained obscured and its gates had not yet opened. When the Sun of Han radiated its light, the teachings of the Buddha were suspended over the Eastern Lands;

it has been two hundred years since that time. The monastics throughout the realm merely knew how to shave their heads and dye their robes, yet they had not even received the five or eight precepts, let alone the full ordination.
It was during the Jiaping era of the Cao Wei dynasty that the Venerable Dharmakṣema arrived.
In Luoyang, the *karmavācanā* was performed according to the Dharmaguptaka school to confer the precepts; thus did the transmission of the precepts begin in the land of China.
Reaching the Yao Qin dynasty, Jueming served as the oral interpreter and Zhu Fonian took up the brush to translate the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Since then, twenty schools have composed commentaries (*śāstra*). Although it is said that each vies with the others like the orchid and the chrysanthemum, none have yet attained the pure and essential essence. And when...
Now, the Great Master Chengzhao of the Great Tang searched out the secret and wondrous mysteries of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and fulfilled the final charge to uphold the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
He produced commentaries, sub-commentaries, and ritual diagrams for the benefit of the people of his time; how could this not serve as a guiding model for future generations? Holding...

Hold this as a mirror for reflection! Indeed, were it not for the illumination of the lamp of wisdom and the bestowing of the raft of Dharma, who could have dispelled the darkness to reveal the broad highway, or rescued those submerged in the depths to reach the further shore?
Its fame has spread throughout the Five Heavens, and its bounty has flowed for a thousand years.
It was intended merely for the four reliances to sustain a single person; yet, as the phrasing is profound and the meaning obscure, it is not easy to unravel.

Nevertheless, there have been no fewer than sixty schools of thought that followed its lead, each vying for supremacy regarding what is right or wrong, clashing like drums in battle over victory and defeat.
Yet, those who merely echo the same arguments are not yet sufficient to serve as a standard for regulation.
As for one who rectifies and encompasses the eternal models and manifests the conduct and rituals—could it be anyone other than the Great Master Vinaya Master of the Great Song?

When the eminent voice of this master’s five hundred outstanding disciples raised a single chant, having already set a precedent beyond the reach of former masters, who indeed shall continue his lingering resonance? It is we of Fusang...
As for the transmission of the precepts and Vinaya in this land, it originated with Master Jianzhen (Jōdo) at Zhaoti Monastery and was revived by Bodhisattva Xingzheng of Xi Daxing Monastery.
Subsequently, it was transmitted by Preceptor Mingren; its lineages have become vast and far-reaching, overflowing throughout the realm.
He refined the *vinaya* to such a degree that he need not feel ashamed before the masters of the past. Previously, Master Guang first brought together their practices.
The *Shichao Ji* (Record of the Essentials). Next was Master Rong, who likewise compiled the *Jie-mo Su Ji* (Commentary on the Sutra of Rituals).

However, what was regrettable was that the *Jieben Su Ji* (Commentary on the Precept Text) and its topical outline circulated as four separate works, which caused inconvenience for readers. I wished to synthesize them; I attempted this twice and even thrice.
Yet, due to a lack of leisure for meditation and recitation, compounded by illness that caused the days to pass in vain, I have not yet been able to accomplish it. Now, there is...
I praise Master Lingzhi Jijing of Donglin in Zhenzhou. He polished himself with the jewel of the precepts and cooled himself with the water of meditative concentration.
Diligent in the Dharma-gate, his resolve was set upon universal salvation. Devoting himself to this assembly, he brought it to completion;

his achievement thus surpasses those of previous generations. Upon hearing of this, I sighed and said: "That the Master has undertaken such an endeavor is like the fainting glow of the setting sun in the final age being restored to its dark depths."
This fulfills my long-cherished aspiration. Thus, I have praised his achievements from afar, so that they may be bequeathed to distant generations. Alas!

The three divisions [of the Tripitaka] are now fully realized, and the radiance of wisdom shines forth; the single path to Nirvāṇa is brilliantly visible. May those who delight in learning and observing the precepts [be inspired].
By means of this, one proceeds: relying on the śrāvaka precepts, one exits the gates of the triple world;

by means of the bodhisattva precepts, one transcends the land of transformation and attains the Tathāgata’s unconditioned aggregate of precepts. Thus, the ocean of the mind turns its current back and suddenly enters the capital of eternal quiescence.
This is the preface.
Written on a day of winter retreat during the first year of the Mingwa era (the Jia-shen year of the dragon),
by the bhikṣu Jisō at the Yugishitsu of Senryūzan Sennyo Ritsu-ji Temple.

Since my youth, I have carried my books and traveled through the monasteries where the Vinaya is studied. I have been singularly nurtured by the compassion of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, allowing me to slightly sprout the seeds of the Five Divisions [of the Vinaya].

To express my gratitude for this grace, I have taken up this single volume; reading it by day and contemplating it by night, I have wielded my brush to model myself after its teachings until I finally attained a comprehensive understanding.
Those who read it all said that I should have it carved upon wooden blocks to circulate throughout the world. I, too, [have agreed].
This was indeed a matter of great joy. The master of Mount Raishan composed this preface and introduction to bring it forth;

however, as the timing and conditions were not yet ripe, it remained buried within the library for over twenty years. His disciples, including Kakuhō and others, consulted with a bookseller and had it announced.
As for me, my years have grown old and decrepit, and the twilight of my life presses against the western mountains.
Unable to wait for the appointed time, I have once again collated this work, added the table of contents and other preliminary matter, and brought it to life through the printing blocks.

Thus it is recorded. On the first day of the moon in the middle winter of the eighth year of Meireki, the year of the Dragon (the Xinmao year), the bhikṣu Jōren bows his head in reverence and inscribes this.
Now, the transformative influence of the Way has gradually spread to the East for some six or seven hundred years.
Among those who have emerged in the world as preeminent masters of the Vinaya in both the North and South, the Great Tang Master Chengzhao is such a person.

His composition of the three great treatises on the *Vinaya* fully embodies the intent of the Tathāgata’s skillful means and opens the gateway to liberation for all sentient beings. The merit of upholding the Triple Gem rests with him.
This is so. Next is the commentary. As for one who can elucidate the profound depths of the *Jiaochao* (Commentary), it must be none other than the Great Master Dazhi of the Song Dynasty.
During the Tianping era of our present dynasty, the Tang monk Dahe Sheng arrived at Zhaoti Temple and transmitted the Vinaya.

In Fusang, the unified tradition generally receives and recites the texts of the Four Divisions (Dharmaguptaka), and when discussing their practical applications, they all rely upon the texts of the Nanshan school.

If one were to follow the scholars of the Sarvāstivāda school, it could be said that their fundamental tenets would be inverted and their understanding of the principles and flavor of the Dharma would be erroneous.

At present, the *Sāmāyika-śīla* (the precept of receiving the vows) is universally observed; furthermore, based upon the *Chao* and the *Shu*, this specific version of the *Śīla-mūla* (Root Text), along with its commentaries (*Shu*) and sub-commentaries (*Ji*), has been particularly circulated in the world. This is the current assembly edition. It was a task upon which my teacher long applied his mind.
Now that its work is accomplished, he has repeatedly subjected it to collation and proofreading before preparing it for publication. He has further commanded his disciples...

I have collated this manuscript (though unworthy). Although my understanding and insight are crude and desolate, I dare not disobey the Master’s command. I simply compared the old version with the new;

having finished a single reading, I was so filled with joy that I could not bear to let go of the scroll. Thus, forgetting my own mediocrity, I take up the brush and prostrate myself in salutation, saying thus much.
Respectfully offered by the mountain disciple, the bhikṣu Qingyue (Yishun), on the middle day of the second month in the second year of An’eng,
the Gui-si year, at the Pavilion of the Yuantong Jingshe on Mount Ru bao within the Great Palace of Zandong. I pay homage.
Śīla is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the foundation of the myriad practices; it is truly the causal basis for dhyāna and prajñā.
In the near term, it is the path to the realms of humans and devas; in the distant term, it is the primary cause for attaining the Way.

Whether one is a lay follower or a monastic within the Śākya school, one must certainly know this. It is here that the three great commentaries on the *Vinaya* composed by the Patriarch [Daoxuan] of Zhongnan Mountain have been circulated.
These have flourished throughout the world. Among them, that which is most urgent to undertake is surely the essential commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Nevertheless, it has been unavoidable that it has been transmitted separately since different dynasties.
My teacher grieved for this in private and applied himself with tireless diligence to synthesize the five recensions into a single text, desiring to make it easy for beginners to examine and compare.
Furthermore, I desire to cause the people of the world to give birth to the seeds of humans and devas, ultimately leading them to the authority and exposition of the Great Way.
On the day this work was completed, I, the unworthy one, had it collated and reviewed. Now, it has been carved in relief and distributed to propagate its influence throughout the realm.
With one heart, I rejoice, for my chest is filled with it. Having no leisure to examine the countenances of others, I exhaust my humble words to offer this brief praise:
The Buddha realized the Truth through the Precepts; By relying on conduct, he became a True Man; Thus the life of wisdom was made continuous.

The title indicates that the *Sifen lü jieben* (Skt. *Caturvargika-vinaya-prātimokṣa-sūtra*) belongs to the Dharmaguptaka school (*Tánwúdé bù*).

The commentary (*hànzhù*) and the sub-commentary (*shū*) were produced by Nanshan [Dōngyǎn]. The *Xíngzōngjì* and the topical outline (*kē*) were composed by Línzhī [Zōngtǐng]. Within these works, the commentary is integrated with the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

Originally, this was a single work; however, the *shu* (commentary), *ji* (sub-commentary), and the topical outline (*ke*) circulated separately according to their respective levels—upper, middle, and lower.

Regarding the sections, there were five; regarding the fascicles, there were four volumes. The *shu* and *ji* each consisted of eight fascicles (as categorized by Lingzhi), and the outline consisted of two fascicles;

together with the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, they totaled twenty-one fascicles. Now, these have been further compiled and combined into thirty-seven fascicles, divided into three sets of seven. One, two, three.
Each of the four [sections] has its upper and lower parts; these have been preserved according to their original form.
To them, I have further added the first, second, and so forth, thereby forming the individual fascicles. This is my own established arrangement.

The commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* was written in small characters arranged in parallel columns in ancient editions. For the sake of easy reading, I have transcribed most of it in large characters and divided it with punctuation marks.

Where the space was insufficient for a column, or where the notes were recorded together without being formally categorized and explained, I have followed the old edition directly by placing the sub-commentary below the main text in smaller script; do not be surprised by this.

In general, those items marked with 【律】 within the topical outline (kē) are from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. Those marked with 【註】 include the commentaries (*zhù*). Those marked with 【疏】 are from the sub-commentaries (*shū*).

Items set down one character lower are from the records (*jì*). These have been arranged as headings above the text of the sub-commentaries so that the five sections may be brought together for a single overview.
Fearing there may still be discrepancies, I leave it to later generations to verify them; this would be most fortunate.
