Consequently, among the texts of the four Āgamas, none surpass this Vinaya; its name is not falsely attributed, and it is held in high esteem today.
Yet, those who propagate it are few, which cannot help but evoke a long sigh.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* was also brought back by Faxian, but he passed away before it could be translated.

When the monks in the capital heard that Kumārajīva was well-versed in this Vinaya, they requested him to produce a translation. In the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty, Kumārajīva arrived in Yangzhou;
it was in this same year that he, together with the Khotanese monk Zhisheng, translated it. Both masters, Sheng and Yan, were disciples of Kumārajīva.

The first four lines of the preceding text demonstrate the superiority [of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*], while the final two lines express lamentation over the fact that, among the four Vinayas transmitted here in this land, only the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* has rarely been propagated;
thus it is said that its circulation is meager. *Shifen lü han zhù jièběn shū xíngzōng jì*, Vol. 1, Part 1.1.
*Commentary on the Essential Meaning of the Precepts of the Four-Part Vinaya with Annotations: Record of the Practice of the School*, Volume One, Part Two.

[Sūtra] From the preceding section, the general characteristics have been briefly revealed prior to the text. Now, we shall proceed according to the meaning of the text by establishing three positions.

Regarding the "marking of the preceding" within the introductory section: "marking" refers to the teaching that elucidates, and "mark" refers to the meanings explained in the general and specific sections of the preceding four chapters.
Now, below, the subsequent [sections] are marked. [Commentary]:

The first part, from "I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas" onwards, is a verse that clarifies the Dharma; it indicates that the realization of the Arhat (aśaikṣa) is about to be transmitted and practiced.
Although the light of the teaching has shone throughout the age, those of dull faculties in this degenerate era are for the most part full of guile and deceit;

they claim that [the Buddha] harbors a different intention and have been unable to receive him as their teacher. Therefore, [the author] first pays homage and extols the efficacy of the precepts, exhorting them to practice them.

Thus, the general introduction to both the extensive and abbreviated teachings has already been manifested. Now, the primary doctrine (saddharma) should be revealed; hence, the second section follows, beginning from "The harmonious Sangha having assembled... and below.

When one arrives at the middle [section] of this treatise, it is titled "The Distinct Introduction, Main Body, and Circulation of the Two Teachings, Extensive and Concise," which extensively opens up the various aspects of upholding and violating precepts, as well as their general and specific applications.
Once these distinct practices have been established and all virtues perfected, they shall subsequently flow forth to manifest inexhaustible characteristics;
therefore, in the third section, beginning with "A person who can protect the precepts," the text generally cites both teachings to exhort practice for the sake of broad benefit.
In the initial summary judgment, the introduction is clarified: "Cunning, deceitful, and sycophantic" refers to having much suspicion and a lack of pure faith.

Regarding "harboring separate intentions," the subsequent explanation clarifies the intent of the dedication, stating: "It means harboring false thoughts because one does not follow the lineage of the school.
Thus, "first paying homage" refers to the first verse; "praising the merit of the precepts" refers to the next verse; and "exhorting practitioners" refers to [the following].

The following verses are intended to exclude [the preceding]. Within the "Correct Doctrine" (*saddharma*), both the Extensive and the Abridged teachings each have their own sequence for the Introduction (*nidāna*) and the Circulation (*pariṇāmanā*);

therefore, they are called "distinct. When these two teachings are combined, they constitute the "General Correct Doctrine," and it is said that both the Introduction and the Circulation are "general" because, in relation to the two teachings, each possesses its own three divisions.
Regarding "penetration and obstruction" (*tong-se*), this refers to opening and closing, as well as upholding and violating. Opening...
The "General Summary" (*Zhētōng*) encompasses both the extensive and the concise versions, subsuming all precepts within its circulation. It states:

"Regarding the 'distinct practitioner' (*biéxíngzhě*), this refers back to the main body of the teaching where the extensive and concise versions differ; furthermore, because the modes of practice (*xíngxiàng*) vary between the two teachings, one who reveres both teachings will have their internal spiritual accomplishments (*dàoyè*) become beautiful and their external reputation manifest, which is why it says 'the multitude of virtues is fulfilled.'"
[Commentary]: Regarding the two preceding introductions, there are three types of distinctions: first, the name; second, the intent; and third, the sequence. [Commentary]:

Regarding the first, the name, there are four kinds of differences: first, the difference regarding the person; the preceding verse concerns the Dharma as the primary subject of compilation, while from "the harmonization" onwards, it concerns the Tathāgata’s dissemination of the teaching.
Second, the difference regarding the time; the preceding verse concerns the future hundred-year period as the primary introduction.

The initial transformation of the three [vehicles] into one, both collectively and individually, differs from the preceding verse; the Dharma is the single orthodox school, harmoniously unified into five hundred sects.
Fourth, regarding the difference in meaning: the former is the exhortation to faith, while the latter is that which is transmitted; this is the introductory sequence of the narrative.

Regarding the establishment of the titles within the first section of the introductory division, the four distinct names are as follows: first, "The Dharma Proper" is named after the person, the Tathāgata;
second, [the title] is named after the time, distinguishing between the future and the present; third, it is named after the central theme, taking the specific first and then the general whole;
fourth, the naming convention is identical to that of other sutras, and its meaning is readily understandable.
[Commentary: Second, regarding the difference in their underlying intentions: if one considers the propagation of the teaching at that specific time, each [compiler] had but a single intention.

Since the Tathāgata himself set forth the sequence, there was no need to worry about its non-implementation; why, then, would there be a need for encouragement to believe? This [encouragement] is merely the cause for initiating [the compilation].

It does not preclude the act of encouraging belief, as it serves both to describe the circumstances of the collection and to initiate [the work]. As for citing later [evidence] to establish [the authenticity], this is not mere conjecture; thus, the "initiation" also extends to this.
Exhortation to Believe.

In the initial section clarifying the specific intent of the composition, it merely recounts that the Buddha did not require exhortation; this demonstrates that when the Dharma is correct, there is no need for laborious initiation.
Since the teaching flourished during the Buddha’s own lifetime, its propagation required only the addition of exhortation; this passage highlights that point.
The two prefaces each have their own specific intent and do not hinder one another; the subsequent section demonstrates their mutual interconnection.

The preceding preface establishes the purpose of the compilation and introduces the main body of the teaching, while the latter preface cites the Buddha’s own words with the aim of providing authentication and inspiration for faith. Regarding the phrase "cited to establish," it means that the Buddha’s preface is cited to authenticate the main body of the teaching.
[Commentary] Regarding the sequence of the three types of introduction: the question asks why the order of the initial arousal [of the teaching] is presented later, rather than at the beginning.

The answer is that if it were placed at the outset, there would be two inconveniences: first, it would manifest that the extensive introduction is separated from the main body of the treatise (*saddharma*), preventing them from being contiguous;

thus, the arousal [of the teaching] would be rendered ineffective. Second, it would fail to fully manifest the original intent of encouraging faith; that is to say, one would only be encouraging faith in the main body, but not in the extensive introduction.
Now, summarizing, both of the preceding two types are reversed to explain "taking" (*upādāna*) as above.

Regarding the sequence of before, after, and middle in terms of time, the question and answer concerning what is "illogical" (*ayukti*) involve two instances of "inappropriateness" (*anupapatti*): first, based on the initial arousal [of the thought], it is inappropriate;
second, regarding the exhortation to believe, it is inappropriate. As for reversing the explanation above: first, it demonstrates there is no interval; second, [it demonstrates]... [text fragment].
Because all [beings] have been exhorted, it is said that they "all" [attain] it immediately.

[Commentary]: Regarding the initial introductory text, it is divided into four sections. The first half-verse clarifies that as he is about to expound the True Dharma, there are many obstacles in this defiled world;
fearing there may be hindrances, he pays homage to the Triple Gem to receive their protection and empowerment. The second half-verse is for taking refuge...

The first section, "Respecting the Original Intent so That the Dharma May Long Endure," explains the three precepts as being like the ocean. The subsequent nine verses extensively enumerate the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the precepts;
when these are fully revealed, the mind is exhorted to uphold them. The final section, "The Worldly [Benefits]," clarifies that the merit of upholding the teachings and practices is not in vain.
In the fourth section of the analysis, the four lines of the verse are generally divided such that two lines constitute one verse and one line constitutes half a verse;
when there is only a single line, it is simply referred to as a "line. All subsequent divisions of the text follow this same principle.
[Vinaya] I bow my head in homage to all Buddhas, as well as to the Dharma and the Sangha of Bhikṣus.
[Commentary] Regarding the first passage, the meaning and the text are divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the Three Jewels; second, the interpretation of the intent of taking refuge.
[Commentary] Now, as for the Three Jewels and their three distinct conditions, since their initial names and meanings are already well known through regular study, there is no need to explain them;
therefore, I shall briefly cite them here.

In the first section of the first half-verse, which provides a brief indication, there are two parts. First, it indicates the distinct objects of the conditions, which refers to the objective realm (*viṣaya*). First...
Next, I shall explain the names and meanings that were previously mentioned.
[Commentary] Regarding the term "Buddha," in Sanskrit it is called *buddha*, or alternatively *budha*, *buddha*, *buta*, *futu*, or *foutu*. These are merely corruptions of the phonetic transmission.
Since there is no such person [in this context], it is translated according to its meaning as "the Awakened One" (*jue*). This possesses two [aspects].

In terms of meaning, "awakening" (*bodha*) refers to the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*); like thieves, these are perceived only by the noble ones (*ārya*). "Awakening to" (*bodhana*) refers to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
like sleep, these are uniquely awakened to only by the noble ones. There are two types of ignorance (*avidyā*):

first, ignorance that is deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu*), which is well-awakened to as the three realms; second, ignorance that is deluded regarding principle (*tattva*), which is the awakening to the true nature of dharmas through universal penetration.
This is collectively termed "Awakening" (Bodhi).
Regarding the Buddha, there are two initial translations: first, the Sanskrit name has seven [phonetic] variations, such as *Mata* or with the character *Jia* added below;

second, the explanation of its meaning: the sense of "awakening" (*bodha*) refers to the realization that the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) do not extend beyond the ten branches [of dependent origination], which together constitute [the state of awakening].

The delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the three realms are coarse and thus easy to sever; they are combined into one dwelling. The delusions of thought (*saṃjñā-kleśa*) within the three realms are subtle and difficult to shatter;
they are divided into three. Thus, there are four dwellings. These obstruct ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) sever them together.

Within the sense of awakening, ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes one dwelling. Generally, it is termed "ignorance," but when specifically distinguished according to phenomena (*vastu*) and principle (*tattva*), the former...

Those who are deluded regarding phenomena obstruct the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); because only a Buddha thoroughly penetrates both mundane and supramundane dharmas, this is called the wisdom of "knowing as it is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Because he is able to awaken all sentient beings, it is said that there are three destinies—humans, non-humans, and animals—which collectively encompass the six realms of existence.
These are all that is to be awakened; this refers to awakening others. Second, those who are deluded regarding principle obstruct the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The truth of the *dharmatā* is the sphere of realization fully realized only by the Buddha; when the aspects of wisdom and its object merge, it is called "wisdom of suchness" (*tathatā-jñāna*), which is self-awakening.
However, these two types of awakening are not realized by the followers of the Two Vehicles, while Bodhisattvas realize them only partially.

The latter two phrases summarize [the preceding] to show that universal awakening is restricted solely to those at the stage of fruition; this is the fulfillment of awakening and practice. As the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states:

Possessing both omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—the two types of awakening according to the *Vyākhyāyukti*—and being free from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—the two obstructions according to the *Vyākhyāyukti*—he is able to awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects (the two truths of ultimate and conventional reality), and is likewise able to awaken all sentient beings (the two benefits of self and others).
He is like one waking from a dream, or like a lotus flower blooming (the dream metaphor represents delusion regarding phenomena; the lotus metaphor represents delusion regarding principle).
Therefore, he is named Buddha (distinguishing him from those still on the path). Furthermore, as I wish to examine this in detail, it is not the primary focus here, so I shall be brief.

[Commentary: That which is called "Dharma" is a local term of this land; in the Great Xia (India), the Sanskrit pronunciation is *dharma*, or alternatively *dharmma*—these are merely differences in transmission.
Because they do not understand the science of phonology (*śabda-vidyā*), their terminology is often erroneous. The Dharma has two meanings: first...
Regarding the method of understanding the nature of reality through the three clusters (*tri-rāśi*) and other such models, we shall now rely on the latter meaning.

When the Noble Ones expound the teachings, their intent lies in the accomplishment of practice—just as a carriage follows its ruts and a vessel follows its mold. The Dharma is not something perceived by the eye; it is established through analogies.
Furthermore, practice must follow the Way, for the Way does not follow the practitioner; the Way is that upon which practice relies, and thus there is no fixed form.
This concludes the preceding section.

Regarding the explanation of the Dharma, the first part demonstrates that in the Western lands (India), there exists the *Śabdavidyā* treatise which distinguishes and determines the correctness or corruption of phonemes;

it now points out that because the translators who transmitted [the texts] were not proficient in that treatise, what they produced differs [from the original]. The following section explains the meaning of the Dharma.
Regarding the initial mention of the "three aggregates" (*triskandha*): first, matter (*rūpa*); second, mind (*citta*); and third, that which is neither matter nor mind (*naiva-rūpa-na-citta*).

Because the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of these three are distinct and do not intermingle, they are called "self-nature. The subsequent meaning is self-evident from the text. First, there is the presentation of the heading, followed by the explanation through metaphors below.

Furthermore, this consists of two parts: first, the explanation using the metaphors of the vehicle and the vessel; second, the explanation using the metaphor of taking the road, which establishes the model of the system.
The meaning is as follows: the first two lines establish the analogy, while the latter two lines provide the application.

[Commentary]: "Saṃgha" is a transliteration from the Sanskrit; it is called "Saṃgha" because that specific term does not exist [in Chinese], and thus it is translated by its characteristic meaning as "the assembly.

Alternatively, there are older interpretations which state that the "harmonious assembly" (andha-saṃgha) refers to the essence and characteristics [of the community]; those who hold such views all possess [this commonality].
The six harmonies and the four types of persons are not merely a single matter, for they collectively establish the dharmas of the Saṃgha;

however, in various sūtras, this is translated simply as "the assembly" (*saṃgha*) without explaining its essential nature, as is explained in detail in the *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā).

In the initial translation of the list of names by Shi Sengzhong, the translation was based on their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); this is the current standard translation. Alternatively, the following presents the ancient interpretation:

the initial translation of the name as "Harmony" (*saṃgha*) refers to its essence (*svabhāva*), while "the assembly" (*gaṇa*) refers to its characteristics. The subsequent explanation of the meaning—that it possesses the six kinds of harmony—interprets the aforementioned essence.
The mention of "four persons" interprets the aforementioned characteristics. "Accomplishing the dharma of the assembly" distinguishes all *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts).

[The commentary] likewise follows the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā), which takes the collective translations as its primary basis; while there are many instances of rejection or establishment [of alternatives], I shall not cite them here at length. [Sūtra]:

These three benefits for the world are: near extraction from the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*) and distant purification of the two types of death (*dvividha-maraṇa*). This rare, unique, and thorough realization is worthy of veneration.

Regarding the Jewel, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* (Treatise on the Nature of the Jewels) explains the six meanings through similes: 1. **The Meaning of Rarity:** Worldly jewels are not possessed by the poor; likewise, those with meager merit do not encounter the Triple Gem. 2.

**The Meaning of Freedom from Defilement:** Worldly jewels are inherently free from flaws and impurities; likewise, the Triple Gem is utterly detached from all outflows (*āsrava*). 3. **The Meaning of Power:** Worldly jewels remove poverty and dispel poison;

likewise, the Triple Gem possesses the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that are inconceivable. 4. **The Meaning of Ornamentation:** [Worldly jewels serve as ornaments; likewise, the Triple Gem adorns sentient beings.]... [The text continues with the remaining meanings.]
The meaning of "worldly treasures that adorn the body to make it beautiful" refers to the Three Jewels, which can adorn the *dharmakāya*.

Among all things, the Three Jewels are the most supreme; they are the "worldly treasures of the six meanings of being unalterable," for they remain unchanged even when refined and polished. The Three Jewels are unmoved by the eight worldly concerns.

Although the preceding six explanations are identical in their general presentation, when one examines the substance through the metaphor, the character for "treasure" (*ratna*) is uniformly defined as "precious."
As for "beauty," it is as previously cited.

Regarding the general name, the middle two [phrases] provide a brief explanation based on meaning; the first three phrases above clarify the benefits. The two terms "near" and "far" must be correlated with cause and fruit, and death.
First is called *pariccheda* (segmented death), which the Three Vehicles abandon in common; second is called *pariṇāma* (transformation death), which [is abandoned] exclusively by [the Bodhisattvas].
The phrase "the Buddha has forever exhausted all that is rare" concludes the name [of this section] as "rare in the world," because such a being does not exist in the world;

"the Solitary Realizer transcends all realms of existence" because he has surpassed all *bhava*. Therefore, the following passage cites texts to explain these points extensively. Now, we employ the four kinds of Triple Gem to correspond with these six meanings.

The first meaning applies to all four: the *dharmatā*-Treasure is not encountered by those lacking faith; the *nirmāṇa*-Treasure is not encountered by those for whom there is no karmic affinity, as in the case of Śrāvastī.

The principle that the three jewels are [conventionally] distinct can be clarified by this: the essence of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is restricted to the distinction between the holy and the ordinary, while the ignorant do not encounter it as a single entity;
furthermore, the two vehicles do not encounter it as the second meaning. Within this context, regarding the Jewel of Principle alone, the *Gongyang yi* (Ritual for Paying Homage) states:

"The essence of the Three Jewels as maintained [in the world] is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and fully possessed of outflows and defilement"; and it further states: "The essence of the manifested form (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*) is impermanent, being transmuted by the four marks of existence and subject to extinction."

Passing over a thousand years, one can only look back to honor the distant past, thereby increasing one's reverent devotion; yet, based on the subsequent principle that those remaining in delusion follow along with defilement, these three types [of beings] all lack this meaning.
In the third analogy, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) reside in humans; they are applied specifically to the manifested marks (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*).

These six—miraculous power (*ṛddhi*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)—are all clear and penetrating, and are collectively designated as such.
Regarding the first [meaning], it is said that jewels can manifest and eliminate poverty and suffering; this is somewhat similar to the present context.

Regarding the fourth [meaning], the four types of *dharmakāya* (abiding and maintaining) are the marks of transformation (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) which can inspire faith; the principle-body (*li-ti*) and the essence-body (*yi-ti*) are one and the same, both capable of being cultivated and realized as ornaments for the body.
Regarding the fifth [meaning], it also encompasses the remaining four; the other three are easy to understand. Although the abiding and maintaining of the Buddha-dharma is indeed... [the text ends].
Among all worldly things, none fail to represent the functioning of the Dharmakāya, which is infinite. The *Yi* (Ritual) states:
"Gold, wood, stone, and earth—though their substance is insentient—are used to create images; therefore, those who honor or revile them personally obtain merit or transgression.
Thus we know that these treasures are named the "Unsurpassed Dharma," and they likewise serve as fields of merit for the world, just like shaven-headed monks among humans and devas.
It surpasses those who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct, let alone others who uphold them; thus its superiority may be known.
The sixth [jewel] is restricted solely to the principle. The *Riyao* states: "These Three Jewels abide eternally in the world and are not subject to the insults of worldly dharmas.
Although their single essence is eternal, from the perspective of delusion, they flow and change according to conditions; the other two are impermanent."

This is not a matter for further discussion. Regarding the "eight dharmas," the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that decline and prosperity, defamation and praise, honor and contempt, suffering and pleasure—these four adversities and four conformities are able to stir the human mind and are thus called the "eight winds.

Since the principles, jewels, persons, and dharmas are all supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) noble paths, they cannot be moved by these eight dharmas; this is the summary of the preceding and following sections.
[Commentary]: Within the Three Jewels, four distinct sections are further differentiated: first, enumerating the various characteristics; second, clarifying the fundamental and the derivative;
third, analyzing the sequence; and fourth, describing the functional efficacy.
Within the first section, the names are initially explained because the names apply to all four positions; thus, the categories of meaning are opened up and analyzed to reveal their distinctions.
Therefore, it is said that they are "repeated.
[Commentary] Within the initial section on the "Various Characteristics," there are four kinds of Triple Gems.
Regarding these various characteristics, all other schools omit the Jewel of Principle (理寶); this present commentary alone provides a detailed classification of its four positions.
[Commentary: First, regarding the essence of principle (*li-ti*): the fivefold Dharma-body is the Buddha Jewel; the unconditioned cessation of principle (*nirodha-asamskṛta*) is the Dharma Jewel;

and the merits of the Śrāvakas, both those in training and those beyond training, are the Saṃgha Jewel. Second, regarding the marks of transformation (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*): for example, Śākyamuni reigning as the King of the Path over the three thousandfold world system is the Buddha Jewel;
the expounding and dissemination of the teachings of the Truths (*satya-dharma*) is the Dharma Jewel; and Kauṇḍinya and the other four are the Saṃgha Jewel. Third, regarding abiding...
That which is upheld—namely, images and stūpas—is the Buddha Jewel; that which is transmitted on paper and silk is the Dharma Jewel; and the precepts, dharmas, and ritual forms are the Sangha Jewel.

Regarding these four as a single essence, as is commonly discussed, it is simply that the substance of the mind is distinguished into three aspects according to its meaning, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* concerning the identical nature of the Three Jewels.
First, the Jewel of Principle is clarified. The text is excerpted from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya). "Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom" receive their names from their causes;

"Liberation and the Knowledge and Vision of Liberation" manifest their titles from their fruits. Because one cuts off delusions through wisdom, the state where delusions no longer exist is called "Liberation.

Emerging from entanglements, breaking through obstacles, and reflecting back to contemplate the mind is called "Knowledge and Vision of Liberation. It is the cessation of the principle of the Four Noble Truths.

Those who study for the realization of the Truths (satya) and those who have already attained the fruits of training and beyond—beginning from the first fruit—are called a "harmonious Saṃgha through the vision of the True Truths.
This treasure of principle (*tattva-ratna*) is also of one essence; however, it is distinguished from the perspective of the Buddha and the Saṃgha in terms of their realization of that principle.
Thus, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha is also the Dharma, and the Dharma is also the Buddha; the Saṃgha is also the Dharma; they are merely one single phenomenon (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*)."
Because there are distinctions, the three jewels are divided; among the manifested aspects of transformation, the "three thousand" refers to the realm of those to be transformed.
Regarding the Truths and the Teachings, although the Dharma-gates of the Four Noble Truths are numerous, they are represented by the foremost.

Furthermore, the Four Truths universally encompass the causes and effects of both ordinary beings and sages, as well as the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings—whether extensive or concise—and their diverse suitability, all of which do not transcend these four. *Kulinda* is translated here as [the name of a king].
The "original limit" (the beginning) refers to the first five persons converted at the Deer Park;
the first was Kauṇḍinya (also known as Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya), the second was Aśvajit, the third was Bhadrika, the fourth was Daśabala-Kāśyapa, and the fifth was Mahā-Kapphiṇa.
To uphold the precepts of the Dharma is the essence of the Saṃgha; its outward form and appearance consist of the tonsure and the dyed robes. Within this single body, it is like...
"Constant Discourse" (Changlun) refers to the essential tenets of the sūtras and śāstras; the three characteristics [of these tenets] will be explained in detail below.
[Commentary: Second, explaining the fundamental and the derivative. Second, explaining the fundamental and the derivative.

[Commentary]: Among the four types [of offenses], the first—principle—is the root, while the remaining three follow from characteristics and are thus the branches. For example, regarding the offense of shedding the blood of a Buddha:

according to the characteristic, there is no fault [in the case of] a manifested Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*), because it lacks a mind, is not a sentient being, and cannot experience affliction. However, because it damages the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) which is its basis, it is classified as a grave *ānantarya* offense.
The cases of benefiting or harming the Dharma and the Saṃgha follow this same logic of root and branch. Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "If one breaks or destroys..."
Whether a bhikṣu observes the precepts or not, the offense of shedding the blood of ten trillion Buddhas is grave;

for is it not because one’s physical form and robes serve as the banner of the supramundane Holy Path that, if they are subjected to contempt or disparagement, the Three Jewels are collectively destroyed?
In the general explanation of the Middle [Section], the first part, the actual demonstration, is as follows: by citing examples to clarify [the subject], it first elucidates the Buddha Jewel.

This clarifies the aspect of transformation (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), which takes principle (*dharma*) as its basis; because the aspect of transformation corresponds to the body, it is called a "transformation Buddha. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:

Why does shedding the blood of the form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) result in a grave offense (*ānantarya-karma*)? It answers: Because the form-body is the vessel for the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*); therefore, [shedding its blood] is an offense against the Dharma-body.

Based on the primary dharma, the remaining two jewels are illustrated by analogy: just as destroying the Wheel of Dharma is considered in relation to the ultimate truth because there is no realization [of it], so too is killing an Arhat considered in relation to the field of merit, as it is the ultimate field for realizing the principle. Thus, the manifested characteristics are all evaluated in relation to the jewel of the principle when discussing offenses and blessings.
Below, the Sangha-jewel is specifically verified; this refers to the "sustaining" (zhuchi) aspect to verify the "manifested" (huaxiang) aspect.

The *Xiang* (Phases) initially cites the scriptural passage stating that the karma of beating those who have broken the precepts or lack them is extremely grave; from this, we know that one does not rely on the formal appearance (*yi-xiang*) when discussing the Sangha.

How could one fail to infer the intent of the sutra? The outward form and robes constitute the "Sangha of Sustenance" (*zhu-chi seng*), while the Noble Path constitutes the "Sangha of the Jewel of Principle" (*li-bao seng*).

Since the Buddha-Dharma is propagated and manifested through the Sangha of Sustenance, to defame the Sangha is simultaneously to defame the Buddha-Dharma; therefore, it is said that [the offense] extends to both.
The *Huài yòu zhì lùn* (Treatise on the Destruction and Rebirth of Wisdom) states:

"Just as the substance of clay or copper is itself indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and does not in itself produce sin or merit, yet when fashioned into the form of the Dharma-body, it becomes associated with sin or merit depending on whether one previously showed respect or contempt [toward it]. (This Buddha of Sustained Presence is also fundamentally based upon principle; this is explained according to the sutras.
When the single essence is in delusion, delusion arises from principle; when awakening occurs, one returns to that fundamental principle. Thus, the beginning and end may be known."
[Commentary]: Question: Do these four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) themselves also possess a beginning and an end?
In the preceding question-and-answer section, the four stages were discussed collectively; now, wishing to explain each stage individually, this question is asked.
[Commentary] Answer: All previous schools have entirely obscured this point; let me now attempt to set it forth. This arises from their habitual failure to reflect—how could they not recognize it?
For instance, in the maintenance of the Three Jewels, the painted images of the Buddha stand upright and solemnly composed, serving as the very foundation of the Buddha Jewel.

The remaining figures of the worthy and holy ones, as well as the eight classes of beings, are arranged around them as the secondary elements of the Buddha Jewel. Therefore, within the halls and corridors, there are gods, ghosts, birds, and beasts...
If even these beasts are not considered treasures, how could they produce merit? They serve merely as adornments; yet the Most Holy Ones equally venerate and honor their virtue.
Therefore, whether they are created or destroyed, all is based on original conditions; the Dharmakāya and Saṃgha maintain them, for there is no lack of root and branch, as explained above.

In the response, the first part indicates the general meaning, while the following section clarifies the specific points: "Tǐ" (峙) refers to the appearance of being lofty and towering; "xiánshèng" (賢聖) refers to the disciples of the Three Vehicles;

"bābù" (八部) refers to the eight classes of beings mentioned in the sūtras, such as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth; "běnyuán" (本緣) refers to the examples of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha. Regarding the superior [categories]:
the Dharma takes the sūtra scrolls as its primary essence, while cases, boxes, and other such items are secondary; the Saṃgha takes the possession of the precepts as its primary essence.

Question: It may be granted that the *zhuchi* (institutional) [Buddha] is the "branch" while the eternally abiding [Buddha] is the "root" in terms of enjoyment; however, how can this be applied to the other three? Answer:

Although the text does not explicitly clarify this, it may be explained according to the underlying meaning. Even the Buddha and Sangha of the transformation aspect (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) are included as "enjoyment" to distinguish between root and branch.

Within the Dharma, among the Four Noble Truths, suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) are that which is to be destroyed, while the path (*mārga*) is that which reveals [the truth]; these three are all "branches. As for the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), it is the principle itself.

That which is revealed is called the "Fundamental Principle. Among the fivefold bodies of phenomena within the Jewel of Principle, the body of phenomena that is the object of realization corresponds to the "Branch.

As for the Dharma-body, which is the fundamental principle, the teaching that expresses it through provisional names is designated as the "Branch," while the essence of the principle revealed by that teaching—which transcends all names and words—is the "Fundamental.
Furthermore, among the Sangha, those who are still training (*śaikṣa*) are the "Branch," while those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are the "Fundamental. Moreover, as for those who are still training...
The exhaustion of afflictions and the remaining basis of suffering in those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are both branches;

they equally realize the True Principle, which is collectively termed the "Harmony of Principle" as the root. Within this single essence, the sentient beings' original nature—quiescent illumination and sovereign freedom—is the root;
now, being in delusion, agitated, and bound, these three states are all branches.
[Commentary] Regarding the sequence of the three parts: it is the sequence of the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*).

[Commentary] If one examines the reality according to principle, the essence of the Three Jewels is identical to the order listed above; however, if one investigates their fundamental realization, it is only then that the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*) is fully present.
In the initial [classification], the principle alone does not manifest itself; it must rely upon practice to be revealed. Therefore, the fivefold division places the Buddha Jewel at the forefront.

Furthermore, the explanation is that the principle is manifested through persons and the Way is accomplished by means of practice. Only when the World-Honored One appeared in the world did we hear of the Three Jewels. Thus, one returns to the conventional manifestations of transformation, and so the principle remains no different.

Regarding the first two lines of the "Jewels of Principle" (*lǐbǎo*), the preceding various characteristics (*zhòngxiàng*) are indicated. If one proceeds downward to explain them through progression and regression, the "conformity with the realized Dharma" (*yuèzhèngfǎhé*) should take precedence;

furthermore, when considering the Buddha as the starting point for practice, he should be placed at the head. Moreover, in the subsequent re-explanation, the analogies for the manifested marks (*huàxiàng*) likewise take the Buddha as the primary reference.

[Commentary]: Second, regarding why the Buddha of Transformation (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*) is explained first, followed by the Dharma and then the Sangha: it is because when Śākyamuni first attained realization, he alone was uniquely honored;

as nothing could be more honorable than him, he is placed at the beginning. Although the Great Sage manifests [in this world] and can move one's ears and eyes, as for the afflictions and delusions, they must necessarily be removed by means of the Dharma.
Next, he expounds the teachings of sound (*śabda-śāsana*) to cleanse the mental afflictions; such is the function of the teaching.
Furthermore, although it is said that those who practice this teaching have a place of refuge, if there is no realization, it is the same as not having taught at all;
thus, when Kauṇḍinya attained the fruit, the Sangha Jewel appeared. This sequence of the transformative ritual must not be violated.

Within the section on the characteristics of transformation (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), first there is the general indication, followed by the detailed explanation. First, the Buddha is presented; next, the Dharma is clarified; then, the Saṃgha is explained;
and finally, this concludes with a summary and demonstration. [Commentary]:

Regarding the three [categories] of maintaining the teachings (*dharmadhara*), the order is Saṃgha first, Dharma second, and Buddha last. This is because the Path relies upon persons for its propagation, and the worldly way of the Dharma depends upon them.

Therefore, when Kāśyapa Mātanga first arrived, he manifested the monastic deportment; by describing the five vehicles as the causes of goodness and the three miserable realms as the effects of evil, he manifested the ritual of the Dharma.
Because this Dharma is profound and vast, beyond what ordinary or inferior persons can reveal, he depicted images upon the Liang Terrace;
by inferring from what he taught, he manifested the ritual of the Buddha.

Regarding the "abiding in the maintenance" (zhùchí), this is discussed in terms of this region [China] to establish the sequence of before and after; one should know by analogy that in the Western Heaven (India), after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma was entrusted to the Saṃgha, which is no different from this.
First, there is a general enumeration of the causes; below, there is a specific explanation. First, the Saṃgha is described;

first, the "lower" section recounts the Dharma, and subsequently, the "lower" section explains it. Next, the Buddha is clarified; "later opening" (hòukāi) refers to the revealing and showing. As for the "cool terrace" (liángtái), it is the ascent.
Lan brought with him a white *mòu* (woolen) image of Śākyamuni and the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*.

Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty subsequently ordered painters at the Qingliang Terrace in the Southern Palace to depict standing images of the Buddha and transcribe the scriptures, which were then sealed within the stone chamber of the Lan Tai.

[Commentary: Regarding the fourth point, the single essence (*eka-tattva*): the Dharma comes first, the Saṃgha second, and the Buddha last. The essence is the essence of mind, which is fundamentally undefiled;

yet because it is obscured by delusion and inversion, the false and the correct arise. Now, having realized that the fundamental principle of the Dharma is in reality without these three, one follows the phenomenal functions and divides them into one direction for the sake of practicing and transforming others.

Thus, when reflecting upon the side of principle, it constitutes the meaning of "Awakening" (*bodhi*); when the essence transcends names and words, it constitutes the meaning of "Dharma" (*dharma*). This is the ultimate truth.

Regarding the meaning of the unimpeded harmony of the Saṃgha: because they do not know what is non-Dharma, this must be mentioned at the beginning; it is not because the Buddha is ignorant that it is mentioned later.

As for those who abide within the Saṃgha, their essence is not yet purely pure; like milk mixed with blood, there are portions that must be separated, so how could they be compared to the *tāla* (clarified butter)? Therefore, they are not the same as the Buddha.

Regarding the four aspects of the single essence (*ekātmya*): first, the enumeration of the essence; second, the sequential explanation. This section has two parts: first, the indication of the three marks;
within this, the preceding passage describes delusion, while the subsequent passage clarifies awakening. The first two lines clarify that the true substance is fundamentally one;
the latter two lines clarify that the provisional [teachings] are known as skillful means. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Good son, you should not now be like the śrāvakas and ordinary people..."
Now, as for the differentiation of the Three Jewels, within this Mahāyāna there is no characteristic of differentiating the three refuges.
Why is this? Because within the Buddha-nature itself, there already exist the Dharma and the Saṅgha (the Dharma being shown as the fundamental).

It is only for the sake of transforming and delivering Śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings that one speaks of the distinct characteristics of the three refuges (clarifying the provisional nature of their respective capacities). Therefore, one should know that the division into three is merely a temporary application.
Because they are all minor, it is said that their transformation through teaching occurs in a single direction; this refers to the specific capacities of beings in the Sahā world.

Therefore, the following section clarifies the meaning of the "one essence": "Illumination" refers to the wisdom that is the subject of awakening, while "principle" refers to the Buddha-nature that is the object of awakening—eternally abiding and transcending names and words because its essence is quiescent, and its principle being unimpeded because it follows conditions of both defilement and purity. Below, the second part clarifies the sequence; first:

The first two lines clarify the Dharma: initial knowledge is itself the realization of the eternally abiding essence of the Dharma, and because one enters it through such realization, it necessarily occupies the first position.
The next two lines clarify the Buddha: only upon reaching the ultimate fruit does one finally exhaust [all understanding].

Below, regarding the Sangha, this refers to those from the stage of the initial resolve up to the level of Equal Enlightenment; these all constitute the intermediate *nirvāṇa*. This is according to the "Kāśyapa-Paripṛcchā" chapter.
It is said that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like milk mixed with blood;
the "blood" refers to all afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), while the "milk" refers to the wholesome five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Thus, for those at the stage of *srotāpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin*, who have severed a small portion of afflictions, the Buddha-nature is like milk. For those at the stage of *anāgāmin*, the Buddha-nature is like curd (*dadhi*). For *arhat*s... [text fragment ends].

The people of Han are like fresh butter; from the Pratyekabuddhas up to the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes, the Ten Directions, and the Ten Grounds (as well as Equal Enlightenment), they are like matured butter.
The Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature is like the finest cream (*maṇḍa*). The three vehicles listed above all represent partial manifestations and do not yet reach the fruit of Buddhahood;
therefore, it is said that they cannot be used as metaphors for equality. This commentary (*shu*) discusses them based on the distinctions between these four stages.

Now, the sequence of these four positions may be clarified by analogy: the principle-body (*li-ti*) and the essence-body (*yi-ti*) are both eternally abiding, thus pervading the three periods of time;

the transformation-body (*hua-xiang*) abides in the present during its tenure and ceases after [the Buddha’s] passing. This is based on the Tathāgata proceeding from the state of an ordinary being to sainthood, appearing in the world and entering extinction;

therein, the essence-body resides at the beginning. Alternatively, if one proceeds from the Buddha outward to initiate transformation and provide guidance, then it is the transformation-body that [resides at the beginning].
The correspondence to the first principle, the first [jewel] as the abiding, and the final meaning as the sustainer can be understood thus.
[Commentary]: Regarding the four functions:
among the four jewels, the Jewel of Principle (Dharmaratna) is supreme because it is eternally abiding; it is that to which the world turns for refuge, while the other three follow accordingly.

If one posits that its essence is a functional dharma (*dharmatā*), the "Excellence of Principle" (*li-bao-sheng*) clearly elucidated therein refers to the principle that penetrates both the Great and Small Vehicles.

While the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*) and true suchness (*tathatā*) belong to the Small Vehicle, the pure mind as the fundamental nature belongs to the Great Vehicle; here, we must discuss their relative superiority and inferiority based on the Great Vehicle.
The *Guijing yi* (Ritual of Homage) states: "Principle (*li*) refers to the ultimate truth, the primordial and eternally abiding reality;

it is the very substance of the mind. If this is so, how does it differ from the 'one essence' (*yiti*)? Answer: "The 'one essence' pertains exclusively to the state of delusion and is spoken of solely in reference to ordinary beings (*fan*). 'Principle-treasure' (*libao*), by contrast, concerns realization and is discussed only from the perspective of the sages (*sheng*).
Therefore, they are distinguished as two. For this reason, the substance of Principle alone is superior to the other three."
[Commentary] Question: Since the mind is fundamentally pure and not defiled by the world, and its single essence is eternally abiding, why is it not considered supreme?
Answer: Although the principle of the One and the purity and constancy of the two stages are not distinct, because the principle alone is supreme, it must be clarified.

[Commentary] Answer: Speaking from the perspective of ultimate principle (*li*), it is indeed as you have asked; however, if we discuss this according to the characteristics of conventional language (*yu-xiang*), how could that which is defiled and impure be identical to the source of the mind realized by the Buddha?
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "There may be a Buddha-nature that both types of persons lack," clearly showing that while cause and effect differ, [the nature] is present in both.
In the initial passage of the response, the first two lines concede the interlocutor’s question, while the subsequent two lines refute it by returning to the previous interpretation.

The first two lines clarify that the essence is inferior, whereas the latter two lines reveal the superiority of the Jewel of Principle (*tattva-ratna*). Although the essence of principle is one, there is a distinction between ordinary beings and Buddhas;
therefore, the following citation from the *Kāśyapaparivarta* serves as proof: "Good son, there may be a Buddha-nature that is [identical to] the icchantika..."

Those who possess roots of goodness do not seek superior gain or offerings for themselves, nor are they bound by being subject to others; they fix their mindfulness on the formless heavens and thus cultivate goodness as such persons.

An icchantika—here translated as "one without faith"—may or may not possess the Buddha-nature. Those with roots of goodness may lack it, because an icchantika has severed the roots of goodness due to the nature of their false views and obstructions.

Alternatively, both types may possess the Buddha-nature, because their fundamental nature is equal. Or, both types may lack it, because both are ordinary beings and are not distinct [from one another].

Because it is the nature already realized by the Tathāgata, it is said to be "non-existent. Son of Good Family, if my disciples understand the meaning of these four propositions, they should not raise the objection that an icchantika either definitely possesses or definitely lacks Buddha-nature.
If one says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, this is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention (*svacittāśaya-vāk*). The sutra clarifies that the Tathāgata exists.

Regarding the three types of speech: the first three phrases of the preceding section on skillful means (*upāya*) constitute speech according to the intentions of others (referring to the provisional teachings).
All [the remaining] phrases constitute speech according to one's own intentions (the true meaning of the present sutra). Furthermore, the sutra says:
"If it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet they cannot perceive it because it is shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), I speak thus."
Your statement is likewise so; this is called the *Sūtra on Speech According to One’s Own and Others’ Intentions*.

This scripture clarifies the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), of which two are briefly cited here to prove the distinction between ordinary beings and Buddhas. These two individuals refer to those with severed roots of goodness (*icchantika*) and those with wholesome roots.

From the perspective of what the Buddha has realized, both types of persons lack [these qualities]; from the perspective of ordinary beings, both possess them. Thus, it is clearly known that cause, practice, and fruit are distinct.
This refers to the *Sūtra on the Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata*, which states that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see their nature only partially;
thus we know that only a Buddha realizes the nature to its ultimate conclusion. How could an ordinary person, possessing nothing more than this, dare to compare themselves?
[Commentary]: Some say that in the final age, the maintenance of the Triple Gem is supreme; its principle lies in mysterious penetration, yet it functions as profound virtue.

In this world, only the phenomenal exists, and through provisional phenomena, the turbid world and its dull dispositions are opened and guided. While non-phenomena do not move, they respond to capacities to engage with the mundane, ensuring that faith is never in vain.
In his response, the first two lines indicate that the superiority of the *dharmakāya* (the sustaining body) is restricted to the period after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa;

however, if discussed in a general sense, the *nirmāṇakāya* (the transformation body) in its manifest state is superior. Since the single essence is eternally abiding and remains untainted even while sentient beings are deluded, how could it not be superior?

Although this applies according to the specific meaning [of each case], the principle is determined as above. The final two lines clarify that the principle is not "superior" in the sense of being a substantial entity, for the essence transcends all verbal expression.
Because it is like an elephant, it is called "dark penetration" (*mingtong*); because its divine function is inconceivable, it is called "dark virtue" (*xuan-de*).
The commentary below [on the term] "abiding" (*zhu*) regarding the excellence of the presiding master seems to be the words of the commentator expressing his approval of this.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the intent behind the homage. If we take the subsequent verse as the basis for expounding the Vinaya-piṭaka so that the Dharma may endure for a long time, then discussing it according to its meaning, there are six kinds of distinctions:
1. Because of the debt of gratitude: The Buddha preached the medicine of the Dharma; the Saṃgha is that which propagates it.

To extract the arrow of poison and cause [the Dharma] to flourish in the world—all of this is beneficial to me. How could I not pay them reverence? 2. Because of their protection: In an age of turbidity, obstacles arise. [...]

As I am now deeply intent upon transmitting and propagating [the Dharma], I have encountered many demonic activities creating various obstacles; were it not for the application of majestic power, there would be no way to distance myself from them.

Because I have developed faith in three respects—namely, that my previous thoughts were merely delusions and that I do not inherit the lineage—I first set forth this expression of reverence, knowing that my receiving [of the teachings] has its source.

The fourfold expressions of reverent etiquette are that which the five assemblies take refuge in, all of whom honor the Triple Gem. Now, as I wish to propagate the Dharma, I must first give rise to [this resolve].
Please approach; this is because worldly offerings are for those who dwell near, whereas the Dharma is for those who dwell afar. Fifth, to manifest its superior characteristics:
as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states, "The Triple Gem is the most auspicious. Therefore, I now list it first to open up in sentient beings mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

Because the great benefits of the Triple Gem bestow welfare upon the infinite, and even a slight inclination toward them remains indestructible throughout kalpas, I place it at the beginning to inspire reverence.
"Mindfulness.
This refers back to the initial passage to clarify the concise summary; below, the six types are specifically revealed according to their meaning.

Among these, the first, second, and fifth—the aspects of superior grace and majesty—belong to that which is revered; the third, fourth, and sixth involve the maintenance of mindfulness through faith and reverence.
Regarding the metaphor of "one who can venerate the poisoned arrow": it is used as a metaphor because the three poisons of ego-inversion (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) can harm the pure mind.
Among the four [sections], "worldly offerings" refers to burning incense and prostrating; among the six, "imperishability" means that the seeds of goodness are not lost.
This concerns the fortnightly recitation of the sacred teachings; through the full observance of reverence and prayer, the six intentions are fully realized within the sincerity of one's inner heart.

[Commentary]: Regarding the explanatory text, the initial "prostrating with the head" (*kāśaya*) constitutes the ritual of veneration, while the subsequent listing of the Three Jewels constitutes the objects of veneration.
This is explained according to the text.
[Commentary: Because one expresses mental reverence through physical form by lowering the head to the ground, it is called "prostration" (*kāśāya*). "Kai" (稽) means to lower oneself.

According to the three grades of reverence found in the sūtras and śāstras, there are nine grades based on secular etiquette; however, *kāśāya*, *kai-sang* (稽顙), *dun-shou* (頓首), and *dun-sang* (頓顙) are all one and the same.
Regarding the first section of "Able to Pay Reverence": the first four lines demonstrate the names and meanings, while the subsequent lines provide an examination of their training.

"Below" refers to reaching down to the ground; as explained below, two teachings are cited to interpret the three grades. These originate from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Chizhi lun): 1. Prostration with the mouth (the act of speaking greetings is called the lower prostration);

2. Bending the knees (that is, kneeling while standing, called the middle prostration); 3. Bringing the head to the ground (that is, the full prostration, called the upper prostration). The nine grades originate from the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), the first.

1. *Jiǒushǒu* (bowing with the head touching the ground); 2. *Dòushǒu* (second: bowing with the head striking the ground); 3. *Kōngshǒu* (third: bowing with the head reaching the hands, known as *bài shǒu*); 4. *Zhèndòng* (fifth: bowing while trembling); 5. *Jí bài* (sixth:

bowing followed by touching the forehead to the ground, performed for auspicious occasions); 6. *Xūnɡ bài* (seventh: touching the forehead to the ground followed by bowing, performed for those in three-year mourning);

7. *Qí bài* (eighth: pronounced *qí jū yí fǎn*; a single prostration used when responding to the bows of subordinates); 8. *Bāo bài* (ninth: pronounced *bào*; a double prostration); 9. *Sù bài* (tenth: simply lowering the hands while bowing).

Regarding "bai" (bowing) and "ji" (prostrating): when one merely touches the ground, it is called "dun"; when one strikes the head, it is "dunshou. This refers to the crown of the head, specifically the forehead;
although the names differ, the substance is no different, hence they are said to be "one."
[Commentary: "Ritual (*li*) is simply reverence. Because one bows out of reverence, one expresses the inner sentiment and exhausts the external forms;

thus it is called "ritual. Ritual is principle (*li*); it means that the performance of affairs accords with correct principle. The rest is as explained by Zheng Xuan in his commentary on the *Zhouli*.

According to the tradition of the ancient sages, "ritual" refers to bowing with the hands. Based on the common understanding of ritual among the people, it encompasses all that cannot be fully described; one need only know this.
This is an abbreviation.
In the initial passage of the following text, it first demonstrates that the root of ritual (li) lies in reverence within the mind;

while the outward manifestation of ritual is seen in the body, if the mind’s reverence is not exhaustive, the body will not achieve true ritual. Thus, ritual primarily consists of reverence and has no other intent; therefore, it says "and."
Having already paid homage, the following section explains the meaning of *li* (ritual propriety). The *Liji* states: "Li is principle; Yue (music) is regulation.
The gentleman does not move without principle, nor does he regulate himself without music. It further states: "Li is embodiment (*ti*).
If the embodiment is incomplete, the gentleman says he is not yet a full person. To establish it improperly is likewise to be incomplete. The remainder follows below.
All that has been cited above is from those very texts. Regarding the three points below concerning the critique of the limited definition as being universal:

first, the ritual of *li* (propriety) is defined by principle and does not consist solely of bowing; furthermore, as in the "Ninth Rite," how could *li* be limited merely to prostrating with the hands? Thus, one knows it is not restricted.
Below, the brief and extensive versions are shown within the "Protocol for Reverent Homage."

[Commentary]: "The many sages are not one" refers to the various Buddhas. The reason for paying homage to the Teacher [Śākyamuni] and including the Buddhas is to manifest that the Way is non-dual and that all must equally offer their respect;

thus, the Buddhas are included. Furthermore, when the seven Buddhas are listed below, this constitutes a general offering of respect. If one follows the principle of universal circulation, one should pay equal reverence to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Next, regarding the explanation of the Jewel of the Buddha whom one honors: the first section consists of two lines which cite and explain the introductory phrase; the subsequent section explains the pervasive meaning of the expression of reverence.

While the *Prātimokṣa* texts of other schools pay homage only to Śākyamuni, the present *Dharmaguptaka* text universally honors all Buddhas. This is because the Path is non-dual; thus, the statement is made from a universal perspective.

However, when distinguished between the provisional and the ultimate, there is a difference between the cultivation and realization for one’s own practice and the skillful means for transforming others. It is with this intention that the present text provides its explanation.

The Venerable One established the prohibitions and permissions of the precepts by observing both the heavy and light offenses, seeing that there is no difference across the three periods of time. Furthermore, the subsequent sections rely on the preceding introductions to explain the various meanings mentioned above.
[Commentary] Question: This teaching belongs to the Hīnayāna and contains no text concerning a present Buddha; yet those items listed here pertain to the past and future. How is this to be answered?

The fact that the Great Vehicle is the fundamental principle is because Master Guang of the *Jie-mo-shu* (Karmavācanā-vṛtti) judged it not to be of the Hīnayāna; thus, the text below on the precepts states:
"The various World-Honored Ones of the present"—this passage is indeed a fine proof.

Regarding the initial intent of the first question within the "Dispelling Doubts" section: it is because the present Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings clarify only the trichiliocosm with Śākyamuni as the sole Buddha acting as the principal teacher of transformation, and lack mention of other Buddha-fields.
Since this textual passage [of the Mahāyāna] applies universally to all Buddhas, its meaning actually deviates from the [Hīnayāna] tenet;

therefore, it must be harmonized through interpretation. This refers back to the initial direct response within the previously cited answer concerning this Mahāyāna school, which is now divided [into sections].

Regarding the general meaning as indicated in the commentary, that [text] clarifies the partial and universal application based on five points: first, the conversion of mind of Trapusa; second, the attainment of Buddhahood through the perfection of giving;
third, the summoning of the Buddha’s sons; fourth, the relinquishing of wealth and the lightness of its use; and fifth, consciousness cognizing objective realms.
As Guangshi extensively explained below, he relies on the judgments of others; thus, he subsequently cites the *Liu-tong* (The Extensive Propagation) as his authority.
[Commentary: Above, "prostrating with the head" was used to express general reverence, while the other two names were connected by the term "and.
Next, the other two are explained.
[Commentary: The Dharma is as explained above.
Regarding the "Dharma Jewel," that which was mentioned above is seen in the "Explanation of Terms" (*Shiming*).
[Commentary: The term *bhikṣu-saṃgha* refers to the provisional construction of function through the gathering [of elements]. As for *bhikṣu*, its original Sanskrit pronunciation is *bhi-kṣu*;

In the first section on the Jewel of the Sangha, the essence of the Sangha is first demonstrated: a person has no self-substance;
it is the collection of the five aggregates that is designated as a "conventional person. The aggregates themselves have no function, yet this conventional person possesses function.

Taking these four types of conventional persons together as the essence of the Sangha, it is said that by gathering these four conventional persons, they are able to accomplish the aforementioned tasks; thus, it is called "accomplishing function. A *bhikṣu* is a specific instance of such a conventional gathering.
Because they constitute a distinct Saṃgha, the names of the bhikṣus listed in two rows are marked below. The *Karmasūtra* states: "Some call them *bhikṣu* (the sound of which is missing).
[Commentary]:
In this land, there is no one who translates [this term] based on three meanings: first, "Terrifying Māra," or "Causing Māra to be terrified" as he reverently practices the Three [Trainings].

Their practice issues forth from the three realms of existence; for this reason, they are called the *Saṃgha*. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Those who have left home for the sake of liberation are called the *Saṃgha*.
Second, they are called "mendicants" (*bhikṣu*), which carries two meanings: first, above, they beg for the Dharma to discipline the mind; second, below, they beg for food to sustain the body.
Having attained the Dharma, they uphold it and verify their realization through the Four Teachings; having received food, they contemplate it with revulsion.
One must distance oneself from the five perversions, as explained in detail elsewhere. Third, regarding "the destruction of afflictions":

this is intended to cause those who rely on names to contemplate their meanings and recognize that they have a source, so that they do not fall into worldly vulgarity but instead rejoice in the essential path of deliverance. Therefore, it is said: "Within my Dharma, joyfully practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) to exhaust the source of suffering."

First, "frightening Māra" clarifies his original resolve; second, "Māra is frightened" refers to his spiritual practice. There are four kinds of Māras: celestial, afflictive, demonic, and death.
Below, the names are explained comprehensively: the three practices are precept, concentration, and wisdom. Thus, the names are concluded.
The citation below serves as proof for this interpretation. It states that all bhikṣus are called "Saṃgha" because the individual is established through the collective designation of the multitude;

thus, the individual derives its name from the assembly. Regarding the subsequent meaning, "begging" (yācana) carries the sense of "seeking. This Dharma is the cause of the Path, while food is the condition (pratyaya) for the Path.

Because the cause is primary and the condition secondary, they are divided into superior and inferior. By clarifying the inferior, it is shown that both are established only by following the primary [cause]. These four categories constitute the four teachings.
These are the Four Reliances of Nirvāṇa: first, rely on the Dharma and not on the person (the first ensures reliance on the Dharma, meaning one does not discard the teaching because of the person);

second, rely on the meaning and not on the words (the second distinguishes reliance on the teaching from allowing literal expression to obstruct the principle); third, rely on wisdom and not on consciousness (the third distinguishes reliance on the meaning from allowing subjective sentiment to hinder wisdom);

fourth, rely on the definitive meaning and not on the non-definitive meaning (the fourth distinguishes reliance on wisdom from allowing provisional means to obstruct the ultimate reality). These four provide a decisive discernment of what is heterodox.

Because those who practice correctly rely [on the Dharma], there are five types of wrongdoers: first, changing one's usual deportment and falsely manifesting extraordinary appearances in order to seek gain and offerings;
second, speaking of one's own merits; third, raising one's voice to manifest authority; fourth, proclaiming what one has attained to stir others into giving;
and fifth, forcibly claiming knowledge of good or bad fortune in order to seek gain and offerings. In the latter part of this definition, the first phrase indicates the name [of the category].

The following passage clarifies that the basis for the intention is the name; "hearing and contemplating the meaning" refers to reflection (*cintā*), while "looking back and surveying" below refers to cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
By means of this single term, all three types of wisdom are fully encompassed. "Looking back and surveying" refers to observation (*vipaśyanā*). "Having a basis" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

One does not fall into worldly vulgarity because one abandons worldly pleasures; one rejoices in the essential departure [from suffering] because one aspires loftily to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). Therefore, the following section provides an illustration.

"Realization" refers to the Buddha’s words for welcoming and transforming others: the first phrase gives rise to right faith, the second phrase involves cultivating the causes, and the final phrase realizes the fruit.
"Suffering" is the source of birth and death, which is to say, affliction (*kleśa*).

[Commentary] Furthermore, it is explained that when [the path] is in the causal stage, it is called "Terrifying Māra," "Beggar for Alms," and "Destroyer of Afflictions"; when in the resultant stage, it is called "Slayer of Thieves," "Worthy of Offerings," and "Non-arising.
Because these names shift and become increasingly superior in relation to one another, they are said to be "extraordinary" (śu-jue).
Regarding the first section on the fruit, the title "Arhat" (A-lo-han) also possesses three meanings that correspond to the reversal of the three preceding causes.

First, "slayer of thieves," because the two types of affliction have been exhausted. Second, "worthy of offerings," because as a true field of merit, his virtues are capable of receiving the offerings of sentient beings;

the character "ying" (應) is pronounced level-tone (ping sheng), meaning "correspondence. Third, "non-arising," because the retribution of suffering has perished forever. Thus, the name of the cause is "Victory over Self" (Ji-sheng).
Because the title of the fruit is even more superior, it is called "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*).
[Commentary] Question: When one seeks the Dharma to refine the spirit, why does it not reach the fruit? Answer: That which is like the parable of the raft is not to be used once one has crossed over;

medicine is for the purpose of curing illness, so when the illness is gone, the medicine is discarded. If one does not eliminate the medicine, it becomes a deep-seated illness itself. One can only rely on the cause according to its form.

There is the aspect of dependence upon requisites; if one follows from the perspective of the fruit and its merit, it should be provided as an offering for sentient beings. This can be understood by analogy with the fact that while there are afflictions to be destroyed at the stage of the cause, there are no afflictions to arise at the stage of the fruit.

In the question, the cause is divided into two meanings, whereas the fruit is specifically contrasted with food; thus, the question addresses this. In the answer, the first part clarifies [the point].

The Dharma does not reach the fruit; this is illustrated by the two metaphors of the raft and the medicine. To show that the causal dharmas are without function once the fruit is reached, the remaining three causes are further demonstrated as necessarily reaching the fruit.
The phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) abbreviates the preceding section on "frightening Māra. Māra is like an enemy bandit:

he is feared during the causal stage, but once the fruit is attained, he has already been slain—meaning that afflictions are completely severed, one no longer undergoes future aggregates, and there is forever no more death.
When the devas and Māras suffer, their fear is equivalent to being killed.
[Vinaya] Now I shall expound the Vinaya rules so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.

it is called *vinaya* because it can extinguish the unwholesome roots (which is to say, it settles disputes), it can extinguish obstructing dharmas (the three obstructions of the three periods of time), and it can extinguish the five hindrances and evil conduct (the afflictions of views and the karma of deluded actions). [Commentary: As for the aforementioned "extinguishing through understanding," this refers merely to what is eliminated by means of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*); as for "eliminating through mutual opposition," it is as explained above.

[Commentary: Furthermore, according to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, there are nine meanings of the Vinaya:

1. Vinaya regarding what has been taught: the four offenses such as sexual misconduct and theft; 2. Vinaya arising from the eight causal conditions as a remedy for the extinction of the five afflictions;

In border regions, one may receive the five precepts and bathe frequently, whereas in the central lands this was not permitted. What was formerly allowed with the three refuges is now not permitted.
Regarding bathing frequently during hot weather and not doing so during cold weather—these and all other such matters constitute the *sarvatra-vinaya* (universal discipline).
Just as with [the prohibitions against] killing or stealing, one must train together in these rules at all times and in all places.

In the first two points of the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, the two groups differ regarding the precepts; in the third, they are identical regarding the precepts. Regarding the eight conditions in the fourth [section]:

1. There are [offenses] that arise from the mind and do not arise from the body or speech (such as various mental transgressions). 2.

There are those that arise from the body and speech and do not arise from the mind (such as when one with a virtuous mind acts as a go-between for men and women to engage in sexual intercourse; this refers to matchmaking). 3.

There are those that arise from the body and the mind and do not arise from speech (such as intentionally emitting impurity). 4. There are those that arise from the speech and the mind and do not arise from the body (such as speaking words of lustful desire to a woman with a defiled mind).
This refers to coarse speech (*pāruṣya*). Seventh, there are cases arising from body, speech, and mind (such as when one with a defiled mind acts as a procuress for men and women).

Eighth, there are cases not arising from body, speech, or mind (such as when one first speaks a great lie to another person who does not understand; if this person later understands the words after having already countered the three preliminary conditions, this person incurs the *pārājika* offense).
Regarding the "five categories" mentioned in the fifth [section], the treatise calls them the "five divisions" (*pañca-varga*); the old records, based on the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, follow this.

[It is said: "The fetters abandoned through seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), the fetters abandoned through [seeing] the origin (*samudaya-prahātavya*), the fetters abandoned through [seeing] cessation (*nirodha-prahātavya*), and the fetters abandoned through [seeing] the path (*mārga-prahātavya*)—these specifically indicate the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya*).

Those who possess the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) are so because they apply themselves to the precepts; those who lack the aspiration are so because they have already reached fulfillment. Among these eight, the *Abhidharma-kośa* treats them as one."
