[The Commentary] states that there are three parts above, which collectively concern the gradual [training]; the eight chapters on the primary precepts (*śīla*) clearly demonstrate the relative gravity of the various rules.
"Cloud" (*yun*) means to spread and manifest.

In the main body of the text (*zhengzong*), the first two lines of the upper section follow up on the preceding gradual conditions, thereby initiating the meaning [of the teaching]. The "eight" below refers to the formal explanation;
"manifesting" (*xian*) here means "to show."
[Commentary]: In the section on the "Circulation of the Extensive Teachings," the text is raised again separately for fear that there may be those who fall into error or deceive future generations;
thus it says, "repeatedly and analytically distinguished.
Within the section on circulation, the first two phrases point to the textual divisions; "raised again separately" means to restate what has already been explained.

I have repeatedly reviewed [the text], fearing that there might be omissions in the transmission of the intended meaning; thus, lest it sink into oblivion and lead to errors in future traditions, I speak of "entirety" (*wangmào*). [Commentary]:

Some say that each of the eight sections of the *Zhengzong* (Orthodox Canon) possesses three levels of significance. How can the broad teachings be comprehensively collected as if they were merely like the beginning?
In this chapter, the four *pārājika* offenses for the various venerable ones correspond precisely to the four aspects opened within the *Pravrajyā-vastu*.

When seated together and hearing them in unison, they are then promulgated, manifested, and finalized; three questions are posed, and the preceding sections are restated and analyzed in detail. Since these are all citations from the words of the Sage, how could one not rely upon them?

In the initial presentation of his interpretation, he refutes [the opponent] as follows: taking the first chapter and correlating it specifically with this [text], he explains it solely from the perspective of the main body of the teaching.
However, regarding the three points previously listed, according to this master, he cites only the single meaning of "initiation" (*samutthāna*), while the other two textual passages are omitted;
yet their meanings must necessarily be implicitly included. Furthermore, the final two phrases appear to be the words of another master concluding the critique.
As the commentators selected and utilized these phrases, they correlated the preceding text with its full explanation based entirely upon the root sūtra;
therefore, it is said that "these are all the words of the Sage. [Vinaya]: Various bhikṣus gathered together in one place.
[Commentary]: Second, regarding "the bhikṣus assemble," this signifies that the Dharma is without discord and clarifies that people are not to be separated.

In the second section, the explanation of the text, "Dharma" refers specifically to the precepts; it means that the Dharma is not partial and no one is excluded from its teaching, thereby clarifying the purpose of assembling within the same boundary.

[Commentary] The Buddha stated that when those who share the same *karmavācanā* assemble in one place, and even those who ought to be rebuked do not rebuke [the proceedings], this is called "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*).

[Sūtra] The note states: "Those who share the same *karmavācanā* come together"—this is called the assembly of the body (*kāya-saṃnipāta*). Since physical obstruction exists while the Dharma is universally applicable, the method of expressing one's consent (*chanda*) must be presented.

It is called the "assemblage of mind" (*citta-saṃghāta*). Although the body may attend the assembly, there may be instances where it is rebuked or restrained; thus, the perfection of the Dharma through silent forbearance is called the "assemblage of speech" (*vāk-saṃghāta*).
Because these three karmas together constitute a single Saṃgha, they are said to "assemble in one place."

The commentary on the first section of the *Śāstra*—from the words "even unto" onwards—is abbreviated; its meaning is fully explained in the *Jíshù* (Compendium of Exegesis) by analyzing it in terms of the three types of action (*trikarma*).
Because the physical body has form and obstruction, it possesses conditions [for transmission]; because desire exists, the Dharma can be transmitted universally;
because the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure) is accomplished, a single monk constitutes a *saṃgha*, for a monk is indeed the assembly.
[Commentary] Another interpretation states: "Those who perform the same *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) clarify that those whose correct observance of the precepts is pure are included;

those with other transgressions who do not count [toward the quorum] do not perform the same *karmavācanā* and need not assemble. Regarding 'one should grant their consent' (*chanda*), this means that these teachings and practices must not be treated lightly;
it is only when one is unable to attend due to urgent and essential circumstances that granting consent is permitted. All other minor matters..."
In minor matters, it is unnecessary; for instance, those with serious illnesses may be brought by sedan chair, while those who are light can be carried by monks—this should be understood accordingly.

Regarding those who ought to be rebuked, this refers to the four types of *karmavācanā* and various disciplinary procedures. When such legal acts are being performed upon a person, there is no room for one to exercise the authority of the Dharma.

Although their physical presence fulfills the quorum, they do not verbally recite the non-faults [of the procedure]. Only through such refinement and training can one become a person of true substance.

This is not so. In the other interpretation, the three sections all concern the selection of the assembly (*parṣad*) and the exclusion of those who fulfill the quorum (*sāmagrī*) yet have committed offenses—namely, those subject to the three types of formal accusation (*tṛtiya-samutthāpana*) and the two types of *pravāsanīya-karman* (expulsion)—as well as members of the fourfold assembly including nuns, and persons who are mute, deaf, asleep, or insane. Second, it excludes those whose desire for [the assembly] is absent.
Regarding the "Urgent" [procedures], these are the three [categories] such as the Three Jewels, and the diseases and so forth;

the three combined [procedures] are the four *karmavācanas* of reprimand (*tarjanīya*), banishment (*pravāsanīya*), dependence (*niśraya*), and prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople (*pratisaṃharaṇīya*). These four are called "complete" in the Vinaya and cannot be further reprimanded.

As for the various miscellaneous disciplinary measures (*pāyantikā* and others), they include those who practice the concealment of offenses (*parivāsa*) and so forth; all of these arise because their capacity for wisdom has been forfeited.

The method for censuring must necessarily not be these [other methods] before it can be called "proper censure. If, at the conclusion, one summarizes the training—that is, the selection of genuine persons—this refers to those who are worthy of the teaching.
[Note: If the voice of the assembly is low, one should arrange a magnificent high seat, ascend upon it, and preach.
[Commentary: To speak of "spreading an exquisite seat" means to revere the True Dharma. To "open and establish the teaching" means to bestow benefits upon others.

The intent is that both speaker and listener shall achieve merit and the roots of the Path shall remain unimpaired. How could it be right for there to be no hearing, such that both parties labor in vain? What benefit would there be in that?
In the first section of this division, the intention behind the prohibition is explained, followed by the intention behind its allowance. Regarding the term "standing to preach":

because the voices of the assembly were loud while his own voice was small and could not be heard by all, the Buddha permitted him to stand and preach; yet even so, they still could not hear him. He therefore had a high wheel-turning throne constructed and stood upon it to preach.
The "root of the Way" refers to the essence of the precepts (*śīla*).
[Note] The remaining conditions for the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) are briefly explained according to the occasion.
[Commentary] What are called the "eight difficulties" refers to kings, thieves, water, fire, serious illness, malevolent insects, and so forth.
What are called "remaining conditions" refer to cold, heat, rain, dampness, and the crowding of many people sitting together, and so forth. The detailed text is as found in the *Shu-chao*.
To summarize the initial section of the middle [division], the eight difficulties are abbreviated; the persons and non-persons are abbreviated;

and other conditions are abbreviated, such as the assembly being largely ill, the *poṣadha* lasting many nights, prolonged disputes, or lengthy discussions on the *Abhidharma*, the *Vinaya*, and the preaching of the Dharma.
Matters such as these, along with the addition of cold and heat, are not explicitly set forth in the *Vinaya* text.
[Commentary: Regarding "briefly explaining according to the occasion": the timing for the application of the holy teachings to various capacities is not uniform.

When the leaders of the assembly and those of wisdom deliberate upon matters of business, the precepts consist of ten sections, yet there are nine brief explanations; because one must weigh what to adopt and what to discard, it is said to be "according to the occasion."

Regarding the subsequent sectioning of time: because the conditions for the timing are as manifold as described above, they are not uniform. Since the first of the ten sections of the precept text must necessarily be extensive, it is merely abbreviated;
however, once the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, it is difficult to rearrange the sequence, so the introduction (*nidāna*) cannot be omitted.

Yet, if one simply states that each person shall rectify their body, speech, and mind, then all ten sections may be abbreviated. This is because the meaning of the announcement within the introduction is essentially the same.
Because it was recited extensively, it is said there are nine [sections].

[Note] Regarding the "guests, residents, and external assemblies," their numbers may vary from few to many; once this preface has been recited for the sake of purification (*śauca*), one may then listen.
[Commentary] The phrase "guests, residents, and external assemblies" refers to those encompassed by the Dharma. If there is any violation or opposition, there will inevitably be transgression.

When people follow the Dharma, if they have previously heard the introductory section (*nidāna*), they do not need to announce their purity (*śauca*) because they have already heard the three inquiries (*tri-praśna*).
Within the eight sections [of the *Prātimokṣa*], however, one must necessarily announce their purity because they have not heard the introductory section.

Among the four [sections], the first explains the *dharmas* that govern the assembly of people, which refers to the regulations for the community as a whole; "people follow the *dharma*" refers to the regulations for individuals.
In the subsequent explanation regarding the eight sections on declaring purity (*śuci-ārocana*), once the three inquiries have been completed, one must immediately declare purity.
[Note] The details are as extensively explained in the Vinaya.
[Commentary] These matters are numerous and cannot be discussed here immediately; therefore, it refers back to the Vinaya.
Regarding the "numerous matters" among the five points, it means that those who are pure declare their purity, and those who have committed offenses confess them, each reporting to themselves.
When many people are listed individually but the total number of guests is few, there is no need for a redundant recitation;
the specific procedures and phrasing for such cases are all found in the "Reciting the Precepts" (Shoujie) chapter of the *Shishi Yaoyong Chao*. This concludes the section.
[Sūtra] "Listen attentively, all of you, and reflect upon this well.
[Commentary] From "Listen attentively" onwards, the text admonishes against false conditions. The ordinary mind is difficult to bind, comparable to a wild deer;
the body of a Sage masters it like a monkey in chains. To incline the ear and seek out sounds is called "listening attentively," according to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
The "net" refers to the activity of deliberation; it is not what is called "wholesome thought.
Regarding the first part of the third section, the parable of the wild deer running and scattering illustrates the intent:

as the *Śāsanānuśāsanī* (Teaching of the Final Instructions) says, "It is like a vicious horse that cannot be restrained by a bridle, a mad elephant for which there is no hook, or a monkey that has found a tree"—all these are metaphors for the discerning mind (*vijñāna-citta*).
The "momentary arising and ceasing" section is the gateway of antidotes; it subsumes the following explanatory text.
At this time of sitting and listening, the mind often wanders toward other thoughts or lapses into sleep; therefore, please read this text carefully to stimulate your dull faculties.
[Commentary] The Buddha said that one should listen to the Dharma with an upright mind and single-minded concentration.
[Sub-commentary] In the commentary, "upright mind" refers to the correct mental discernment; "single-minded concentration" refers to listening without error.
In the commentary, the first part [“above”] excludes deviant thoughts, while the second part [“below”] excludes distracted conceptions.
[The Vinaya states: “If one knows for oneself that there has been an offense, one should immediately perform repentance.

[The Commentary (Shu) states: Regarding the fourth point, “knowing for oneself that there has been an offense”: the intent of reciting the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* lies solely in the removal of offenses; therefore, upon hearing it, one should act accordingly.
This refers to the passage stating, "one should immediately rise," which is what the text means by "one should immediately repent.
Regarding the first section of the fourth commentary on the text: it describes the original intent to demonstrate that repentance is necessary;

because one has just heard the announcement of the *nidāna* (preface), there is no room for delay, hence it says "immediately proceed to rise" and "immediately repent. It is named after its metaphorical source.

They are the same. [Commentary: "Hui" (repentance) is a term from this land; "chan" (confession) is a concise expression from the Western Regions, corresponding to the sound *kṣamā* in the Sanskrit original.
The character "chan" is not found in the *Cangjie* or *Yayi* lexicons; it is merely a term transmitted through recent secular usage.
Next, the *Cang* (倉) and *Yá* (雅) are names for secular dictionaries and glossaries, such as the *San Cang* (三倉) and the *Er Ya* (爾雅).
[Commentary]: The meaning of repentance (*chànhuì*) should be explained here; it may be as subtle as in the *Shìchāo* (事鈔).
The *Zhilü tongchao* (Brief Commentary on the Essential Points) is identical to the "Chapter on the Confession of the Six Classes of Offenses.
[Note] The Buddha said: Regarding an offense that has not yet been confessed, there are two kinds of wise persons who, when they have committed a transgression, are able to recognize it;
having recognized their transgression, they are able to confess it according to the Dharma. If one wishes to repent, one should go before a pure bhikṣu and state the name of the offense committed.
Once the names have been removed according to the Dharma, one may then hear the precepts; this applies likewise even when there is doubt regarding an offense.

If the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense and there is no one available to perform the confession, one should perform a formal announcement (jñapti) for both what is known and what is suspected, and subsequently explain the matter.

[Commentary: The note regarding "offenses not yet repented" explains the characteristics of being possessed of guilt. It is simply that, with beginningless ignorance and inverted perceptions as the root, one moves the mind and conditions objects;
how could one then remain serene? Only those with wisdom can perceive this and perform repentance.

As for others whose delusions are heavy, by what means could they attain awakening? Therefore, the Vinaya text states: "Those who have attained the fruit of No-more-learning do not intentionally violate the precepts."
That those in the three fruits of the path remain identical to ordinary beings and have not yet escaped the bonds of conditions—should this not be contemplated?

In the first section of the commentary, the preceding part restates and indicates [the point], while the subsequent part provides a detailed explanation. First, it describes the abundance of transgressions;
the first two lines indicate the delusions, while the last two lines clarify karma. "Purifiedly" (xiāo rán) refers to the state of being clear, still, and unattached. "Only" (wéi) below clarifies...

Because the confession is slight, the following cites the admonitions of the Noble Ones for ordinary persons: first, regarding the two fruits [of the path], one commits a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (offense by nature) through the mind—as in the case of the two nuns, Sūrasā and others, who experienced pleasure when coerced by an enemy;

second, regarding the three fruits, one commits a *pratikṣepana-sāvadya* (offense of prohibition) through the mind; third, regarding the four fruits, one commits a *pratikṣepana-sāvadya* through a mistaken mind.

[Commentary]: The note enumerates wise persons who have perfected the method of repentance and approach those who are pure, thereby manifesting that their entrustment to the object and clarification of the mind mean that the names and characteristics of transgressions they declare are not false.
"Removing [transgressions] according to the Dharma" clarifies that one initiates repentance based on the teachings, rather than acting in a superficial or indiscriminate manner.

Next, regarding the method of repentance (*pratideśanā*): first, there is a general indication of approaching [the preceptor]; second, the formal citation and explanation of the entrustment to the object, which refers to the person one faces;

and third, clarifying the mind, which means resolving the offense committed. [The Commentary] states: "Recognizing that doubt constitutes an equal offense, one opens up and confesses. Regarding the confession, the offense is based on concealment; one presents one's circumstances before the assembly and makes a formal announcement of repentance."

The procedure for severing [the offense] is the same as the Great Confession (*mahā-vaiyāvṛtya*). Regarding the first section of the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the offense is based on concealment; because the fault is established through concealment, it ceases upon disclosure.

Thus, it is the same as the Great Confession, as it does not differ from the methods for repentance within the *Saṃgha* found in the preceding chapter. Therefore, the text of the announcement, like that of the *Karmavācanā*, consists of the recognition of the offense and the formal announcement.

Once the doubts regarding transgressions have been purified, one subsequently resolves them through a grave repentance (*gurvī-pratikramaṇa*). Furthermore, all categories of offenses from *sthūlātyaya* downward are extinguished, while the two aforementioned [categories] are not opened for such purification.

[Commentary: How is this known? It is because when an ordinary person commits a transgression, it is subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); thus, one knows suffering and abandons origination upon entering the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).
How could one immediately silence this karma by merely speaking?

Next, regarding the first section of the inquiry into the underlying intention: the first phrase poses the question, while the subsequent portion explains that the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is the cause of the world. The "Path of Vision" (*darśana-mārga*) refers to the first fruit;

this clarifies that it is only upon reaching the state of a Noble One (*ārya*) that the karma of origination is severed. How could an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), by mere verbal expression, be able to achieve this immediately?
The *Duan-yi* (Severing the Intent) reveals that according to the Vinaya, confession can purify transgressions because it does not clarify the underlying principle of karma.

[Commentary: Now, at the beginning of each precept, one is required to confess. Once the listener has repented for past offenses, severed subsequent continuity, and exposed their faults before them so that there is no concealment in the mind, they are as if attaining purity;
thus they may participate in hearing and upholding the teachings, regardless of the retribution produced by past karma.
Increasing delusion.

In the first section of the following chapter, the reason for purification through repentance is clarified; the fundamental purpose of repentance according to the Vinaya is most clearly demonstrated in this text.

It does not fall short of showing the boundaries of instruction: "karma" refers to the path of karma that brings about rebirth, "rebirth" refers to the path of suffering, and "increasing delusion" refers to the path of affliction. This...

The judgment of the three mental activities as belonging to the *Huajiao* (Transformation Teachings) or the *Lüjiao* (Vinaya Teachings) based on violations of regulations is not a subject for discussion here.
[Commentary: This merely involves the repentance of the event to subdue the karma; ultimately, one must practice purity and cultivate deep insight.

One realizes that the inversion of the self is fundamentally equal to empty space, existing only due to delusive conditions that entangle one within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). When this principle is clearly and thoroughly perceived, there is no longer any doubt.
If one attains right view through the elimination of doubt, one will then tilt away from the realms of suffering; such repentance is called the "extinction of karma. How can karma be extinguished?

It is called "extinguished" because it is obstructed from producing further retribution. Even those who have attained the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa) must still repay past causes, as seen in Śāriputra’s affliction by illness and Maudgalyāyana’s encounter with suffering;
these cases may be used as analogies to understand that one's thoughts must not be deluded.

Of the three [types of repentance], the first two lines follow upon the conclusion of the preceding ritual repentance (*vidhi-pratikramaṇa*), while the latter initiates the subsequent repentance based on principle (*li-pratikramaṇa*). First, it demonstrates the contemplation of principle;
for now, it relies on the school of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to analyze the view of selflessness through the contemplation of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

Since the characteristics of phenomena are empty and consciousness is fully present, the "self-inversion" (*ātma-viparyāsa*) is fundamentally non-self; thus, empty space is cited as a metaphor. Below, the stage is definitively judged.
Regarding "attaining a portion," this refers to those from the stage of the Inner Worldlings (āryapudgala) upward, who are not reborn in the evil realms.

This concludes the previous section by demonstrating that while the former [stage] merely suppressed the phenomena through practice, this [stage] extinguishes them through principle. Regarding the subsequent explanation of the meaning of "extinguishing" as "not producing rebirth":

this means that while there is no longer a collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*), individual retributions (*prātibhedavipāka*) are not entirely absent; even fixed karma (*niyatavipāka*) does not cease until it is repaid at the stage of Buddhahood.
Therefore, practitioners should take pleasure in self-observation, constantly perfuming and training the mind-consciousness with wholesome conditions. Do not say that there are no sinful karmas;
the principle is crystal clear. A verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Even if [an action] were performed across hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it is not forgotten;
when the causes and conditions meet, one must personally undergo the retribution. The Buddha’s words are true; do not deceive yourself. Thus it is said below.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites the case of Śāriputra, who suffered from a wind-disorder that caused one eye to swell, and Maudgalyāyana, who was beaten by a brahmin while begging for alms until his flesh and bones were completely mangled;
these are both said to be retributions for past karma. Based on this, it can be known that even through rational repentance (*yili chan*), [karma] is not extinguished;
thus it is said, "it can be... and so forth.
[Commentary] Question: Should there not be two types of practitioners of purity? Regarding those who do not commit offenses, how should one first act before asking about them?

Since those who do not commit offenses are rare and naturally accord with the teaching, while those who commit offenses are numerous and habitually conceal their transgressions, it is said that one must first eliminate the offense;
therefore, one asks first about those who possess offenses.
In the dialogue, the discussion of purity, excellence, defilement, and inferiority is based on practice;

the holder [of the precepts] ought to be mentioned first, yet here the order is reversed to demonstrate that the Sage’s regulations were established with a specific purpose, as can be seen in the explanatory text. The two individuals are categorized as follows.
[The Vinaya: One does not commit an offense by remaining silent; "remaining silent" means that one knows the various venerable ones are pure.
[The Commentary: Regarding the five instances of not committing an offense through silence: it refers to responding with silent assent while not boasting of one's own virtues.
In the fifth section of the text, there is the fault of boasting about one's own virtues, which diminishes one's merit.

[Note: The Buddha stated that there are two types of cases where there is no offense: those who have not originally committed the transgression, and those who have committed it but subsequently repented.

[Commentary: Regarding the two ways of not committing an offense mentioned in the note, the first consists of remaining free from offense through single-minded diligence; the second consists of being able to repent after having committed an offense.

There is no wholesome dharma (*śukladharma*) that does not result in one being without blemish within oneself, such that one collectively achieves the state of being "one who has not committed an offense."

Explanation of the Second Note: Regarding "white dharmas" (*śukla-dharma*), this refers specifically to the confession of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. It applies generally to all subsequent categories of offenses, as they are all termed "capable of being repented.

Because the substance of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is destroyed by its commission, yet through confession one is restored to the status of a monk—functionally equivalent to receiving the precepts again in contrast to the initial reception—it is called the "second [reception of] the precepts.
Because it is pure and wholesome, it is called a "white dharma. In various sūtras and śāstras, the two types of karma, black and white, refer precisely to these.

In the first chapter on good and evil, there is no returning to the original state; when the conduct of the lower assembly is deficient while the substance remains intact, one performs repentance without manifesting this [deficiency], for name and form are merely categories.
[Vinaya: If others should question one, answer in this manner (the Buddha said: as when two bhikṣus question and answer each other).

[Commentary]: Sixth, "if there is another who questions" means that when a bhikṣu who has been formally accused (a *codaka*) interrogates one according to the Dharma, if one has committed an offense, one answers openly;
if one has not committed an offense, one remains silent. This principle is the same as common worldly speech, as illustrated by the example of two bhikṣus questioning and answering one another.
Among these six, this refers to one who has committed an offense and is confronted by others through the manifestation of the three bases of accusation;

he is commanded to answer truthfully. First, regarding the resolution of the matter, it concerns two types of responses—speech and silence—to explain the case of "two bhikṣus," which uses a specific instance as a comparison.
[Commentary] Another interpretation states: Since the three faculties are not dull and the five virtues have been heard, how could one remain silent when being accused before the assembly?

Therefore, it is necessary to clear one's name regarding both the facts and the falsehoods to manifest the circumstances of both self and other; thus, the Buddha’s resolution through questions and answers according to the nature of reality is precisely this.

Regarding the explanation of the second [of the three] among these, it is answered by means of speech; the three roots—namely, what has been seen, heard, and suspected—are called "roots" because they arise from these [three modes].

Regarding the five virtues, the Vinaya regulations stipulate that one must possess five virtues when accusing another of an offense: first, knowing the proper time; second, being truthful; third, acting for the benefit [of the accused];

fourth, being gentle; and fifth, having a mind of loving-kindness. This is explained in the *Chao* (Commentary) within the section on *Pravāraṇā* (Self-Examination), where "cleansing" (*jie-xue*) refers to analysis.

[The Vinaya: "In this way, if a bhikṣu remains in the midst of the assembly and, even after being questioned three times, does not confess a fault he remembers having committed, he commits a deliberate lie.
Regarding such lying, the Buddha has declared it to be a dharma that obstructs the Path."
[Commentary] Seventh, the passage "Thus, this bhikṣu among the assembly... clarifies that failing to repent entails harm.
In the seventh section, it states that failing to repent constitutes concealing transgressions; such karmic bondage is harmful, meaning it violates the regulations and obstructs the Path.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "therefore, one who speaks falsely," since silence already signifies purity, what offense would one incur? The various masters of antiquity have also deliberated upon this;
as it is one aspect of the correct principle that must be known, I shall first clarify it through reasoning and subsequently provide a detailed analysis.
In the initial passage of the commentary on the exegesis, although it specifies *duṣkṛta*, the question is raised as to what offense it constitutes;

this is because ancient authorities considered it a preparatory act (*prayoga*), whereas the present [text] treats it as a fundamental offense (*maula*), and thus a question is posed to introduce the definitive judgment in the subsequent section.

[Commentary: Now, in explaining the introduction, there is a sixfold analysis: first, determining the gravity or lightness [of offenses]; second, clarifying what is common or obstructed; third, correlating with the conditions of the questions;
fourth, distinguishing according to the offenses; fifth, discussing in terms of persons; and sixth, regarding the location where an offense occurs.
[Commentary] First, regarding the determination of the offense:
Former interpretations state that the silence regarding falsehood in the introduction is merely a skillful means (*upāya*). How is this known?
Because the offense—namely, deceiving the Saṃgha by feigning purity—has not yet been manifested, it is therefore a skillful means.
The principles established in the *Zhonggu* (Middle Commentary) regarding the determination of offenses are evident here.

[Commentary] Question: If the words have not yet been articulated, even though the monk has mentally resolved to undo the formal act (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), this constitutes a preparatory act (*prayoga*) of speech. For example, when one physically commits a verbal act or initiates a manifest action through silence, the mental resolution is the same.
By what cause is it that, according to this analogy, one would incur a *pāyattika* offense for resolving [the act] through silence? It should entail an offense.
The statement that verbal expression differs from bodily action is because the Sage observed that their characteristics do not overlap; thus, it is a grave offense.
Now, silence expresses purity within the assembly, encompassing all members without partiality toward oneself; therefore, one should know this as a skillful means.

In the initial objection, it is argued that because bodily actions that produce verbal karma—such as silent false speech—are identical to those that result in the attainment of karmic retribution, they should be taken as the basis for the objection.

However, this interpretation is untenable; below, the text distinguishes between what is "confused" (*lān*) and what is "not confused," establishing that while the former constitutes deception, the latter does not. The subsequent sections systematically and exhaustively refute this interpretation by examining each phrase.

[Commentary] Question: If it is said that the falsehood of silence has "silence" as its essence, while other false speech has "vain discourse" as its essence, then since the falsehood of silence is now considered a skillful means for speech, should "cessation" (śamatha) likewise be considered a skillful means for "activity" (pravṛtti)? Yet cessation cannot be a skillful means for activity;
how then can the falsehood of silence be a skillful means for speech? Answer: The meaning of false speech consists in words and phrases being clearly articulated.
Now, silence merely indicates its characteristic; if it has not yet manifested before others, how can it be determined to be ultimately established?

Regarding the second objection, first the nature of the offense is established: since an offense must necessarily involve action as its preparatory stage (*upāya*), falsehood should likewise be explained as having speech as its preparatory stage.
Why, then, do you reverse this in your interpretation by claiming that silence indicates speech?
[This] deceptive expedient (upāya) does not constitute an obstruction.

[Commentary: Question: For one who has committed the offense of silence, their private mind is already resolved and satisfied; the matter is limited to three inquiries, and if they remain silent in response to each question, the meaning of their feigned purity is complete.
What is lacking that would require this expedient? If silence were sufficient to signify purity, why must verbal expression still be required for the matter to be finalized?
As for "conclusion," even at the time when the *saṃgha* remains silent during the *karmavācanā*, it should merely be an act performed as a provisional means (*upāya*) by those in harmony;
yet this is not the case here. Since [the act] is completed and finalized according to its performance, how can it be called a provisional means?

Now, in explaining the first section of the initial argument, we address the previous objection: the ancients claimed that because there is a fruit to be attained through skillful means (*upāya*), the path has not yet reached its ultimate consummation;
however, this present [state] of silence and delusion lacks any distinct fruit, and therefore it is not a skillful means.

Below, we provide an analogy to further demonstrate that the former is not [a valid means]. Next, we shall clarify the present judgment. Question: Is the offense of this silence and delusion distinct?

If there is a skillful means to avoid answering, yet one remains silent when summoned for questioning with the intention of refusing, this case must likewise be classified as a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;

if there is no such means, it is a single offense (*pāyattika*). [Commentary]: Merely remaining silent in falsehood is a *duṣkṛta*. The Vinaya text contains this fully; however, because the ancient masters established the structure of the chapters and limited the meaning to three equal categories, they [treated it] accordingly.

These offenses are subsumed under the section on "preparatory stages" (*prayoga*); however, because this treatise has a distinct purpose, they are not discussed here, as may be seen below. Regarding the three types within the section on "manifesting intent," they are all as explained later.
That is to say, when complete, it is called a "section" (*varga*); when incomplete, it is termed a "cluster" (*khandha*); and when excluding the multitude, it is called a "group" (*gaṇa*).

The external training, evil conduct, and evil speech are ultimately not uniform; they are all subsumed within the categories [of offenses]. Since silence and falsehood reside within these categories, they are considered preparatory acts (*upāya*).

Now, below, the distinctions are clarified by pointing to the two names established in the subsequent section on the "Categories of Offenses" (*pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*). These two names manifest each other’s presence;

they are not absent from the two divisions—the fifth and the seventh—where they are equally mixed and do not overlap (the term "uniform" refers exclusively to the root offense, while "mixed" applies to both the root and its causes). Herein, this silence and falsehood are the fruit within the category of the "mixed."
[Offense].
[Commentary]: Furthermore, as you stated above, that which is light because the bodily form remains unmoved when questioned before an assembly is also not fixed.

If one commits a verbal karma through speech alone, such that the words are clear and the person before whom they are spoken understands them, it constitutes an offense regardless of whether there was doubt or certainty in the listener's cognition; it is fully established.
Throughout one's entire life, if one commits verbal karma regardless of its quantity and does not doubt its pervasiveness beforehand, it is not an "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Regarding the mutual commission [of karma], the initial passage is divided into two parts. First, it cites the ancient interpretation, which states:

"As previously mentioned, because it applies universally to the assembly and is not restricted to oneself alone, it is an expedient means. Below this, the text clarifies why this is incorrect. First, it describes the individual commission of [karma]; below that...
The phrase "regardless of how many mutually create [it]" is precisely used here to refute the previous argument.
[Commentary: How is this known? Because the meaning of the sentence is fixed: for example, when many people are sitting together and someone asks, "Has a noble one arisen?
if one person alone arises, the preceding people do not doubt it; thus, the conclusion is reached that if many were to arise, the preceding person would [be affected].

Out of doubt, one employs a stratagem or many people stand up to question [the practitioner]. If the noble one remains seated once, he commits a grave offense; if he sits down many times, he commits a light offense.
Because the preceding phrases involve movement, an offense arises; now, with the following phrases, even though there is no movement, an offense is still committed.

For example, if many people are seated or standing in an assembly and say, "He is not a noble one," if he moves his body once while many do not move, it is light; if many move while he alone does not move, it is grave.

"Immovable" (*acala*) is more serious than "mine" (*mama*); because one is clearly practiced in the characteristics of the noble ones (*ārya-lakṣaṇa*) and thus there is no error, one incurs a grave offense. One should understand the phrases according to this analogy.
Regarding the first two phrases of the sequence of clauses, as indicated below, we first clarify the "movable" (*cala*) phrase; ancient commentators say that if one moves the body, it is grave.

Now, based on the two positions of sitting and standing, each having one or many, four permutations are formed; the first permutation involves one heavy and many light offenses, which can be understood by consulting the text.
Following this, the next section clarifies the "immovable" (aniyata) category. First, it concludes the preceding and introduces the subsequent, as shown in the following list:
that refers to the immovable being equal to the light; now, we shall again demonstrate the indeterminate nature by means of one heavy and many light offenses.

This analogy is as follows: it is said that among the sages, some do not move their bodies at all, while others move them frequently; those who move them lightly are many, while those who move them heavily are few.

[Commentary]: Some say that since the three karmas are performed in mutual interdependence, there is certainly no confusion or overlap; yet even if one acts alone, the sages of former times had doubts.

One must not form a heavy offense, or [assert that] it is light simply because many people are present—meaning they are not ordinary persons. Only by applying this principle to subsume the preceding characteristics can [the classification] be correctly established.
Among the ancient commentaries, this master does not discuss the matter in terms of one versus many, but rather distinguishes based on whether there is doubt or no doubt.

Regarding the mutual inclusion of light and heavy verbal expressions: this means that although a single instance may be combined with a heavy offense, if there is doubt, it must be considered light; whereas although many instances may be light, if there is no doubt, they are also heavy.
[Commentary] Question: When one has the intention to deceive another, the mouth completes the act of false speech; when one has the intention to see a form, the eyes should respond accordingly.
Establishing the View.
In the initial section of the question-and-answer, the root and object are raised to challenge the previous argument regarding mutual creation.

[Commentary] The answer states that false speech involves the faculty of mind (manas-indriya). When seeing a form, it proceeds by means of visual consciousness; it is not the eye-consciousness itself. Why, then, is it so named?
"Seeing forms.
In the response, the first two phrases contrast with and clarify the latter two phrases by means of a counter-interrogation. [Commentary:

If that were so, since the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*) is not visual consciousness, it would not "see forms"; likewise, mental action (*manas-karman*) would not be [considered] verbal action (*vāk-karman*). This should not be the case.

When one answers with false speech, the three karmas are mutually produced; in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), false speech is established, for the six consciousnesses do not function interchangeably, as the mind does not perceive visible forms.
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states: "The four karmas of the mouth can also be performed by the mind. This is excellent evidence [for this principle].

In the "Rebuttal of the Difficulties," the previous objection regarding the mutual production of seeing is addressed; in the initial response, the difficulty is resolved by distinguishing between mutual and non-mutual production, and subsequently, scriptural evidence is cited to prove mutual production.

[Commentary] Question: Why is it that while the three karmas of ordinary beings mutually produce [results], the six consciousnesses have fixed functions? Answer: Although the three karmas differ, they share the same intention as their essence;
the six consciousnesses are not so, for each has its own distinct essence and characteristics. Thus, the treatise states: "The sense organs do not have the fault of mutual interchangeability."

Regarding the subsequent question: because the sages of the Middle Way can employ their six sense organs interchangeably (*ṣaḍ-indriya-para-vṛtti*), the question is framed from the perspective of ordinary beings.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the Buddha is able to employ all his sense organs interchangeably, as are the great Bodhisattvas and others; this refers to those from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) onward, who have attained the state of purity of the six sense organs.

In the answer, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun) states: "Apart from the mind, there is no thought, and thus no karma of body or speech. Therefore, it is known that they are identical in this regard.

The essence consists of mental volition (*manas-karman*). Because the objects of the six consciousnesses—seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing—are each distinct, the following citation of scriptural proof [in the original text] does not specify which treatise it refers to.

[Commentary: Question: Since the three types of karma share the same essence of mental volition, how are they distinguished from one another? Answer: They are distinguished based on their specific manifestations; the details of these mutual distinctions are as explained extensively elsewhere.
This was explained in the "Establishment of the Meaning" (*shuji*) section of the first chapter.

The third question and answer can be understood as referring downward to the topical gates (*immon*) of the first chapter; that is, the second [section] on the completion of an offense through the three types of action (*sagyō*), which clearly elucidates both individual and combined [factors], and "establishment" (*ju*) refers to the formal setting forth [of the rule].
[Commentary] Second, explaining what is general and what is specific.

[Commentary] As the former interpretation states: "In the introduction, the questioner asks about what is general regarding the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, because those who have committed such offenses are not permitted to hear the precepts;

therefore, the question in the introduction is general, intended to prompt confession and disclosure. Why is it that this does not encompass the other three types of questions? These are all specific."
Question: Since this section contains both pure and impure offenses, we know that the preceding questions differ from the general inquiry [found] in the Introduction (*nidāna*).

Regarding the distinction between what is comprehensive and what is restricted, the ancient commentary on the first section states: "The first of the three questions regarding the nine locations belongs to the general inquiry of the Introduction."
The final eight sections of the *Sarvavastu* do not interconnect with one another. [Commentary] Question:

The introductory section asks questions that apply generally to the subsequent sections, as discussed previously. Since the eight sections ask about specific offenses, and one must first state the actual transgression before asking the question, does this not contradict the teaching?

Answer: In the introductory section, the general inquiry for purity through silence is intended to reveal that no offenses have been disclosed; had there been any, it would have been feared that they would remain hidden. Thus, there is no contradiction.

To claim that one does not recall or recognize [an offense] while falsely asserting it to be pure conduct is logically untenable; therefore, each section [of the Vinaya] is presented to demonstrate the characteristics of offenses.

Although the precepts were previously expounded, this does not constitute concealing an offense, for when the mind is deluded regarding purity, there is no fault in the conduct—just as in the case of the "Dharma-speech" (dharmavāda) regarding persons.
In the initial inquiry, questioning the subsequent section would contradict what precedes it; therefore, this is presented as an objection. The response is twofold:
first, an explanation through the categories of confusion and forgetfulness to resolve the difficulty; second, an argument based on the absence of concealment to refute the challenge.

Regarding the analogy of "persons and dharmas," this refers to the *Pudgala-vastu* (The Chapter on Persons), which states: "There was a bhikṣu who committed one offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; he remembered one [aspect of it] and did not remember another."

If one is conscious of being conscious while concealing [a transgression], it is called "concealment"; if one is not conscious of it, it is not concealment. Taking this as proof, delusion regarding the offense opens the possibility for hearing [the precepts].

[Commentary] Question: If there is an offense when the mind is deluded regarding purity, yet there is no basis for opening [the rule] when the mind is not deluded regarding the hearing of the precepts, why is this so?

In the Vinaya, regarding the response that one may hear the recitation of the precepts through the "confession before another" (*pratimukha*) or "mental recollection" (*manasikāra*), this refers to an exceptional allowance (*anujñāta-kāraṇa*) where repentance is not permitted;
it does not mean that this applies universally. This is determined by the general principle of those who have committed an offense and did not hear the recitation of the precepts.

Next, the question is raised regarding the difficulty of confessing one's offenses while remaining within the assembly; in the response, the initial section provides a direct explanation of the inquiry.

Regarding the phrase "as for those who have committed an offense," although the Vinaya states that such individuals are not permitted to hear the *Prātimokṣa*, this regulation is not without its exceptions or general allowances;
hence the use of the term "generally speaking" (*dàyuē*).

[Commentary: Now, I shall explain the meaning of the preceding "cannot be contained" (*bù róng*). There are nine positions in total; in each case, the question is answered by referring to what follows, as will be explained in detail later.

Here, in explaining the first two phrases of the middle section, I clarify the intention of citing ancient authorities. The term "cannot be contained" (*bù róng*) indicates that [the former view] is not to be accepted.
Master Rong (or Rong) may have said that [the term] "stagnant and obstructed" (*zhìsè*) refers to the fact that [the offenses] do not exist [in the current context], and thus he mentioned them first.

Following the text below, I shall briefly indicate my own interpretation. As for the question posed below: many in the world do not understand this and claim that when the first section was being expounded, one only asked about the *pārājika* offenses down to the *śaikṣa* rules;
yet they also ask about the specific sections of the present [text]. Now, one should raise the following objection: regarding the commission of various minor offenses, it should...
If one hears the preceding section, how can it be reconciled with the Vinaya text which states that those who have committed an offense are not permitted to hear the precepts?

The present statement regarding "inquiring about the subsequent" means that when about to recite the subsequent section, one asks the assembly whether there are minor transgressions of the disciplinary codes within the seven groups of offenses (*sapta-āpatti-skandha*);
it does not mean that one merely inquires about the preceding section itself. This will be seen in the following text.
[Commentary: Third, regarding the number of offenses incurred based on the conditions of the questions asked.

[Commentary: As the ancient interpretation states: "Although three questions were posed, they collectively constitute a single formal act (*dharma*); therefore, one who remains silent now incurs only a single offense.

This is like various requests for alms or the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations), where although the words are repeated, they all together constitute a single formal act."

Regarding the threefold inquiry within the context of the causal conditions, the initial establishment of the principle is as cited below in the examples, such as the acceptance of various requests for alms or the performance of repentance (*pratideśanā*).

As for the previous cases where there are three requests followed by a formal motion with four parts (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), take, for instance, the reception of the precepts: four rounds of *karman* together constitute a single reception;
other cases are to be understood by this analogy.

[Commentary: Now, as there are three distinct questions and the interpretations differ, one incurs three offenses according to each question—whether by responding, remaining silent, or returning [to the offense].

This is like the *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part) procedure for admonishing, which together constitutes a single formal act (*dharma*). However, regarding the four *sthūlātyaya* offenses incurred through the *karmavācanā* (formal motion), they are not merely in response to the questioning or the admonition;
since there is a mind of resistance in both cases, multiple offenses are incurred.

Now, regarding the first section of the middle part of the explanation: the preceding establishment of the principle is as follows; the examples cited include the *śuklā-vastu* (white matter) and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for admonishing.

Following the general rule that a *sthūlātyaya* offense is incurred for each instance, here, with each of the three questions, a *duṣkṛta* offense is incurred. [Commentary] Question: Since the questioning is modeled after the process of admonition, one incurs multiple offenses. Furthermore, by violating the admonition on the fourth [stage], one would also incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, would it not?

To remain silent while falsely accusing [another] constitutes four offenses of *pāyattika*; to answer back when being admonished; to disobey the community’s command; and to recite the *Prātimokṣa* again after it has already been recited.

Since the prior transgression was not yet manifest, the formal procedure of the Saṃgha proceeds, and the questioning ceases after three rounds. Because one remained silent within the Saṃgha, this constitutes an offense of *dukkaṭa*.

According to the rule for confession before another (*pratideśanīya*), if one confesses a fault while possessing pure requisites, there are three [offenses]; the cases of mental reflection (*manasikāra*) should be understood by analogy.
In the section resolving objections, regarding the comparison of the fundamental offense with the formal admonition, an examination of the texts reveals four general differences:

(1) the distinction between an individual and the monastic community; (2) the difference between defiance and silent concealment; (3) the difference between admonishing through exhortation versus direct questioning; and (4) the difference in circumstances regarding whether the fault has been manifested or not.

These factors cannot be treated as analogous. Below, the distinctions are clarified: the "mindful" (*smṛti*) method involves internal reflection, whereas the "oral" (*vāk*) method is expressed aloud; both are applicable.
Regarding the analogy for the deluded thoughts of speech: it is said that if one does not address others, one obtains three types of merit.
[Commentary] Fourth, concerning the discussion of committing offenses.
[Commentary] Question: Now, if there is one who commits many offenses, since this violates the sequence of questioning, how many offenses does he incur?
Regarding the fourth point, concerning the interrogatory formulas within the offenses, I have cited the case of violating the proper order; the remaining eight cases are likewise so.

[Commentary] Answer: Silence, purification, and deceiving the Saṃgha result in only one offense. This is because the offense arises from the conditions of the interrogation itself, rather than arising from the offense of deception.

Since there is an offense when there is an interrogation, but no offense is incurred when there is no interrogation, it is known that this single offense is not the same as the offense of concealment (*pārājika*), which arises from the act of concealing a transgression.
If the offense is committed merely by the appearance of dawn, the transgression is incurred accordingly.

There are two ancient responses: first, regarding the establishment of the doctrine, although there are three questions, they collectively constitute a single dharma; since they arise from the questioning, there are no multiple offenses.
Second, regarding the prevention of obstacles: because one fears that the concealment of the offense might lead to further transgressions—whether few or many—one must act accordingly.
Because it is difficult [to distinguish], they are pre-screened.

[Commentary: Now, the explanations differ. Regarding the conditions for inquiry (*praśna-pratyaya*), both the appearance of light (*āloka-lakṣaṇa*) and the acquisition of multiple offenses result in the commission of many transgressions.

Since these two conditions constitute the stage of formalizing the offense (*āpatti-samāpanna*), and since concealment (*tirokaraṇa*) already allows for the arising of further offenses from an existing offense, would it not be the case that the condition for inquiry is itself the arising of further offenses from an existing offense?

If sin did not arise from [failing to] respond to a question, then all those who heard the inquiry would likewise have committed an offense, since there was the occasion for questioning that could have been disregarded.

However, this is not the case; for one who has committed a sin violates the duty to respond, whereas one who is innocent does not. Thus we know that having committed a sin, one harbors silence and falsehood.
How, then, can it be said above that "sin does not arise from [failing to] respond"?

Now, regarding the first point of the initial section, it clarifies that silence, concealment, and the commission of an offense share the same meaning in terms of the nature of the transgression. As for the inquiry into the conditions [of the offense]:
if one does not descend [to answer], the subsequent establishment of reasoning serves to refute and dismantle [the opponent's position] based on the loss of meaning resulting from the questioning.
[Commentary: Thus, we know that "silent falsehood" (*mò wàng*) is also a specific synonym for "concealment" (*pūti*). However, it may only persist through the night or until the questioning occurs.
In both cases, the concealment of the offense is identical and not dual.

The initial section of the subsequent analysis first demonstrates that while the names differ, it concludes below that the offenses are the same; this is because both silence and concealment alike violate the requirement of disclosure.
[Commentary]: If one commits ten offenses and for each there is a silent purification (*tūṣṇīka-śuddhi*) performed three times or nine times, one incurs two hundred and seventy *duṣkṛta* offenses.
It is also like a single person being accused of three charges; by receiving offerings from each, one incurs three offenses. Such are the categories [of these rules].
Among the three [sections], the first provides the direct exposition; for now, one should understand this by taking the number of the ten offenses as the standard.
Furthermore, the following citation of similar cases refers to a single person who is subject to all three types of punishment simultaneously.
[Commentary: Fifth, regarding the characteristics of the formation of offenses based on the number of persons.

[Commentary: Since one has committed the ten offenses, one desires to let the multitude know that one’s own conduct is pure. If I were to reveal [the offenses], they would know my conduct is non-virtuous and would not include me in their ranks;

therefore, one hopes for many people [to hear of them] so as to incur multiple offenses. This is like the rule for false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*): a single word deceives many, and each person who hears it incurs an offense.
The procedures for confession before another (*pratimokṣa*) and mental recollection (*manasikāra*) are to be divided accordingly, as explained above.
Regarding the first part of the explanation based on the number of persons, "registering" (*chil-luk*) means that the person’s name is not recorded;
thus, the following indicates the number of offenses as illustrated by the examples cited below. As for the question regarding confession before another (*dui-shou*), that may be so;

however, how can one apply the same principle to mental recitation (*xin-nian*) or private confession (*du-shuo*)? The answer is that, according to the *Shan-chao* (Commentary), one must confess toward the Sangha of the four directions.
If one knows [the truth] yet does not disclose it, this constitutes deceiving the Sangha. However, since the object is not present before one, by what means could it be restricted?
Nevertheless, to speak privately is contrary to the proper decorum and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; as this is likewise determined by the number [of those present], it may be cited by analogy.
[Commentary] Sixth, clarifying the number of locations where silent offenses (*tūṣṇībhāva-āpatti*) are committed according to the sūtras.

[Commentary] As the ancient interpretation states: "Of the seven classes of offenses (*sapta-varga*), six offenses are committed in three locations. Alternatively, it is said there are eight offenses;

that is to say, the two offenses of sexual misconduct (*maithuna*) and physical contact (*sparśana*), and the two offenses of the private (*rahas*) and public (*prakāśa*) places—these four applied to both nuns and laywomen—making these eight offenses, each situated within its respective section.

The two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules, together with the initial sequence, constitute the offenses of the three locations; these are established by combining the nun and the female lay follower within the *aniyata*.

Thus, the ninety rules are separated, each having its own purpose. If one wishes to confess, it may be done in only one location. Regarding the single category of *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), this refers only to the offense of the sequence;
it is settled through the *pāpadeśanā* (confession of evil). This single *sthūlātyaya* occurs within the sequence and constitutes an offense among the seven *vinayas*.

Sixth, clarifying the scriptural sources for the previous explanations: first, the general clarification of the various *saṃghāvaśeṣa* groups; second, the specific indication of the *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding the six offenses [of the first group], they are categorized by whether they occur in private or in public;

regarding the eight offenses [of the second group], they are divided according to whether the victim is a nun or a laywoman. This refers to the offenses listed below. From here on, the locations where these offenses are committed are shown.

Ancient commentators maintain that within the introduction there are general inquiries, while within this specific chapter there are distinct inquiries; thus, both general and specific inquiries apply to all chapters and groups (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), and in each case there are two types of offenses.

Since these two indeterminate offenses (*aniyata*) include all eight of these transgressions, they involve three locations; the distinctions regarding their concealment or disclosure in private or public settings will be clarified individually below.
Next, regarding the indication that confession requires only one location—where neither [concealment nor disclosure] is required—it need not necessarily involve three locations.

Furthermore, among the *sthūlātyaya* offenses, the first two phrases provide a general indication, while the subsequent section specifically distinguishes the "quarrel settled by a verdict of wickedness" (*adharmasamatha*). That is to say:

The *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti* (majority decision) and the *vinaya* for resolving disputes regarding Devadatta’s schism distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox; because following the heterodox to destroy the orthodox entails the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.

[Commentary: This is an ancient interpretation still taught today. If it were not recounted, there would be no means by which to establish the teaching or to distinguish between what is to be promoted and what is to be refuted.

It is possible to understand this within the initial section of the "Refutation" (Jiechi), where the author first specifically refutes those who limit the offenses to their respective chapters alone to explain the "silent falsehood" (*mowang*).

This interpretation is established because, by examining the underlying intent of the citations below, one sees that the correct meaning was not realized until after the errors of former scholars had been addressed.
This is because it refutes the capabilities of ancient commentaries.

[Commentary: The present explanation is not so; if one has committed an offense, it is improper to hear the precepts. How could one who has committed a *pārājika* (defeat) be permitted to hear the remaining sections?
Therefore, we know that this is difficult. Regarding the nine locations mentioned in response to the question, if there is a concealing mind in each case, then it constitutes an offense accordingly.
[This is] a fault.
Now, in the explanation of the middle [section], the initial pointing out of the non-objection still constitutes an obstacle; subsequently, the correct meaning is demonstrated.
[Commentary]: If this were so, the introduction consisting of the thesis and the question would suffice; why then are there nine distinct locations for questions and answers within the introduction?

The questioner is about to expound the eight chapters; fearing that there may be those who have committed offenses, which would cause discord between the speaker and the listeners, he follows the same procedure for questioning regarding the four matters.
Because he intends to expound the subsequent precepts, he first sets forth these questions, fearing there might be forgetfulness or error.
He asks again according to each chapter while asserting that his conduct is pure, so as to ensure a correct exposition; for one who has committed an offense is not fit to hear [the teaching].

In the initial question-and-answer section, the first question follows upon what was established above: since [the offenses] do not follow the sequence of the chapters (*pāda*), they are already fully contained within the Introduction (*nidāna*).

As for the remaining eight locations, their faults lie in excessive prolixity; therefore, they must be explained comprehensively. In the response, the first part clarifies the questions in the Introduction;

the four subsequent sections explain the later questions. For now, four matters are raised as examples, with the remainder to be understood by analogy. The term "later precepts" refers generally to the seven chapters (*sapta-varga*).
Regarding the "Thirteen Intermediate Questions," these refer to the six sections; thus, when discussing their meaning, there is no difference.

To establish the correct exposition, the pure conduct and the assembly of listeners do not deviate from the Dharma. Examining what is explained here, it differs from the former [tradition] of the *Tiān* (Heaven/Treasure) school.

Herein, the term "questions" refers specifically to the questions posed by the Saṃgha. Since the offenses of purity pertain to all seven categories of transgressions (*sapta-varga*), and one asks first before speaking, it is called "questions."
The latter nine sections are all likewise; let the student examine them with precision. [Commentary] Question:

After the seven methods for extinguishing offenses (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), there are no further precepts to be taught. Why, then, is there another question? Answer: The characteristics of offenses are like dust;

when examined closely, they are clearly seen. When the mind of recollection and awareness becomes turbulent before and after, one must immediately confess and reveal them as soon as understanding arises, in order to attain tranquility.
Thus, when in the presence of a multitude, one should keep in mind the collection of the Nuns' Vinaya and the summary teachings of the seven Buddhas;

Before composing this text and its exegesis, I first provide a general overview of the meaning to clarify the essential body of the orthodox teaching; herein, the principles of maintaining and violating the precepts, as well as the characteristics of such violations, are established.
Modeling it after the *Piñjū* (Articles of the Vinaya), I shall briefly establish its path through four sections: first, clarifying the primary fruits in five articles;

second, clarifying the gravity of offenses in seven groups; third, explaining the characteristics of transgressions regarding preparatory acts; and fourth, explaining the methods for upholding and violating the precepts.

In the first section of the opening chapter, the first two lines indicate the primary subject, while the subsequent lines introduce the exposition. The first two lines show the essence of the teaching (*śāsana-tattva*);
the next two lines clarify the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), namely the transgressions, conditions, rules, and determinations, which constitute the model.

Briefly stated below, the four sections are divided into four gates in sequence: the first concerns only the fundamental fruit; the second pertains to both cause and fruit; the third is restricted to causal offenses; and the [final] three are specific distinctions.

[Commentary: Now, regarding the term "pian" (chapter) in the phrase "jie pianzhang zhi pian": it refers to the uniformity of categories and the equivalence of meaning with the various chapters and sections.
Generally, the establishment of a chapter must possess three types of uniformity: uniformity of name (*ming-jun*), uniformity of substance (*ti-jun*), and ultimate completion (*jiujing*).

This is the definitive definition. In the first chapter, the shared title constitutes uniformity of name; the necessity of expelling and subduing [defilements] constitutes uniformity of substance; and that which is not a provisional means constitutes ultimate completion.
Because the three grades [of offenses] extend even to the fifth grade and are not absent therein, this is titled the "Chapter on Grades" (*piān*).

[The Commentary] states: Some say that only when all three [factors] are fully present can a section (pian) be so named; however, why must secular books possess all three factors in order to establish a chapter?

[Commentary: Now, regarding the term "pian" (section/chapter), it begins with the four *pārājika* offenses and ends with the seven *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, thus constituting eight sections. A collection of text and meaning is what is termed a "pian.

[Commentary] Regarding the second interpretation, which derives the meaning from the radical "grass" (艸), this too is a self-delusion; how can it lead others to enlightenment? The characters in these sections derive [their meaning] from...
"Cǎo" (grass) is merely the name for grass; "biān" (end/limit) is its opposite. In the world, they are called "piān" (tablets). Bamboo can also be eaten by humans;
the character "piān" follows the radical for bamboo and is thus the name for a bamboo slip. Prior to the Han dynasty, there were originally no examples of paper or pens;
bamboo and wood were used together with silk (*wán-sù*). Later, during the Later Han, Cai Lun invented paper, making it easier and simpler than the silk and ancient bamboo slips.
A single chapter may consist of what is termed a "leather-bound" (weibian) section, as when Confucius read the *Yi*, the leather bindings were snapped three times;

this refers to that. The subsequent explanation merely refutes the character "delusion" (*mi*) regarding the established uniformity of meaning, for the following text correctly takes the initial indication rather than the end of the chapter.

To provide a further explanation of the preceding commentary on the character "bamboo" (*zhú*) from the section on "Grasses" (*cǎo*): the *Erya* commentary states that it resembles the small jujube (*lí*), has red stems and nodes, grows well by roadsides, and is edible.
Following the character "bamboo" in the next section, there is an explanation of "bamboo" as a type of wood; "bamboo" is the name for the *jiǎn* (slip), while "wood" is the name for the *dù* (box).
Cāi Lún was a person of the time of Emperor Huán of the Han dynasty—some say he lived during the reign of Emperor Shùn—who pounded fish nets to make paper.
To employ plain and simple materials was the beginning of this practice. "Weī" refers to processed leather; "Xuānní" is the courtesy name of Kǒng Qiū, whose style name was Zhòngní.
During the Yuánsī era of Emperor Píng of the Former Han, he was posthumously titled Gōng of Bāochéng Xuānní, and it was for this reason that he was addressed by that title.

[Commentary]: Now, the meaning of the chapters is established as three equal divisions. This may be analogous to the *dharmaskandha* (aggregates of dharma), where categories of meaning are not confused;

since the *dharma* and *śīla* (precepts) each have their own distinct groupings, they are called *khandhaka* (sections). This is also like that [the *dharmaskandha*], for name and essence ultimately coincide in a single position.
What fault would there be in using the term "chapter" (*pǐn*) to encompass these five grades of progression?
