Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, those who can purely maintain the precepts and understand the retribution of karma;

second, those who fear the consequences of actions in future lives and possess a sense of shame, modesty, and remorse. Such persons are themselves free from sores (where "sores" is a metaphor for the evil karma of breaking the precepts). These two types of pure individuals are without such afflictions.

[Commentary: Regarding the initial theft from the Three Jewels, speaking of it in general terms, if there is a guardian, stealing [an object] valued at five *kārsāpaṇas* or more constitutes an extremely grave offense.

In the case of property belonging to the Buddha that has no guardian—such as when a donor’s gift is severed, as in the case of the *piṇḍola*—it is otherwise. The details are extensive as found in the *Chao*.

The subsequent text provides two judgments. First, regarding the stealing of banners, canopies, and so forth from a Buddha’s stūpa or a Śrāvaka’s stūpa, these are all judged from the perspective of severing the donor's merit;

thus, one incurs the grave offense of *pārājika* (abandonment and non-acceptance). The *Vinaya-mātṛkā* states: "If one steals from a Buddha stūpa or a Śrāvaka stūpa, such as banners or canopies, because it severs the donor's merit, one incurs the offense of *pārājika*.
If one follows the precedent in the *Chao*, which states that the Buddha has no sense of "mine," this would not apply to non-humans.
Since the current text of the *Jielan* (Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu) does not provide [this detail], it refers back to that [source].
[Commentary: It is said that among the property of the Buddha, there are four distinctions.
First, regarding items used by the Buddha: these include halls, buildings, clothing, as well as metal, stone, clay, and earth that have previously been [used by him].
That which is used by the Buddha image must not be treated with negligence; it should always be prepared for offerings, as this generates great merit for those living in the world.
Thus, the Vinaya states that if items such as seats are used in the Buddha’s garden, all devas and humans regard them as objects of worship equal to a stupa.
The reason they are not permitted [to be used otherwise] is that these things are the very manifestations of the Dharmakāya; their outward form is profound and must not be treated lightly.

Therefore, within the section on the Buddha’s requisites (*buddha-vastu*), the first part is divided into three: first, showing the characteristics of the objects; second, citing the Vinaya to corroborate what has been stated; and third, investigating the underlying reason.
Since the Dharma-body is formless, it manifests through these objects; thus, these various objects are themselves the substance of the Dharma-body.

[Commentary]: As for the reason why items belonging to the Buddha may be diverted [for other uses], it is because the original donor intended them generally for the Buddha’s utilization; thus, they may be traded or exchanged.
This differs from the former case, where because the object had previously served as a superior sign (liṅga), it was fixed exclusively to one specific purpose.
Of the two [sections], the first provides the heading; that which follows clarifies the reason for permitting the exchange of items such as money, treasures, people, and livestock.
It does not provide a comparative distinction from what precedes it.

[Commentary]: Third, regarding objects of offering—such as banners, flowers, and so forth—if they are obtained through trade, their status is identical to that which belongs to the Buddha; this can be understood through reasoning.
[The text] seeks [the following]: regarding the three types of objects, their distinct transformation and exchange are as stated above.
[Commentary: As for the fourth point, "objects offered to the Buddha," it is permissible for attendants to use them because they share the same status as being subsumed within the Buddhist community.
As in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, those who provide the requisites for the Dharma—such as the Dharma-preacher, the teacher of the Dharma, and the reciter of the sūtras—also receive their share;

the details are as explained at length in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*. Among the four [categories], the first indicates the substance itself, namely food, drink, fruits, and so forth; the second clarifies its usage and bestowal; the third determines its ownership.
The attendant is one who currently manages the Buddha’s temple; this principle applies to both monastics and laypeople.

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that when food is offered before the Buddha, the bhikṣus attending the Buddha may eat it, and laypeople attending the Buddha may also eat it, as illustrated by the examples cited below.

The *Śāstra* says: "If one gives a portion of the Dharma, it should be divided into two parts: one part is given to the scriptures and the Dharma, and one part is given to those who recite the scriptures."
The Dharma-preacher says that although he bestows the Dharma, the person receives a share of it; just as one who now serves the Buddha undoubtedly obtains food, so it was in ancient records.

A question asks: "If one uses the food belonging to the permanent endowment of the Sangha (*sthavira-saṃghika*) to make offerings to the Buddha, does this apply to all such uses? The answer, as stated in the *Fayuan*, is:
"In the end, it returns to the permanent endowment of the Sangha."
[Commentary]: It is said that there are likewise four types of stealing objects belonging to the Dharma.

First, those items used for the Dharma refers to sutras, images, or boxes, containers, and bags written upon paper, silk, bamboo, or wood, which have already been used for storage and are designated as permanently dedicated, not permitted to be diverted; these are fixed and revered in the same manner as the Sages.
Since all teachings are the support for the principle of cessation (*nirodha*), there is both loss and benefit; both [actions] give rise to demerit or merit in relation to *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the objects of the Dharma, the first section presents the physical entities, while the subsequent sections demonstrate the reasons [for their use], concluding with paper, silk, and storage containers.
These worldly objects are merely things designated by names; because the Ultimate Truth (*tathatā*) is priceless, [they cannot represent it]. [Commentary:
There are those who, lacking discernment, burn and destroy sutras, claiming that by "purifying them with fire" they will gain merit. This is a false calculation.

Even a half-verse of the Dharma was sacrificed for the sake of the body, yet two characters from the Illuminating Canon (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*) that remove delusion are listed in the authentic scriptures. How can one burn these?
The omission of this matter is due to [the text] being located within the section on merit (*puṇya*).

Next, the previous section pointed out erroneous views (such as the false worldly tradition claiming that one obtains rebirth by burning oneself, which is not seen in the sutras; how could such a commentary lead others astray?).

Hereafter, based on the text, the following refutes the aforementioned citation of the half-verse regarding the sacrifice of the body: first, it manifests the Tathāgata’s diligence in seeking the Dharma; second, it demonstrates...

The Tathāgata values the Dharma and thrice reveals that the True Dharma is difficult to hear. [This section] first cites a sutra as proof; second, it removes delusions to reveal the profound merit of the Buddha-dharma.
By citing a small case to illustrate the great, the gravity of the transgression becomes even more severe. If you fear future suffering, do not follow the followers of Māra.
These two conditions both appear in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where it says: The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, saying: "In the past..."
In that world, before the Sun of the Buddha had yet risen, I dwelt upon the Snowy Mountains at that time, subsisting solely on various fruits.
Having eaten, I focused my mind in contemplation and sat in meditation for countless years, without even hearing the name of the Tathāgata’s Mahāyāna sūtras.
While I was practicing these ascetic penances, Śakra-devendra transformed his own body into the likeness of a rākṣasa and descended.
On the Snowy Mountains, he recited a half-verse spoken by a past Buddha: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the nature of arising and ceasing.
Upon hearing this half-verse, his mind was struck with alarm and doubt, and he said, "It would be fortunate for you now if you could complete this verse.
The rākṣasa replied, "I am currently tormented by the suffering of hunger; I truly cannot speak it. He then asked:
"What do you eat? The rākṣasa replied, "Only the warm flesh of humans; what I drink is only the hot blood of humans.
I spoke to him again, saying, "First recite half a verse of the gāthā; once I have heard the verse, I shall offer this body of mine as a gift for your sustenance.
The rākṣasa then recited half a verse, saying: "When birth and death have ceased, nirvāṇa is bliss. The Bodhisattva [leaned] toward...
Having inscribed this verse upon a stone wall and a tree along the path, he immediately climbed a tall tree and cast himself down from it.
Before his body reached the ground, various sounds issued forth from the midst of space, reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
At that time, the rākṣasa returned to the form of Śakra and, from mid-air, caught the Bodhisattva and placed him on level ground.

...and so forth. Furthermore, a sutra states: "Good son, if there are those who do not know the profound realm of the Tathāgata, and thus wander through birth and death, increasing their fetters and undergoing much suffering;

yet if there are those who can know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change, or who hear even the two characters 'eternal-abiding' (zhǒngcháng) but once pass them through their ears, then immediately..."
Only at the time of liberation after being born in the heavens can one realize and know such matters as the Tathāgata’s permanence and immutability.

Regarding the statement that "matters reside in merit," this refers to acts such as a donor building bridges or wells; as long as the conditions for generating that merit remain intact, the name persists, but once those conditions perish, it is lost.
Now, because these matters reside in *avijñapti* (unmanifest action), even when burned, the matter remains so too, as described in the sutras.
[Commentary]: The remaining three characteristics may be inferred from what precedes.
Regarding the first two of the remaining three, they are subject to change; the latter is identical to the previous judgment concerning the attendant.

*Commentary on the Essentials of Practice for the Annotated Sūtra of the Four-Part Vinaya*, Part Two, Upper Section, Chapter Three.
[Sūtra] Within the property of the Saṃgha, there are four distinctions.

Regarding the first two types of Saṃgha property, their locations are fixed and permanent; they are collectively termed "perpetual property" (*changzhu*). However, while the former has no sense of being divisible, the latter... [text fragment ends].
Because this [former category] is divisible, the phrase "permanently present throughout the ten directions" is added to distinguish it;

the latter two are both instances of applying the general term "presently manifest," yet because the former is restricted to its own location while the latter extends both internally and externally, the phrase "presently manifest throughout the ten directions" is added to differentiate them.

[Commentary: First, regarding permanently fixed property: such as halls, buildings, fields, gardens, people, livestock, rice, or flour—once these have been assigned to a specific location, they may not be divided.

If one intends to bestow them upon another monastery, they must be granted through a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) with the consensus of the assembly; to send them directly otherwise is termed "theft and damage.

Alternatively, if there is a designated custodian who steals from it for themselves without seeking the consent of the ten directions, the offense is calculated according to the value of what was taken; once it reaches five *māṣaka*, the full penalty is incurred.
It is extremely grave because, as stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, even if a community (*saṃgha*) were assembled, it could not be divided.
This section is initially divided into four parts: first, the substance of the object is presented; second, the name and meaning are indicated; third, the formation of the offense is clarified;

and finally, regarding theft with respect to the owner, since this meaning is easy to understand, the text merely presents the case of the owner stealing from themselves, as will be shown by the citations below.

[Commentary]: Regarding the property permanently held for the ten directions, such as cooked food like rice or cakes, which was originally intended for the ten directions, if one hears of it and steals this food while treating it as common rice, the offense is grave in relation to the protectors and light in relation to the Sangha; this is because the portion belonging to the Sangha does not reach the full five *kārṣāpaṇas*.

Of the two [categories], the first lists the physical objects; below, their specific and general names are shown. Since these are the same as those mentioned above, they are not repeated here. Below, the characteristics of the offense are clarified. There are two types:

those that are grave when viewed in relation to the owner, meaning theft by another person; and those that are light when viewed in relation to the Saṃgha, namely the commission of a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
This also includes cases where both the resident and the guest steal together, or where the resident steals alone. Question: Regarding both types of permanent property (*dhruva-vastu*)...
Regarding the phrase "pervading the ten directions," why does it not refer to the Sangha beforehand? As for the reference to the Sangha afterwards, it can be understood by following the text.

[Commentary] Question: When the bell is struck to summon the assembly, it is the Sangha who all eat. I do not know whether slaves or livestock from other monasteries may participate. Answer: It is not appropriate.

The Sangha possesses the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-āveṇika-dharma*), and wherever they are, humans and livestock are distinct entities belonging to specific individuals; the principle is not one of universal application. Since the messenger...
The same applies to the case of food restricted to a specific location.

Regarding the meaning of the question: it is intended that since the slaves and livestock of one monastery belong to the Sangha in common with those of another, they should be permitted to receive food.

In the answer, the first sentence establishes that this belongs to the Sangha; the subsequent section explains the reason for this, first demonstrating the principle of commonality among the Sangha and then clarifying the status of the slaves and livestock.
The *Bùtōng chāo* states: "If one travels to another temple and privately uses the property of the Sangha belonging to humans or livestock, it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*).

Since the donor intended it for the monks of that specific location and not for others, and because those others are not a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), using the property of the Sangha’s family members or their livestock constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
(Nowadays, many people carry servants on private business and consume the food of those monks; according to the explicit texts, this constitutes a grave offense.)"

[Commentary]: Third, "present before" (pratyutpanna) refers to items currently present, such as those offered today by various laypeople to the Saṃgha—whether robes, medicine, or housing supplies—all of which belong to the Saṃgha present before them.
This is similar to the *Madhyama Āgama*, where it speaks of donating a cell for the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha of the four quarters), meaning the donation of a separate room.

Furthermore, regarding the term "Saṃgha-mālā" (Saṃgha-ornament/garland) found in the sūtras, according to the Sanskrit original, when translated into the language of Tang, it corresponds to "that which is face-to-face" (*pratyakṣa*).

"Things" refers simply to the offerings presented before one's eyes. The *Shier Yao* (Twelve Essentials) quotes an ancient interpretation stating that [the term] "flowers and fruits" reveals their characteristics according to their literal names, which deviates from their actual meaning and purpose.
Among the three [sections], the first indicates the name and substance, as evidenced by the following citation from the *Madhyama Āgama*: "Ānanda received a separate room."
Regarding the practice of giving to the *cātuddisa-saṃgha*, this refers to the gift of a separate room (*biéfáng*), which is a reversal of the name [of the recipient].
That is to say, one gives a separate room to the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the present community). Furthermore, as for the scriptural passage, it refers to the opening section of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

The *Xiǎnxiàng Chāo* (Exposition of Manifested Characteristics) below points out that the former interpretation was incorrect, stating that the *Shìchāo* (Commentary on the Essentials) erroneously employed the former understanding by claiming that "rooms and buildings are the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha*."
Flowers and fruits are items for the *saṃgha-mālā* (monastic garlands); because they are taken and used to tie these garlands, it is said that the characters reveal their characteristics.
To fail to distinguish between the Chinese and Sanskrit terms is precisely what constitutes a deviation from the meaning of the matter.
[Commentary]: Regarding "objects present from the ten directions," this refers to offerings received by the Saṃgha as well as the property of deceased members of the five assemblies.
Since these items are offered for the sake of the monks throughout the ten directions, all who are present may receive them; thus, the share of this merit is vast and boundless.

Furthermore, concerning the establishment of the rules, they cannot be fully enumerated. These regulations are established as universal legal procedures, and regarding their application across the ten directions, whoever is present at the assembly has a share in them.
Therefore it is said: if one steals before the *karmavācanā* has been performed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*, because the Sangha of the ten directions does not constitute a quorum of five;
if one commits theft after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, the offense is determined according to its gravity based on the present circumstances.
Once the formal judgment is established, the subsequent procedures for sentencing are largely explained in this section, which cites the commentary (*chao*) for clarification.

Of the four [sections], the first distinguishes the characteristics of the objects; from below, it demonstrates the names, meanings, and the application of the rules. That which constitutes the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) is as follows:

regarding the determination of the gravity of offenses according to the *Śraddhākaravarman-sūtra*, an initial offense constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* because the person has not yet performed the formal act;
this is determined by the infinite number of beings throughout the ten directions. Subsequently, once the formal act has been performed, the gravity of the offense is judged accordingly.
Since persons have numerical limits, two offenses are established according to the gravity of the theft.

[Commentary]: Regarding the second [category], stealing another's property, it is divided into three parts based on the conditions: first, explaining loss through negligence; second, explaining the manner of being stolen by thieves.
[Commentary] Regarding the first point, the *Miaotongchao* cites the *Sudarsana-vinaya*:
"If one guards wealth and property with diligence and without negligence, yet a thief secretly steals it or takes it by force, the offense is incurred against the original owner.

This is because the theft does not fall within the scope of what the guardian could have prevented. Conversely, if the opposite is the case, the guardian must compensate for the object, as the original thief is no longer the one responsible."
Because it would be a deception regarding the protection [of the object], it must be returned to the other; if one does not return it, an offense is committed.

Next, in the first section of the explanation concerning the property of another person, the first phrase refers extensively to that [topic], which is divided into seven types based on two categories of owners:
(1) the owner who suffered loss while guarding [the item], (2) the owner to whom it was entrusted, and (3) the owner of the stolen object. Fourth...

1. A thief who gives an object to a bhikṣu; 2. The owner of the object; 3. Five types of prisoners; 4. The leader of the thieves; 5. One who gives an object while insane; 6. The owner of that object; 7.
The person guarding and watching over it. These are all explained in detail therein. Those who require them should seek them out below.

The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (or *Samantapāsādikā*, as indicated by "善見") first clarifies, in its initial section, the meaning of guarding and being cautious with regard to the original owner, for which there are two senses. First:
It is not that one is able to prohibit [theft], for there is no compensation; rather, if the original owner demands restitution, one instead incurs the offense of theft.
Next, the following section clarifies "concealing with arrogance," which reverses the two meanings mentioned above; therefore, it proceeds from the perspective of guarding [the object].

[Commentary]: Second, regarding "being robbed by thieves," as cited in the *Chao*, the meaning establishes two positions: namely, whether the offense is incurred at the time of the actual taking or at the time it is not manifest.

This depends on whether the two owners have severed their claim to the property. If the original owner has already severed their claim, the thief’s ownership becomes fixed; in such a case, it cannot be recovered, as stated in the Vinaya.
If the thief subsequently robs another thief, although the second thief’s ownership is fixed, the first thief’s ownership is not yet fixed; in this case, [the property] may be recovered.

If one seizes [an object] because the conditions are incomplete, the three masters of wealth (the owner, the thief, and the king) will hesitate; since the master of the theft is already determined, this cannot be seized, for the conditions have not been fulfilled.
Why inquire about the original owner? All four parties are indeterminate; thus, it is recovered because the mind is unsettled and the karmic action is not fully manifest.
Now, this may be judged by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Next, regarding the initial general summary of "manifest" and "non-manifest" within the analysis of the phrases:

this refers to the two types of theft—direct face-to-face theft and indirect theft—as well as the two owners, namely the owner of the property and the owner of the thief. If one proceeds to the subsequent specific enumeration, the first and last cases are both easily understood.
As for the second phrase, because the thief’s mind is hesitant and the karmic act of theft has not yet been completed, it is said that "the conditions are incomplete."
Third, because it is the reverse of that, one may not take it away. [Commentary] Question:

Now, if there is a thief who offers a gift, may one take the object? Answer: Judging by principle, it is established that one may. This is because the object does not belong definitively [to the thief];

rather, he becomes its master only subsequently. It is like worldly currency, which cannot be definitively owned; it belongs to whoever uses it, wherever it is used, and wherever it is determined to be.
The cases of "according to the damage" and "according to the bond" may be understood by analogy.

In the question, there is a concern that one might suspect this constitutes joint theft; therefore, it is questioned and explained. In the answer, the initial section establishes the determination, while the subsequent portion explains the reasons.
Below, examples are cited to apply the principle universally.
[Commentary]: Third, regarding the object stolen, this brief enumeration comprehensively includes both sentient and insentient paths, encompassing them all.

Fearing that [readers] may not have seen the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā* (the *Chao*) from which this is cited, I have again quoted the explanation from the *Vidyāmātrasiddhi-śāstra* (the *Míngliǎolùn*) as found therein.
Among the three [sections], the initial general indication of the text is as follows, arising [from the context].

[Commentary]: As that commentary explains, the meaning of "theft" is extremely manifold; for now, we shall consider it in relation to the six sense faculties. If one commits unrighteous acts through these, or if one steals the six great elements, one also incurs a grave offense (pārājika).

In the first section of this commentary, the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) are categorized according to that which steals, thereby encompassing that which is stolen; the six great elements (*ṣaḍmahābhūta*) are included as that which is stolen, thereby revealing that which steals.
Thus, one knows that the objects of theft are pervasive and infinite.

[Commentary]: How is this clarified? For example, there were certain sages who were masters of crawling on their chests; when someone was bitten by a snake, they would consult the sages’ texts, and all who saw them were healed.
However, if a bhikṣu steals to look at them and is harmed, he commits an offense at the very moment of looking, regardless of whether damage was actually sustained.
By this analogy, regarding secret formulas and essential techniques that are not permitted to be transmitted to others, stealing to view them constitutes a transgression.
How could the offense of causing distress be limited to these five cases? One should apply this principle by analogy to others, such as reciting mantras to cure illness.
If one wishes to learn, one must pay the value directly; if a bhikṣu listens secretly, he incurs a grave offense of theft. This also applies by analogy to smelling, tasting, or touching [the object].

If one requires a specific technique or remedy for an illness and it is cured, one should pay the value upon obtaining it. If one obtains it by listening to or transcribing [a text], the bhikṣu who receives and studies it does so with a focused mental intention.
If one obtains a cure but does not pay the price, one commits a grave offense.
Regarding the first phrase among the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the inquiry is raised as follows; the detailed explanation of the eye faculty is set forth below.

According to the *Śarīraprasthāna-śāstra*, the "chest-crawling" [snake] is explained as follows: the snake crawls on its chest (*uraḥ-prasara*). The term "sting" (*daṃśa*) is also reversed [in meaning]; it refers to an insect.
[The text] "Practicing poison" and the following examples apply to the remaining five sense faculties.
[Commentary: Next, regarding the six elements, the preceding ones—earth, water, and fire—are understandable. As found in the Vinaya, there are cases of stealing wind:

for instance, when a monk uses incantations, fanning, medicinal ointments, or shaking to take what is not given without paying its value; or when a multi-storied pavilion is built at an angle, encroaching upon and obstructing another's construction.
This is called the "stealing of the element of consciousness" by those who possess the wisdom of emptiness. When a person possesses skillful means, they do not pass through life empty-handed;
rather, when they receive payment for their services, if a bhikṣu employs expedient means to learn from them without paying the price, this is the theft of consciousness.
Consciousness itself cannot be stolen because it is formless; one can only steal its functional wisdom through conditions.
Next, regarding the "Six Greats," "Great" refers to the six being vast; "pervading the realm" refers to the six aspects being distinct while their substance is identical yet their names differ.
Each is designated according to its position in the text. First, the three preceding [stages] are briefly indicated as in the Vinaya, followed by citations and explanations.
Regarding the latter three: first, the theft of wind is explained; next, the theft of space is explained; and finally, the theft of consciousness is explained. As for the "artifice," it means...
Regarding the arts and crafts, "cannot be stolen" means that they cannot be physically carried away; however, because their skillful mechanisms can be learned by others, it is said they are "stolen.

[Commentary] Regarding the three types of non-material things, as the established principles above have already clarified, one may consult the *Chao* (Excerpts) for details on the gravity of the offenses.

Furthermore, regarding the establishment of the meaning based on the middle finger: "near" refers to when the conditions for the full offense (*sāmagrī*) are present; "far" refers to when the conditions are lacking or when the object before one is mistaken for another category (*pūrvapada*).
As for the reference to the *Śikṣāsamuccaya-bhāṣya* below, it clarifies that stealing what is not the property of a person—namely, that which has an owner—is considered with respect to that owner.
[Regarding] the *pārājika* offense of harboring expectations toward a non-human without an owner, and the *sthūlātyaya* offense of stealing the property of animals:
those of old claimed these constituted a *pārājika*, but our Master, following the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*, concludes that they are merely *duṣkṛta*.
[Commentary: In this text, the term "locations" (*sthāna*) is used as a general heading to encompass their specific characteristics.

[Commentary] Regarding "in the first bhūmi": fearing that people might not understand where this location is situated, the characteristics are listed here so that one may know the object of the offense and avoid confusion.
As explained in the Vinaya, if there is a hidden treasure beneath the ground that has an owner who guards it, stealing such an object constitutes a grave offense when the value reaches five [units].
Now, according to the Vinaya, if there is a hidden treasure on a Buddha-site or a Sangha-site, it is considered as it emerges from the ground.

The two categories of those belonging to the Buddha and the Sangha likewise have no returning master nor can they be given to a king, as explained in the *Śarīra-vibhāṣā* (or *Vinaya-śarīra*) regarding the precept on seizing precious objects.

Next, concerning the location of the object, the first part of the explanation of the ground initially clarifies the reason for enumerating the characteristics, as follows: [the subsequent] citations and explanations point this out as...

The Sub-commentary (*Chao*) states: "That which is on the ground belongs to the king; that within the ground is not so considered. For instance, even the noble Anāthapiṇḍika took such items [from the ground] without fault;
thus one knows there is no offense. [Commentary (*Shu*)]:
Second, regarding "that which is on the ground," this refers to items obtained from the surface of the earth, as in the present day.

[Commentary: Third, regarding "vehicles" (*yāna*), this refers to vehicles such as elephants and horses. Within the context of these vehicles, if one intends to steal property and separates from the vehicle, the offense is grave;

thus, the vehicle itself constitutes the locus [of the theft]. If one intends to take the property but has no means to separate from the vehicle—whether traveling by it for a hundred or a thousand *li*—one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);

the offense becomes grave only upon separation. If the intent to steal the vehicle is combined with the intent to steal the property, the offense becomes grave at the moment of separating from the vehicle.

If one commits the grave offense of stealing quadrupeds according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it constitutes a grave offense for every step taken toward the designated destination; if the animal does not follow the direction, it is a light offense.

The original intent is indeterminate, but once the full distance is covered, it becomes a grave offense. If the original owner comes to pursue the animal and the thief’s mind has not yet succeeded in acquiring it, it is a light offense.

Riding [a vehicle] is first presented as the object; descending [from it] is then analyzed regarding theft. First, it clarifies that stealing an object while riding involves both the act of riding and the theft of the object;
furthermore, there are two parts: first, the formal judgment regarding the Sangha, and second, citing analogous cases.
[Commentary]: Regarding the four terms, "carrying" (*dāna*) refers to all items belonging to one’s own carrying; its meaning is the same as the previous "riding. These can be divided into two parts.

Within "carrying," there are also distinctions regarding the offense based on whether the stolen object is on the carrying device or is carried along with it; thus, it is said that there are two [categories].

[Commentary]: Regarding the five words "empty" (*śūnya*), the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (or *Vyākhyāyukti*) distinguishes emptiness based on existence; the determination of the offense is as stated above. Now, the present Vinaya clarifies "emptiness" as follows:
when there are items such as clothing or birds that have been blown by the wind, and these belong to an owner, one commits the offense of theft by taking them.
Regarding "leaving the place": when one leaves the empty space of another location, it is called "leaving the place. Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:

"If one steals [a bird] in the air, whether its left wing passes over its right wing, or its tail reaches its head, or moving up and down—[in all such cases] one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If one uses a staff to block it and it does not comply, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one steals a bird that has a master, it is a grave offense; if one steals a bird that has no master, it is a *duṣkṛta*."

Regarding "in space," this initially distinguishes [this system] from other treatises. Because those treatises define space based on the construction of pavilions that encroach upon the space belonging to others, they speak of "discerning space" in relation to what exists.

Now, below, the text provides the formal explanation; first, it clarifies the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Therefore, it cites and demonstrates [the following]: the left wing passing over the right refers to flying horizontally;
the tail reaching the head refers to flying vertically. The terms "above" and "below" are easily understood, for space has no spatial divisions.
Furthermore, by taking the flight and movement of birds as an analogy, one clarifies the characteristic of "separation from its place. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states in full:
"If it is a caged bird belonging to an owner, and the object [the bird] has departed, and a bhikṣu steals that bird's property, it is a *pārājika*.
If it is a wild bird, and the object [the bird] has departed, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, seizes that bird's property, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. This refers to the seizure of a bird.
Since the object of public expectation and the person’s accumulation of demerit should likewise be analyzed by way of emptiness, this is cited here.
[Commentary: "Sixth, 'from the rack' refers to goods and property located on various racks or walls. If one steals them by separating them from the rack, that constitutes the locus of the offense.

As in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one takes clothing but not the rack, or carries away the rack itself, it does not constitute a grave offense unless one subsequently separates the clothing from the rack."

The timing for when the offense becomes grave is also judged as above; the meaning is similar. Therefore, the fact that it is "further specified" (*punar-nirdiṣṭa*) indicates that there is no difference.

When the initial location is shown within the framework [of the rules], if one subsequently analyzes the offense and points out its correspondence below, this means it is the same as the previous dual judgment regarding riding and carrying or separating and joining.
The purpose of clarifying the gravity [of the offense] below is to know that there is no difference; if the characteristics were not further specified, one would not know they are the same.

Therefore, [the commentary] states: "Regarding the term 'village' (grāma) in seven-syllable verses, it refers to designating a village as the location. In the Vinaya, first there is the theft of objects;

subsequently, regarding the substance of the village itself—whether by means of mechanical devices, forceful attack, pouring water, or through verbal persuasion and deception to take it—all such acts are grave offenses."

Regarding the first of the seven types of theft, the Vinaya states: "If there is gold, silver, or the like within a village, and one takes it by pulling or dragging it away, one incurs a *pārājika* offense at the moment it first leaves its place.
Regarding the theft of the village itself, this refers to the aforementioned acts of attacking, drenching with water, or causing damage.
Regarding "forceful means," the Vinaya states: "One takes [the property] by relying on intimacy or physical force. This refers to eloquence in speech.
The term "shuō" (說) means to deceive, entice, or take; its pronunciation is "shuì" (稅).
[Commentary] Regarding the eight types of *araṇya* (阿練若): the two categories of "empty land outside the village" and "within the village" can be understood as being similar to the village.

*Araṇya* is a Sanskrit word translated as "empty place" (空處). The two categories of "within the village" refer to stealing objects and the substance itself; the Vinaya states: [Text follows... [End of Text]
"An empty place contains gold, silver, and so forth," and it is also said, "If one uses skillful means to destroy another's 'emptiness' (boundary-markers) and so on.
[Commentary]: Regarding the ninth, "field boundaries," there are many kinds of fields; any place where the hundred grains grow is collectively termed a "field.

The two types of boundary markers are as explained above regarding villages. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If, for the sake of a field, one says that one has gained the superior [boundary]," it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
If one's victory is not decisive, it is considered light; if one's victory is excessively superior, it is considered heavy. The same applies to monastic dwellings.
One must not speak of the merits or demerits of the case as a nun would when confessing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; one may only state the facts for the magistrate to deliberate.

There is no offense in this, provided one does not speak recklessly. Now, judging by the principle: if the subsequent owner’s intention is firm, then [the property] should belong to oneself; if it is not certain, [it remains with the original owner].
It should not be subject to a double penalty.

Regarding the initial presentation of the names and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within the *Vinaya*, the commentary on the original *Vinaya* states that "two characteristics" refers to the physical substance itself.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* explains that "characteristics" refers to winning a legal case when one has approached the authorities; "winning heavily" means obtaining [the victory] through improper means.
It is not as [some] say; the error in the character is that it should read "not superior" (*asādhika*). If one were to treat it as a distinct characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then [the text] would say:

"If, having already failed to be superior, one further creates a characteristic"—that is, if what is obtained is a site, up to and including five *pūrṇa* [in measure], one incurs the offense of *pārājika* (meaning the taking of a marked site).

Since the determination of a dwelling is based on the measurement of the field, it is said "likewise. It does not mention the lower limit, for the text is incomplete. Furthermore, there are two [parts]: first...

The *Zhunli jue* (Decisions on Analogous Cases) clarifies the rectitude or crookedness of principles regarding whether an offense has been committed or not. In the passage concerning nuns, the character "xiang" (mark/aspect) has been omitted;

it should read "ni-xiang" (the marks of a nun). This is because the text describes the opening of the precepts based on principle. Next, the decision is made according to the meaning, which involves determining the gravity of the offense based on whether the primary intention was fixed or unfixed.
Even if it is on monastic grounds, if the primary intention was previously determined to be one of seizure, it constitutes a grave offense.
[Commentary: Regarding the ten locations, these may be shops, workshops, or other such places, and they are not limited to one kind; furthermore, there are two categories as listed above.

Among the ten, the first indicates the location of the dwelling; since the term "location" (sthāna) applies generally, it is said to be "not uniform. The *Lü* (Vinaya) states: "Whether it be a house or a marketplace."

Furthermore, whether it be fruit orchards, vegetable gardens, or places such as the front of the courtyard or the back of the house, as well as any other locations, the determination of the offense is likewise established as theft;
since the two categories of the substance of the theft are the same as before, they are here briefly indicated.
[Commentary: Regarding the eleventh category, "the place of boats," there are also two divisions. First, when one steals goods from within a boat, the boat itself constitutes the locus.

Second, if one steals the boat's structure itself—as explained in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*—when dismantling a boat or raft, at the moment it is moved, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; even if the ropes have been cut but not yet separated [from the ground], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Only when the ropes are cut and the object has left its original location does it become a grave offense (*pārājika*). According to the *Śrīghanācārya-śāstra*, if one dismantles a boat in flowing water and separates it from its mooring, it is immediately a grave offense.
Eleventh, first a general indication regarding the boat, followed by a detailed explanation. First, it clarifies the theft of goods;

if [the text] below clarifies the theft of a boat, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* explains the sequential characteristics of the limits of cause and effect. The *Sūtra on Good Birth* (*Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*) likewise clarifies the "stake" (栓); "栓" is pronounced as *jùyuè* (巨月) in reverse, meaning a wooden pile or post.
[Commentary]: Regarding the twelfth offense, stealing water: the Vinaya merely clarifies the damage caused but does not specify the exact measure.

As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, for example, regarding irrigation from flowing water, even if the value is as little as one coin for a single night’s use, or if four or five bhikṣus, acting for the sake of the Buddha, the Saṅgha, or themselves, steal and destroy that channel, they incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the water enters the field and the value reaches five [māṣakas], it is a *pārājika*; according to the *Mātṛkā*, it is a *thullaccaya*.
It is said that if one calculates that the work on the dam was excessive and uses more water than allotted, a heavy offense is incurred.

First, to show the general principle of our own school (Mūlasarvāstivāda): within the Vinaya, it simply states that stealing gold, silver, clothing, or fish and turtles from water, as well as destroying another's water source, constitutes an offense—as illustrated by the citations from other schools below—and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* clarifies this point first.
The master calculates the value; if a bhikṣu steals or damages [an object] for the sake of the Buddha, it constitutes an offense even due to other conditions.

According to the *Jiǔshuǐgōulú* (Water Channel Gaṇḍī), there are two meanings that determine the offense: first, calculating the labor of the embankment work; second, exceeding the proper measure of use.
[Commentary]: Thirteen, those who cross passes and barriers privately. [Commentary]:

According to the Vinaya, a bhikṣu is exempt from customs duties, whereas a white-robed layperson should pay duties. Because the bhikṣu carries goods for the latter’s transgression, a heavy penalty is prescribed;

as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu fails to pay duties when they are due, it is likewise a grave offense. Even if not acting out of transgression, if one shows another person a different route [to avoid duties], [it is also an offense].

One commits an offense because one is transporting goods for another that are subject to taxation. As stated in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, carrying forbidden items across a border constitutes a capital offense;
thus, it is called "grave" (*guru*) because it violates the king's edicts and results in a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Furthermore, the *Sātyaka-sūtra* states: "Not paying the king’s tax is not theft.
Additionally, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "All monastics are exempt from taxation, provided they do not engage in buying or selling."
Regarding "people should pay tax":

among the thirteen cases, the first category in the root Vinaya states that monks do not pay tax, meaning that the authorities do not tax the property of monks, yet they [the people] pass goods on for others.
In the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), the first part clarifies "self-taxation," meaning there are territories where taxes are levied upon monks.

Although the objects themselves may be of low value, because they are exempted from taxation for others, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) presents two conflicting views. It states:

"If a country prohibits goods from leaving its borders, bringing them [into such a place] constitutes a capital offense. If a bhikṣu carries them out, the Vinaya masters first say he incurs a grave offense (*guru-apatti*), but later say he does not incur a grave offense;
there is only a *duṣkṛta* (misdeed) for violating the royal decree. Based on this, even if one were to pay the official tax on a bhikṣu’s belongings...
Therefore, those who do not pay taxes obtain only auspiciousness; this resolves the previous passage from the *Daśa-śīla* regarding the gravity of the offense.
The following citation from the scriptural and disciplinary texts further clarifies this. The *Saccaka-nigaṇṭhaputta Sūtra* states: "What things should not be taxed?
The property of the World-Honored One’s disciples—monks and nuns—as well as all renunciants of external paths; these are what is so named."
One should not pay tax on [items] being sold or purchased; rather, the seller should pay it. This is called the "limit of taxation" (*śulka-vibhāga*); "tax" (*kara*) is synonymous with "taxation.

(According to this principle, there is no offense for not paying tax [on items] that are merely personal belongings. However, if one does not pay tax on items for the purpose of making a living, then according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it constitutes a grave offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is the same as above.

[Commentary]: If a monk uses skillful means to exempt himself from official taxes, he does not commit an offense. This is for two reasons: first, it is not a common agreement; second, the tax is levied unreasonably upon me.

Therefore, the preceding text states that monks are subject to no taxation laws. If [exempting oneself] were to constitute an offense, then when bandits come to plunder me and I use skillful means to hide my belongings, I should also commit a grave offense.
However, there are cases where laypeople have their goods taxed by officials, and the monk acts on their behalf...
The hidden [meaning] is as important as the formal rules of the Vinaya.
Next, regarding the middle section, the first part clarifies that there is no offense when no tax is levied; this further divides into three sections: first, defining the meaning through principle;

next, citing the texts for reference, namely the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-śāstra*, and other such works; and finally, citing specific cases by way of counter-questioning. Following this, the second part clarifies the case of acting for the sake of laypeople.
Therefore, for a deliberate offense, it is as prescribed by the Vinaya: the first four *pārājika* offenses.
[Commentary] Next, the substance of the object is explained.

[Commentary] Regarding the initial mention of "taking an object of trust," according to the Vinaya, if an object belonging to another person is held in one's right hand, the gravity of the offense is determined by the point at which the connection with the object is severed.
If one originally holds an object in the left hand with the intent to steal and does not return it, one must first relinquish that intent before moving the right hand;

if one moves it without relinquishing the intent, this is called "repeated stealing. Cases of this kind are similar. Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Ten Recitations) states: "If one borrows another's property and falsely claims not to have borrowed it, one incurs a *pāyattika* for lying.
According to the *Samantapāsādikā*, because it is a preparatory act of theft, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* states: "If one uses [the item] first..."
When the subsequent [offense] has been severed and one has already attained the severance of the prior [offense], one only attains the *pārājika* at the point of departing from the place.
The same applies to receiving goods entrusted by another. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If a bhikṣu takes away a debt he owes another, there is no theft and thus no offense."

Next, regarding objects, the first category of objects of faith refers to items entrusted by others. The previously cited *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* establishes the basis for this with respect to the body;
the text specifies the left and right hands to clarify the characteristics of the offense, and the same applies to other parts of the body. Therefore, one should apply this principle accordingly.
The Vinaya states: "Moving [an object] from the head to the shoulder, from the shoulder to the head, or from the left shoulder to the right shoulder [constitutes an offense]."
Shifting [the burden] from the right shoulder to under the left shoulder refers to the initial section on borrowing among the various schools;

the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* clarifies that lending is a *pāyattika* offense, while the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* establishes it as a *duṣkṛta*, showing their differences. Next, the section below clarifies the grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*).
"First using up" means having already used what was borrowed from another. "Subsequently refusing" means when the owner comes to demand it back, one refuses to return it.

"Refusing to return" means that when one seizes what is rightfully due, because the borrowed object still remains in one's possession, the offense is committed only when there is a separation from its original place;
the same applies to receiving deposits. Furthermore, the characteristics of the offense for resisting and seizing what is rightfully due are identical.

Next, citing the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (Shanjian lü piposha), it states that if a monk, while owing debts to others, takes property belonging to another to repay those debts on their behalf, this does not constitute the act of stealing (*steya*), yet it should still entail an offense.

[Commentary]: Second, regarding the taking of water: according to the Vinaya, if one takes water from a vessel off the ground and steals it, a grave offense (pārājika) is incurred as soon as the vessel is full.
According to the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, if one uses a tube to drink from a hole until it is full, it is a grave offense; if one drinks only slightly, there is a sthūlātyaya for each swallow.

If the vessel was previously sealed and one steals it by pulling out the seal, the water flows into the vessel; if it overflows and becomes full, it is a grave offense; if it has not yet overflowed...

If it is full, one immediately feels regret and fear, and pours it back into the original vessel; although the thūlaccaya offense occurs when the rope is cut, it does not occur if the object has not yet left its place, nor does it occur if the rope has not been cut even though the object has left its place.
The same principle applies to cases involving ghee, oil, honey, and so forth.

Regarding the two cases concerning the *vinaya* rules on vessels containing liquids, the text states: "Whether it be large or small jars, or various other types of water vessels—whether containing scented water or medicinal water—if one takes them, it is a *pārājika* offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* clarifies this further: the first case concerns stealing by drinking through a tube, where the amount is relatively small;
the second case concerns stealing by taking the vessel itself, which, although minor, involves carrying it away along with its contents. The latter serves as an analogy for [stealing] butter.
The oil is judged in the same manner as the three [preceding items].
[Commentary: Regarding the three types of *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks), the meaning is the same as above. As for "whatever is available according to the rules," one speaks of them accordingly.

Regarding the three being the same as above, this is also for the sake of following the rule that constitutes a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) when the theft reaches five *māṣaka*. The Vinaya states: "Whether it be one or two..."
Whether it be many, or a handful, or a shoulder-load, etc.—this passage from the Vinaya provides a general indication of the intent behind the enumeration of characteristics in the Vinaya texts.
It means that the items mentioned before and after are stated according to what actually exists, and do not limit the number to only these specific quantities.
[Commentary: Regarding the fourth point, the fruits, trees, and grasses of the gardens, these have been extensively cited above in the *Chao* (Excerpts) section on the property of the Saṃgha.

Of these four categories, the first refers back to the aforementioned "permanently fixed property of the permanently fixed" (*changzhu changzhuyong*). Furthermore, it refers back to the *Chao* regarding the precept against stealing;

therein, it quotes the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, which states that one who steals the property of the Saṃgha commits a sin equal to the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), and that even the theft of a single hair’s breadth [of such property] constitutes this offense.
One should contemplate the offenses incurred by each of the ordinary and holy beings throughout the ten directions; furthermore, the Vaipulya sutras state:

"I can even save those who commit the five heinous crimes or the four grave offenses, but I cannot save those who steal the property of the Sangha. One should also consult the various Vinayas extensively cited therein to examine what is permitted and what is prohibited regarding its use.
[Commentary: Regarding fruit trees in monastic gardens, many bhikṣus commit offenses; yet they do not consider themselves at fault, thinking, "This is within my own monastery.
However, those who establish a monastery do so because it is intended for monks who embody the absence of self (*anātman*), and whatever offerings are made there are for the sake of liberation.
Now, failing to reflect on this, they take property belonging to the community of others to protect their own interests. This is a grave offense, as in the case of Saṃgharakṣita.
Within the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta*, this section is particularly terrifying; therefore, one must contemplate it deeply.

In the first part of the following section, the initial passage describes the joy of committing offenses, while the subsequent part reveals the gravity of the karma. First, the fundamental purpose of establishing monasteries is clarified;
next, the circumstances of theft are explained. As instructed below, one should reflect upon the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*, for its causes are as follows.

The *Sheshan* (捨遊) states that while traveling along the seashore, he saw more than fifty locations of hells, most of which were places where those who had misappropriated monastic property were currently undergoing retribution for their suffering.
The *Rizang jing* (日藏經), a Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtra, records the Buddha’s discourse to the Bodhisattva Rizang regarding various matters such as the suffering endured by those who violate the precepts.
The *Chao* (鈔) states: "An individual may use monastic firewood or grass. This refers to...
One who wishes to possess pure precepts and accord with the Dharma of the Saṃgha will incur immeasurable offense if their practice is even slightly deficient.

[Commentary]: As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, regarding the planting of fruit upon monastic grounds, if one has performed labor, it is permitted to give one portion of the ripened fruit; this applies by analogy to vegetables and melons, where one may give one "cutting.
However, if one shakes a tree in the garden and the fruit falls to the ground, one must wait until they have been gathered before taking them again. This applies even when within the garden itself.

Regarding those who have eaten their fill: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is a grave offense [to take more]. Flowers from trees in the monastery garden may be used for making offerings to the Buddha;

large timber may be used for the Sangha; bark and leaves may be used according to the needs of the bhikṣus. Wood from trees within the *Saṃghika* (monastery) compound may be used as fuel for the Sangha’s meals; if there is no fixed limit, one should take only dry wood.

Among the three types of *saṃghika* (monastic property), the first clarifies the rewarding of merit: "one ripening" refers to a single cycle of ripening; for this, one may take a portion, which is also based on a single cycle of harvesting.

Next, the second clarifies the theft of fruit: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if flowers from a tree belonging to the Saṃgha are used by the Saṃgha to make offerings to the Buddha, it does not constitute mutual misappropriation.
However, regarding the bark, leaves, and firewood from trees belonging to the Saṃgha, these are all permitted to be taken and used by individuals, as established by precedent.
The preceding section clarified that it is essential for the precepts to be pure.
[Commentary] Regarding the "five types of unsatisfied beings," the Vinaya lists snakes and fish as the first; because these have owners who steal them, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If one steals a dragon, a snake, or the like, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*). However, if one speaks with anger and abuse, saying 'Why are you caging and binding this? and then immediately releases it, there is no offense."

If one bypasses the five [factors] or destroys the implements for killing, there is no offense; however, one should not act in such a way. In the *Śaikṣa* section of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it states that destroying a net with a compassionate heart constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
In the text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, after first listing snakes and fish, it continues by saying "and other legless sentient beings," which is why it is stated [as follows].
In the first section of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the taking of what belongs to others by theft is first clarified; it states that "those without feet" refers to snakes and pythons.
If a bhikṣu steals a snake, or a basket full of them, all five cases constitute a grave offense (*pārājika*). The present text’s mention of "dragons" (*nāga*) is likely a textual error.

Furthermore, the subsequent section clarifies the release [of captured animals]; it cites the Vinaya and Śāstras to show that destroying their equipment constitutes only a light offense, as it does not constitute theft.
[Commentary: Regarding "six-footed beings," those with two legs are primary, beginning with humans.
Regarding "beings among humans," the Vinaya states that among humans, non-humans, birds, and other two-legged sentient beings, stealing those who have an owner constitutes a grave offense.

[Commentary: According to the Vinaya, one may cause a thief to leave the household life as explained above; since he is not a slave, he does not belong to anyone else, even though this violates the royal decree, as stated in the aforementioned *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Stealing from one's own household becomes a grave offense at the first light of dawn; this is as explained above regarding the determination of gravity based on the existence of an owner.

Having thus established the gravity of the offense, the text now distinguishes lighter cases: because servants and the like cause harm to their master, the offense is grave; for others who cause no such harm, it can only be classified as a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

Therefore, it refers to the treatise (*śāstra*), which states that those crossing a pass [with stolen goods] and so forth are not guilty; the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* also says that a person stealing from their own master incurs no guilt.
"If a child has run away and is taken by those sent by his parents, there is no offense; this is what is meant. [The Commentary] explains:

If another person's son is forcibly abducted by thieves and taken away, thereby damaging the parents' reliance on and utilization of their physical support (*upabhoga*), the child belongs to the thieves through force.

One may not instruct him to flee; however, if he comes running back of his own accord, he does not owe anything to the thieves. Thus, it is stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) regarding thieves: [text follows].

If a teacher seizes a disciple and takes him away, and the disciple subsequently recovers him, it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). If the thief has not yet reached a definitive decision [to steal], there is no offense.

If the disciple comes back of his own accord after having been stolen, there is no offense. As explained in the past: if the teacher cannot recover the person’s body and the person escapes on their own, or if the parents, moved by the child's strength, cause a thief to seize them, the gravity of the offense depends on whether the teacher was strong and the thief weak, or if the teacher was weak and recovered the thief; thus it is grave.
The child’s report states that the true nature is the strong thief; when it is employed, the weak flees. This is the sign of the strong pursuing the weak, which follows along without transgression.

Among the three [cases] of being robbed by thieves, the first is judged according to principle. The preceding clarifies that if the robbery is completed, it constitutes a grave offense; this refers to what was taken from one's parents.
Relying on the provisional [classification], because the place where the force and function are damaged is grave, it is categorized as a "robbery" (caura);

because one does not descend to instruct a bhikṣu regarding the protection against theft, and because one runs away, it constitutes a grave offense due to the damage caused to the robber. Coming of one's own accord is without fault, as it is not intentional.

Therefore, the subsequent citation of evidence can be seen as follows; the initial citation of the ancient interpretation first restates the two previous judgments regarding the father, and below that, it explains what was previously stated.
First, it clarifies that when the master commits a grave offense, the child does not incur guilt; next, it clarifies that there is no offense for one who comes of their own accord.

Regarding the strong person, they are reported as such because their own body belongs to themselves and is not subject to another; the weak person is so reported because they are neither a biological relative nor an employer.
As for the mutual pursuit of strong and weak retribution, the strong follows its own will, whereas the weak is used according to whatever comes before them, for the thief has no choice.

[This is] because it is divided [into categories]. [The *Shu* (Commentary) states: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "If one sees the speech of another’s male or female slave and says, 'Why do you not run away?'—if one speaks such words, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong speech).

If one lifts one foot, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one lifts two feet, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If the slave has already fled, and one urges them to go faster, one incurs a heavy offense according to the words spoken."
Some say that if there is scarcity here and abundance there, and a slave immediately flees, it is not an offense because he was not instructed [to leave].

Or, if one asks whether it is an offense if a bhikṣu leaves a prosperous and joyful place, the answer is that it is not an offense if he is driven out by an official, or if he runs away when encountering difficulties and calling out for help.
Among the three [sections] and four [sub-sections], the first two teach that running constitutes a grave offense, while the latter two do not teach it and thus there is no violation.

First, "if one entices" clarifies the act of luring; next, "if one urges them to go swiftly" clarifies the act of hastening. Alternatively, the phrase "the third" refers to the bhikṣu speaking to the other person;
"or if he asks" refers to the fourth, based on that person questioning the bhikṣu.
[Commentary]: Regarding the seven categories of four-footed and many-footed animals, these are discussed in the Vinaya in relation to domesticated livestock;

they may also be understood by analogy with the above. Among these seven, the Vinaya states that elephants, horses, oxen, camels, donkeys, deer, sheep, and other four-footed or many-footed creatures—such as bees or centipedes and other many-footed beings—are all considered grave offenses if they have an owner.
Therefore, let it be governed by the above.
[Commentary] "Co-owners of property" refers to those who violate their formal agreement; this is cited here. Based on this co-ownership, its manifestations are manifold:
for instance, sharing the means of livelihood, such as when a teacher and disciple live together. If one takes five [units], one commits an offense without needing to wait for half.

Because they have been completely deceived regarding shared wealth, or because they were living together and jointly managing their livelihood and business—if one should conceive the intent to steal, it must be calculated according to the full value;
since ten parts constitute a grave offense, five parts are my share, and five parts are the deception of the other.
Regarding the first section within the distinctions of shared commitments (*samayika*): it first demonstrates the underlying intent of the offense.
Although there is no offense regarding the common property or activities themselves, because violating the commitment constitutes the sense of theft, this is cited here. The Vinaya states:

"When one obtains wealth through joint activities, it should be shared" (this is the essential agreement). To take five *kārṣāpaṇas* or more with a thieving mind constitutes a grave offense (that is, the violation of the commitment).
The following section distinguishes the characteristics of offenses. The first two phrases provide a general heading, while the subsequent portion provides a detailed explanation.

First, it clarifies "shared livelihood" (*sādhāraṇa-jīvikā*): this refers to cases where both parties possess wealth without any distinction between them; thus, taking five items constitutes a grave offense. Next, it clarifies "shared livelihood through labor" (*sahajīvika*):

this refers to cases where they jointly conduct business and the resulting wealth is divided equally; thus, taking ten items constitutes a grave offense (the term *sahajīvika* may alternatively be a scribal error for *sādhāraṇa-jīvikā*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "mutual agreement," "agreement" (yào) refers to the "requirement" (yāo) among the two [factors]. [Commentary]:

[Commentary] The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "When making appointments to go together at specific times—whether before noon, at noon, or after noon;

today, tomorrow, this year, or next year—if the mutual agreement is not broken, that which is more serious is equivalent to a formal undertaking (*samādāna*), while that which is less so is considered light."

Among the three [categories], *Sudṛśa* (Good Vision) is superior. The upper section clarifies the essential points, while the lower section indicates the characteristics of transgressions. Regarding "correspondence of time," the treatise states: "If the timing corresponds, one incurs the offense together with the instruction;
it is not as light as [the case where] he does not follow the instruction. This means: if one takes [an object] in the middle or later when instructed to take it earlier;

or if one takes it in the latter part of the night when instructed to take it during the first watch; or if one takes it during the dark fortnight when instructed to take it during the bright fortnight.

Regarding the taking of a month and then the taking of a year: if one instructs another to take [the property] after a year has passed, it is a minor offense (sthūlātyaya); if one takes it oneself, it is a pārājika offense.

This is stated with reference to a specific, fixed time; however, if the original intent was general and indefinite regarding the date, the offense becomes grave (pārājika) according to the violation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the term "waiting in ambush" (*sìhòu*): it refers to plotting for the convenience of obtaining wealth by spying on the location and agreeing to advance together; even if one does not obtain the wealth, because they must share it, if they do obtain it, failing to share it constitutes an offense as well.
Even if one does obtain it, failing to share it constitutes an offense. Furthermore, even if one obtains it, failing to share it while acting as a lookout also constitutes an offense.
Among the three [categories], the first concerns the offense of "conspiring" (chàn, pronounced chàn; the character is read as yàn in this context) to spy upon or look into [a place].

The Vinaya states: "If I go to observe that village, city, town, ferry crossing, mountain valley, or inhabited place, and obtain anything there, taking it all together constitutes a grave offense (heinous theft), etc.
Regarding the subsequent section on the offense of "receiving instructions," although one does not share in the division of the goods, [the offense is established].
Regarding the precept against stealing, because both the teacher and the student share equal responsibility for its observance, it is said that "one also commits an offense.
[The Commentary] states: "To 'guard' means to take charge of and record its location, seeking it out until it is found, at which point one shares it with others; this is what is meant here.
If one previously did not consent to it but merely guarded it, since there was no shared intention, in principle there is no offense."

Among these four, the first clarifies the offense of common theft; the Vinaya states: "If one obtains wealth from outside, thinking 'I shall guard it,' yet whatever is obtained is entirely held in common, [there is no offense].
The following section clarifies that which is not common, which constitutes no offense.

[Commentary]: Regarding the term "watching the road" (*lùdào*): it refers to looking out for whether the path is passable or obstructed, guarding against outsiders, and sharing whatever wealth is obtained.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when two people commit a theft together—one guarding the gate and one entering to take the goods—they all incur a *pārājika* offense upon their release; they all incur a *thullaccaya* upon their entry;
and they all incur a *saṅghādisesa* upon their departure.

Among the five [types of travelers], the *luó* (pronounced *láng-zuǒ*) are those who patrol and guard the roads. In the Vinaya, they are sometimes referred to as "those who watch the road" (*kàn dào*).

Initially, when indicating the common rules regarding offenses, it is said that if there are no people, one should raise suspicion; if there is an obstruction, the opposite applies. The Vinaya states: "I shall watch the road.
If a royal army arrives, or a bandit army arrives, or an army of elders arrives, you must inform one another. If there is... [text ends]... 若 (ruò).
"All that which has been obtained is common to these" [is the principle]. Below, one can understand through the cited texts that the offenses are identical;

it must not be the case that they act with mutual consent for the purpose of guarding [the property], as explained above. Of the five types mentioned above, the first two apply generally to thieves who mutually disagree [regarding ownership], while the latter three concern only whether those who steal together share or do not share [ownership].
[Vinaya]: "Not given. [Commentary]:
The text states "not given" to clarify that the master’s failure to relinquish his mind constitutes my theft through private appropriation.
Regarding the third phrase, the commentary explains: "mind's private appropriation" means considering [the object] as one's own independent possession; "private" means not giving it to others.
