Regarding the establishment of the categories (*padārtha*): if one expects to protect the owner, it constitutes a grave offense; this is theft of five [measures].
In the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, the initial establishment of the principle is as shown below: "The mutual instruction of four people refers to different times.
If they stop at the same time, one person may be the instructor and three the instructed. If the instructor takes one [measure], that is the theft of one."

Regarding the principle of constituting a grave offense: when one commits it oneself, the action is established through one's own karma; when one instructs another, the fruit is achieved through an external condition.
Because these two types of karma have distinct conditions, they do not merge.

[Vinaya]: If one is seized by a king (who possesses sovereign power and does not belong to others) or by a royal minister (one of the various ministers who assist the king), and is either killed or bound.
"If you are driven out of the country, you are a thief; you are deluded; you know nothing"—this is a *pārājika* offense for a bhikṣu.
[Commentary] In this text, the passage beginning with "If for the sake of the king" describes the seven forms of punitive treatment for thieves and the verbal abuse used to rebuke them.
The fourth phrase can be understood by examining the text within the heading.

[Commentary: The reason for listing this is that it seeks to clarify how theft brings harm to both monastics and laypeople alike; since nothing surpasses this in its capacity to diminish benevolence and thin the bonds of righteousness, these characteristics are listed here to serve as a warning against future transgressions.

This clarifies the first phrase of the central section, which poses a question; following this, the subsequent citations provide an explanation. First, it is addressed by way of admonition, and subsequently, "corruption" (*biè*) is explained.
Because all possess these evils, they are said to be "equally corrupt. "Neglecting benevolence" (*qīng rén*) means having no heart for providing relief or kindness;
"thinning righteousness" (*bó yì*) means taking what is not right. *Chéng* (懲) is pronounced *chéng* and means "to warn" or "to admonish."
[Commentary] Furthermore, some explain it thus: regarding the four grave offenses (ānantarya) of the first category, the remaining three involve no great transgression when committed by oneself;
yet even for stealing the King’s timber—which is openly known as theft—one cannot escape punishment. How much less so for ordinary commoners? Thus, the meaning is clear:
he cites the noble to illustrate the lowly, and the difficult to illustrate the easy.

The subsequent section explains the gravity of the offense by means of illustration; since there is no greater offense than that against a king, and no greater offense regarding royal property, it cites these extremes to illustrate the rest. [Commentary]:
Regarding the four phases of seizing and killing, the sequence of the text is disordered. To rectify this, one should state them as: seizing, binding, driving away, and killing.

In the first section of the commentary on the text, the treatment of the second offense—killing—is placed out of sequence; logically, it ought to be listed later for the purpose of establishing the correct order.
[Commentary]:
Regarding the term "seizing," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that King Bimbisāra’s distant ancestor, when dealing with criminals, merely ordered the Caṇḍālas to...

Striking his head and grasping [the thief’s] hand, he felt immediate shame and never again committed theft. As for what is called "binding," because the world is turbid and human sentiments are lax, even though one has been caught, the person still acts as before;
therefore, in a place where many people gather, the King’s ancestors sent men to surround him with ashes.

When it came to his father’s time, this practice of surrounding him with ashes ceased, and instead the method of expulsion was employed. This continued until King Bimbisāra ascended the throne, at which point the practice of expulsion was repeated seven times, after which they returned.

When he entered [the palace] to steal, he cut off one of his fingers; his grief and remorse were boundless. The Buddha explained to the king that in the past, for the sake of supporting a thousand fools, he had committed such acts, which led to his current state where he must now carry out slaughter at the hands of Ajātaśatru.
In the explanation of the four characteristics, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi) text is cited throughout: "Caṇḍāla" is translated here as "killer" or "one of base character";
"surrounding with ash" is equivalent to "binding. Furthermore, the explanation of the third [characteristic], "driving out," resembles the modern practice of banishment.
Finally, regarding the fourth, "seven times returning," that text states: "At one time there was a thief who, having been driven out seven times, returned again."
During a time when villages and cities were being plundered, there was a man who was seized and bound to be presented to the king, who requested that he be punished with torture.
The king ordered his little finger to be cut off. The man immediately felt remorse and thought, "As a ruler, one should cherish and care for the people and their possessions;
how can a king injure and cut off another's finger? He went at once to question the Buddha. The Buddha said, "In a past age, there was a city..."
There was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī, belonging to the Kāśī people, whose king was named Mahendrasena.
The citizens all made their living through various crafts and skills; those who lacked such skills or were thieves were all designated as "fools.
At that time, some thieves were brought before the king, who said, "For the first time there has been a fool; if the number reaches a thousand, I shall hold a great assembly."
While he was still suffering under their punishment, the king commanded his ministers to grant him the kingdom of Aśoka and provide him with the pleasures of the five senses.

Later, when the fool heard that the king had bestowed these pleasures upon him, he soon gathered a full thousand followers and reported this to the king. The king then provided them with food and bestowed treasures upon them, commanding the fools, saying:
"Return to your homes, support your parents, diligently attend to your household affairs, and do not commit robbery again."

At that time, having heard the command, the foolish man received it and respectfully carried it out. The King then bestowed the throne upon the crown prince and entered the mountains to study the methods of the *ṛṣis*, speaking these verses:
"Originally I sought a thousand fools to hold this assembly, thinking them difficult to find;
how is it that before long, the number of thousands has suddenly been reached? Evil dharmas increase day and night; the great assembly must now cease, for I wish to depart."
"In this degenerate age, it is fitting that people should leave the household life at the proper time.

The Buddha said, "O Bhikṣus, at that time King Bimbisāra was one who, from previous lives until now, has always feared the retribution for sin; even now that he is king, he continues to fear sin, and thus he gave rise to doubts and questioned the Buddha.
According to the five principles [of karmic retribution], since his finger has already been cut off, he ought to return home and wait for his execution later."

[Commentary] Question: As stated in the section on the conditions for the precepts, if one steals five coins, the offense should be punishable by death; why then does the text point instead to subsequent killing? Answer:

When the amount reaches five coins, death was prescribed according to ancient law. However, when the King wished to mitigate punishments, he reduced the penalty from death to exile, as is the case today in this country.
Where the theft reaches the full amount and would normally incur strangulation, because the administration is lax and the penal code is lenient, the punishment is reduced to forced labor.
The intent of the question is that since there are four remedies (*pratipakṣa*), it is inconsistent to single out only the last one as the condition for violating the precepts (*śīla*).

In the response, the first two phrases explain the condition for violating the precepts by clarifying "the King of Death," while the subsequent passage demonstrates the listing of the four remedies in the text.
[Commentary: The remaining three abusive expressions and the subsequent text on the determination of the offense are easy to understand.
"The first phrase among the others" refers to the current phrase, while "the latter two phrases" refers to those that follow.
[Note] If a bhikṣu obtains goods from any of the aforementioned locations and the value of the theft is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*;
if he employs the means of theft but the value is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If he fails to obtain them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he instructs another to steal and that person obtains the goods, both are *pārājika*. If the one who received the instruction takes other goods himself...

If one takes an object from another location, the taker commits a grave offense (pārājika), while the instructor commits a serious offense (sthūlātyaya). If one instructs another to take an object without the intent to steal, the instructor commits a pārājika offense, whereas the person who receives the instruction is not guilty.
If one instructs a person to take an object by saying "send someone to steal it," the person who receives the instruction commits a grave offense, while the instructor is not guilty.
If there is the perception that the object has an owner, one commits a grave offense; if there is doubt, one commits a serious offense; if it is an ownerless object, there is no offense.
Regarding the offense of *sthūlātyaya* arising from the perception or suspicion that an object has an owner:

for the four assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs and others, as with the aforementioned precepts, there is no offense in cases involving the perception that it is one's own property, the perception that it is refuse, the perception of taking it temporarily, or the perception of a close friendship.

[Commentary: Regarding the analysis of the characteristics of offenses and non-offenses within the *Zhù* (Commentary), the characteristics of offenses for the five groups of practitioners (*pañca-varga*) are divided into sections according to the upper and lower parts [of the text] and are not further subdivided;
they are explained directly according to their characteristics.

Within the first section of this analysis of characteristics, one should first divide it into two: namely, offenses and non-offenses. Within the category of offenses, there are again two: namely, [the offense itself and its] comparison...

The Buddha and the rest of the bhikṣus further divided this into two initial sections: first, one’s own action, and second, instructing another. Within the section on one’s own action, there are again two parts:

the first clarifies the gravity of the offense when the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is completed, while the latter clarifies the lightness of the offense when it is not; these are contrasted in this manner. Within the section on instructing another, there are likewise two parts: the first clarifies the gravity of the offense when the preparatory effort is completed, while the latter clarifies the lightness of the offense when it is not; these are contrasted in this manner. Regarding the case where the object is of inferior status, there are again two parts: the first clarifies the gravity of the offense when the preparatory effort is completed, while the latter clarifies the lightness of the offense when it is not; these are contrasted in this manner. Finally, regarding the case where the perception of the object is mistaken, there are again two parts: the first clarifies the gravity of the offense when the preparatory effort is completed, while the latter clarifies the lightness of the offense when it is not; these are contrasted in this manner. Thus, they are contrasted accordingly.
[Commentary] The first section clarifies the characteristics of the gravity and lightness of actions committed by oneself.

Within self-commissioned acts, "heavy" refers to cases where the amount reaches five *kārṣāpaṇas* or more at the point of completion; "light" refers to the characteristics of preparatory effort (*prayoga*) involving less than five, and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the persons who receive the teaching, this is divided into two parts: first, the correspondence between the initial intention and the object, which constitutes the same offense;

second, the distinction between heavy and light offenses based on the difference in the location of the objects. If one receives the teaching and takes another's property, this is further divided into two: the first two phrases concern the presence of the intent to steal, where the objects are identical but their locations differ, hence the distinction between heavy and light;
the latter two phrases concern the taking of the object, where the intent is the same but its presence or absence differs, hence the distinction between guilt and innocence.

Next, in explaining the section on instructing others to take [things], the first two phrases constitute taking a different object oneself as the first case, and taking an object from a different location as the second.
The latter two phrases consist of taking an object for another starting from "if one takes for the sake of...
as the first case, and instructing another person to take an object as the second case.

[Commentary: Regarding the first case, where one receives the instruction and takes another's property for oneself, the agent is the same but the object is different. In the latter phrase, the agent is different but the object is the same.

Since the act of taking [the object] once it has left the ground is precisely what was instructed, the primary offense is incurred; however, because the instructor’s intent diverged from the actual state of affairs, only the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) of the fundamental offense is formally concluded.
In the commentary, the first section divides the preceding phrases to demonstrate the gravity or lightness of the offense. [The Sub-commentary] states:

Regarding the presence or absence of intention in the subsequent parties, first, if the instructor possesses the intention while the instructed person lacks it, when the object is obtained, one must take half;
this is because the original agreement was to share the proceeds of the acquisition. As for the latter case, if the instructed person also possesses the intention, it is likewise required.

Although it was my own garment that was divided into two halves, because I perceived it as belonging to another when taking it according to his instructions, the conditions for theft were fulfilled and thus an offense was committed.
How could it not be divided? If he does not give it back, the thief will seize it again; the logic of the thief is evident here.
Next, regarding the previous commentary on the first phrase, the character "teaching" (jiao) is missing the character "to" (zhe); one must divide it in half.

That which is taught must necessarily be given by the one who teaches, as there was originally no intention to withhold it, and thus no transgression occurs. The subsequent phrase is also divided in half:
whether this [gift] must be given or not constitutes a further grave offense of theft. Regarding the thought of another's property, it is based on that person's intent.
This means that because one intends to take [the object], even if one mistakenly receives one's own property, it must still be divided and given away, as in the aforementioned *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

[Commentary] Regarding the categories of perception concerning the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), the Vinaya text fully enumerates both the light and heavy degrees; however, as this commentary is abbreviated, it cites only the heavy cases.
Regarding the "perception of the object" (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*) within the classification of light and heavy offenses, the *Vinaya*’s precept on stealing contains two types of heavy cases.

First, when the value is full five [units], there are four permutations as cited in the commentary; second, when it is less than five, the four permutations are identical, except that the first permutation results in a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), while the remaining three are all *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

[Commentary: One might expect five categories, including the case where there is a sense of ownership regarding what is ownerless; however, this is not set forth because it would lead to confusion. To clarify how the nature of such confusion arises:
if one is entirely without intention from beginning to end, it cannot be considered training in the precepts, as it is due to delusion and thus not subsumed under an offense.

If the perception changes before and after the act, the subsequent state is not an offense; yet, if one were to claim that the prior intentional act was "ownerless" and thus non-offensive, this would confuse the case of a change in perception with the absence of intent.
If one says that "stūlan" (thou-lan) is confused with the original [term], it is because they are taken together and do not appear in the subsequent examples;

this can serve as a general mirror for understanding. In the next section, which demonstrates the reason, the first part presents the heading and raises the question regarding the confusion of meanings; the subsequent part applies the meaning to provide a resolution for the initial sentence.

This provides a brief indication of the characteristics of confusion; the following sections provide a detailed explanation. First, there is a double interrogation; next, the characteristics are shown.

Previously, two types of mind were listed to determine whether an offense is committed. Next, the two types of confusion are described to clarify that they cannot be distinguished. Finally, the examples are pointed out:
this is because all four permutations within the category of "perception regarding the object" (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) are identical to this case.
[Commentary] Question: Since these [subsequent precepts] are obscured due to being confused with the former, why is it that the subsequent precepts are able to fully enumerate the five points?

In the initial objection, the subsequent precept—the precept against killing in the Vinaya—already lists all five phrases; this too would involve confusion, and thus it would be improper to list them.

[Commentary] Answer: Offenses differ based on whether they have a specific object (*sālambana*) or lack one (*anālambana*). Because one perceives something as having no owner, it is considered equivalent to refuse-rags (*pāṃśukūla*);

thus, although the objects of perception—whether conceived as a human or a non-human—are heavy or light, they are identical in that they constitute the conditions for generating an offense. This is why such offenses exist. They arise because they are governed by the same restrictive rules regarding the conditions that generate an offense.

In the response, the initial section provides a general answer regarding conditions (*pratyaya*), stating that the preceding objects constitute the conditions for committing an offense; this is followed by a specific explanation.
First, the precept against stealing is explained as having no such conditions, while the precept against killing is explained as having conditions.
[Commentary] Question: If this is the case, then the perception that there was no formal authorization when there actually was one would not be a condition for the arising of an offense;

why then are five factors enumerated? Furthermore, in the subsequent objection, while the factor of formal authorization is established as an offenseless condition, the listing of five propositions contradicts the previous principle.

[Commentary] The answer is: Because both the action (*vastu*) and the dharma (*dharma*) can be learned, although there is intentional activity (*abhisamskāra*) and an instruction (*avijñapti*) upon which one may rely, there is no room for confusion or forgetfulness;

even if one were confused, since it is not a matter of learning, the offense is not established. Furthermore, because the action is difficult to commit, there is a possibility of a major transgression; therefore, it is listed as the third [category].
In the response, the first part describes matters that may be practiced without error: namely, transgressive acts (*atikrama-dharma*) and disciplinary measures (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

Since each has its own established regulations regarding what is permitted by the teachings, there is no room for confusion or negligence. Next, it clarifies those matters that may not be practiced, explaining the reason why:

because there are formal teachings, and a deluded mind is not easily corrected; thus, it is said that such matters are difficult to handle. However, if one acts out of forgetfulness due to delusion, there is no offense.
However, because there is the possibility of erroneously relying [on such a pretext] and thereby committing a root offense, it is said that "there is the possibility of a grave offense.

[Commentary] Question: If this is the explanation, then regarding the Vinaya rules where one perceives what is not ground as ground, or perceives what is not dusk as dusk—these are also cases of confusion and are not considered training offenses.
Why, then, are they listed [among the grave offenses]?

Among the three difficulties, digging the earth and the setting of the sun both constitute delusions of mind regarding specific matters; there is no offense [in the former], and it should consist of only four propositions rather than five.

[Commentary] The answer is that, similarly, by means of a transformed perception (*vikalpa*), one incurs the offense of the preceding mind, as explained previously in the section on the mutual relationship of the four and five propositions regarding the perception of objects.

In the response, the phrase "the same applies" refers to both of the preceding two cases, as they share this same principle; since this has already been explained under the section on sexual misconduct, it is referred back as "as before.
[Commentary] Question: What is meant by "ownerless property"? Answer: As cited in full in the *Chao*, one should read and understand it as being consistent with the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*.
A son who hates his father and flees after being driven out is like one who, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, abandons an object when it is lost; such an object is considered ownerless.
As the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If one takes [an object] with the intention that it is full [of value], one commits an offense."

Regarding the clarification of "that which has no master," first is the question and next is the answer. The first two lines refer extensively to that [passage], citing the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (Shanjian wen), which is the same as the following citation;

it further cites the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Duolun). When the kingdom between two countries is destroyed and the king flees, and a successor has not yet been established, it is all termed "having no master.
This can be understood from the brief indication of the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* below; however, if one discusses this region [of China], the government officials constitute the master.

Regarding the principle that one may take [an item] once it has been relinquished by the *saṃgha*, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* cites this to demonstrate that while one is not the owner, because the item still belongs to another, taking it constitutes an offense.
It states: "If one has already relinquished it with the intention [to give], even if it is one's own property, one must not take it;
however, if it does not belong to another, there is no fault in taking it."
[Commentary] Regarding the section on non-offenses:
[Commentary] As for "taking with the perception of another's," it means that although it is actually another's property, one intends that it belongs to oneself; therefore, there is no offense.

As for "the perception of one's own property," it means that although it is actually another's property, one intends it to be one's own property and lacks the perception of it being another's. As for "the perception of refuse," it is actually...

This refers to the section concerning "having an owner" within the thought-pattern of "opening up" an object that is actually without an owner; it is the first phrase among those regarding the perception of an owner.

To say "taking temporarily" means that since it is not for permanent use, one takes it on loan; this permits the aforementioned case where an owner has not relinquished it, whereas "not taking temporarily" does not.

Regarding the "intention of a kinsman," it is said: "If the heart is like lutes and cymbals, what difference is there in wealth? In antiquity, when eating, one necessarily shared with others, and the same applied to clothing."

The principle of wearing worn-out robes and accepting food from two people applies to the term "friend" (*mitra*) as well. Because they possess genuine affection, it is permitted for them to be superior to non-sentient companions.

As stated in the *Vinaya*’s Seven Dharmas, those who can act as friends are those who are able to do what is difficult to do, give what is difficult to give, endure what is difficult to endure, and who disclose secret matters to one another and conceal each other’s faults;
who do not abandon one in times of suffering and do not despise one in poverty or low status—this is what is meant.
Regarding the five non-offenses, the first three clarify the exemptions based on the mind, while the latter two clarify the exemptions based on the matter.

Within these three, the first phrase concerning the perception of the object refers to taking the preceding "not given" and pairing it with the following three "non-[offenses]"; these three constitute the exemptions.
Regarding the first of the five, explained according to worldly convention: "lute and zither" is a metaphor for being harmonious and not discordant; this also applies to food.
"Person" (ren) refers to those who eat together; "clothing" (yi) refers generally to those who wear together. The character for "clothing" (衣) consists of two people;
according to its seal-script form (zhuanti), it was originally written as "zhong" (衆). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it represents the shape of two people covered [by a garment].

The character for "food" (shi) was originally composed of "ji" (音集) and "zao" (音急); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the subsequent "ji" represents the shape of three things joined together, and "zao" refers to grain.
The *Xiang* (Fragrance) [commentary] now takes the meaning of the upper three [stages] being combined; thus it says, "it is also like this.

As will be explained below when citing the Vinaya, these seven dharmas must first accord with one another before one enters the stage of opening (*kaishi*). Of these, the first three difficult matters can constitute four [stages]: (1) cutting and chipping (*qiecuo*), and (2) carving and polishing (*zhuomo*);
(3) the fifth refers to concealing faults and extolling virtues; the final two preserve the beginning and the end.
[Vinaya] Not living together (the meaning is as explained above).

[Commentary] Regarding this precept, many people secretly violate it without realizing it is a grave offense, considering it merely a matter of negligence. Although the *Chao* and *Shu* commentaries are extensive, I fear that some may still not understand;
therefore, one should use this as a model to deliberate upon the characteristics of the offenses. Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Within the precepts, one should follow..."
One must urgently protect this second precept; as its specific characteristics are difficult to understand, there is no choice but to provide a detailed and analytical explanation of its meaning.
You should carefully contemplate the treatise; otherwise, how could you possibly avoid transgression when faced with actual circumstances?
In the initial section of the concluding exhortation, the reason for the frequency of transgressions is set forth; the commentary below points to the author’s own composition to encourage practice.
Thus, the following citation from the treatise urges study: after citing the treatise, the final two phrases point to that specific passage to provide encouragement.
Commentary on the *Sifenlü hanzhu jieben* (The Four-Part Vinaya with Annotated Precept Manual) by Xingzong, Part II, Upper, Section 3–4; Part II, Lower, Section 1 [Vinaya]:
The Three Major Precepts on Killing.
[Commentary] The third major precept: the explanation of the precept against killing.

[Commentary] The Sūtra clarifies that among the offenses of intrinsic gravity (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), this precept is most frequently placed first; is this not because the body is the precursor to karma, and thus the karma of killing?

This is because it is based on the primary factor (the object). Regarding what is called "grave by nature," this means that the nature itself encompasses both the grave and the light. When grave, it pertains to the human realm;
when light, it pertains to non-human animals. Since the mind is differentiated according to the object, the offenses are ranked into three levels.
In clarifying the gravity of offenses, first we demonstrate the differences between the *sūtras* and the *vinaya* to show that the transgression is particularly grave.

The *sūtras* clarify that among the ten courses of action (*daśa-karmapatha*), killing is listed first; likewise, among the ten heavy precepts of the Bodhisattva *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, it is also so. What is the meaning of this? The answer is:

the teachings for conversion clarify the sequence of actions within the category of physical deeds, wherein killing takes precedence. Furthermore, killing causes affliction and violates the compassion of a Great Being (*mahāsattva*). Specifically:
One must strictly prohibit sexual misconduct because it causes violation and affliction; therefore, it is listed at the end.

If the precepts were not established in this way, they would be for the sake of the Path, yet among those things that obstruct the Path, nothing is more profound than sexual desire. Those of lesser capacity seek only self-benefit and do not consider violating compassion;

thus, this is the opposite of what precedes it, each having its own underlying purpose. This is the case across all sutras and cannot be pointed out by a single example. Therefore, the text simply says:
How could the Sūtra fail to clarify the three karmas? Among these, the two karmas of speech and mind depend upon the body for their formation;
since the body occupies the primary position, it is called "first. Furthermore, among the three karmas of the body, killing is the most grave, as explained above.
For this reason, the Sūtra places it at the beginning, hence the phrase "firstly. Next, the text proceeds to explain its gravity.

The term "nature" (svabhāva) generally encompasses both the Sūtra on Opposites (*Pratipakṣa-sūtra*) and the statement: "The gravity [of an offense] depends on the mind; it is distinguished according to the object.
Since the teaching is established based on the mind, the offenses are also distinct.
[Commentary: Now, regarding the human realm, we divide karma into four categories: first, those that are neither acts of nurturing nor fields of merit; second, those that are acts of nurturing.
1. Not a field of merit; 2. A field of merit but not one who provides nurture; 3. Both a field of merit and one who provides nurture; 4. Neither a field of merit nor one who provides nurture.
In the detailed explanation of these four propositions, ordinary people, parents, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and Buddhas are contrasted as the four categories.

Although they are all alike in being human beings, their distinctions in terms of karma, the path of practice, the gravity of the precepts, the combination of single and multiple factors, and cause and effect are all unique; therefore, they must be distinguished individually.
To avoid confusion, these are roughly divided such that the first [category] consists solely of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the latter two consist solely of noble ones (*ārya*).
Regarding the second [category], parents, they include both ordinary beings and noble ones, as explained in detail later.
[Commentary: First, the initial phrase is explained.
[Commentary] Regarding the intent behind the formulation of this precept: because [human beings] are neither one's parents, they do not provide the nourishment of gratitude;

nor are they those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they do not constitute a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Since they lack these two qualities, it is for this reason that harming them is not permitted among other human beings.

This is because the retribution of the human realm is superior, being summoned by wholesome causes; both their physical form and mind are vessels capable of receiving the Path. For those who have left the household life, it is logically appropriate to observe the four [refuges].

Those who, while professing to cherish compassion and save the lives of sentient beings, instead harbor anger and resentment within, severing the continuity [of life], violating compassion, distressing others, and damaging the vessels of the Path—this is the most extreme of transgressions; therefore, the Noble Ones universally prohibit it.

In the first phrase, regarding the intention behind the prohibition, the initial paired sentence distinguishes the object; the subsequent portion correctly demonstrates the intended purpose of the prohibition.
This section further divides into two parts, the first of which clarifies that the object harmed is superior. Within this, there are three points: first, the superiority of the present retribution;

second, the superiority of past causes; and third, the capacity to receive the Path. Among the six realms of existence, only the single path of humanity possesses the conditions for being transformed through teaching; therefore, it is so stated.
Regarding the vessel for the Way and leaving the household life, the following clarifies the gravity of the offense of killing.

First, it clarifies the practice of the four immeasurables—namely, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—which are called "immeasurable" (*samā*) because they are impartial toward all beings. Now, the following clarifies the contrary practice.

The first two lines clarify the formation of karmic bonds; the next two lines reveal the faults of emotional afflictions. The metaphor illustrates that the physical and mental retribution of life is capable of containing the Noble Path.
The latter two lines of the verse demonstrate the established teachings.
[Commentary] Second, explaining the name of the precepts.
[Commentary] An ancient said: "Regarding the precept against killing, whether it concerns humans or animals, they are identical in terms of life; what is now called 'great killing'..."
Regarding the subsequent [category], if a small harm results in great [retribution], it is heavy; if a small [harm] is treated as insignificant, it is light—this is the meaning of the name.
In the first section of the explanation of "Great Killing," there are two parts: first, the citation of ancient [views] which are common and indiscriminate;

second, the clarification of the present intention for listing [the offenses]. According to the cited "Great Killing," non-humans are excluded; however, although the text provides an extensive explanation, there are no separate precept articles, and this is merely presented in contrast to...
The "ninety" [categories] distinguish [this realm] from the animal realm.
[Commentary]: Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that there are two kinds of birth: first, birth with form (*rūpa-jāti*), and second, birth without form (*arūpa-jāti*).
Birth with form is subject to destruction, whereas birth without form is indestructible. Nevertheless, birth without form depends upon birth with form, for matter and mind are mutually dependent.
The practitioner’s endowment constitutes a provisional life; now, by means of the wheel of blades, one destroys that arising of form and the arising of the formless, causing both to perish together.
By ensuring that the former does not induce the latter and the latter does not follow the former, one severs the continuity of retribution—this is called killing.

The next section is divided into two parts. First, the citation and demonstration regarding form and formlessness: since the five aggregates and four aggregates are all mind, they are called "formless.

Form refers to the coagulated and fluid [state], while mind refers to the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). These two depend upon one another to constitute a provisional life; therefore, both are termed "birth.
However, in the following formal explanation, the first part clarifies the meaning of birth, while the first two lines clarify that the mind is the basis.
Regarding the phrase "in regard to form" (*rūpe rūpe*), read the following two lines as a six-character sentence;

this reveals that [the body] is formed through mutual dependence and constitutes the retributive life-span (the ancient text reads *yi-zhu* for *yi-xing*). Now, the following explains the meaning of "destruction":

taking the sword as a wheel refers to various instruments of killing, such as King Kṛṇika becoming a thousand-headed fish with a wheel of swords encircling his body. Question: It was stated above that there is none...

Regarding the statement that "form cannot be destroyed," this [text] says "both are destroyed together. The answer is: because the mind relies upon form, when form is destroyed, consciousness has no basis;
therefore, it is said that both are destroyed. This does not contradict the fact that the mind and consciousness are actually indestructible.

As for the former, since the past mind and form have already been severed and extinguished, they do not induce subsequent [moments]. As for the latter, since the future mind and form do not yet exist...
Because it is a continuous succession, it does not proceed forward.

[Commentary] Regarding "precept" (*śīla*): it is called the "precept against killing" because it refers collectively to both the practice that can counteract [afflictions] and the object to be counteracted.

The explanation of "precept" is the same as before; since all are designated as precepts by virtue of preventing transgressions, one cites the characteristics of the transgression and, by grasping them together, designates them as a "precept. This is termed "naming."
All [cases] are identical to this and need not be further explained.

[Commentary: Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha-nature of sentient beings dwells within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). If one destroys these five aggregates, it is called 'killing.
If there is killing, one falls into the evil realms. There are three kinds of form; that which is past and present cannot [be destroyed].
Because it obstructs the future, it is called "killing. Now, sentient beings are defined by their inhalation and exhalation;
because these breaths are severed, it is called "killing. We Buddhas likewise speak in accordance with worldly convention when we say "killing."
In the scriptural citation, because that sutra states that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding and cannot be severed or destroyed, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva raised the act of killing as an objection;
the present commentary merely cites the Buddha’s response. This is simply because the name "killing" is derived from the destruction of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);
furthermore, it is because the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) perishes that the other four aggregates perish accordingly. Therefore, the following text [provides] the correct [explanation].

The three types of form—past, present, and future—are indestructible. Past form has already passed away; present form is subject to transformation and extinction, ceasing without pause from moment to moment.
That which has not yet ceased is the future, and that which has already ceased has returned to the past. Since present form does not persist as a fixed entity, it cannot be killed.
To preclude the future is to sever the continuity [of rebirth]. Sentient beings have no substantial reality; they are constituted by the appropriation of the aggregates (*skandhas*).

There is only a name; however, because consciousness relies upon the breath and follows the breath as it ceases and continues, thereby distinguishing between existence and non-existence, sentient beings are termed "in-and-out breaths.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there are truly no sentient beings; even when seeking them within the aggregates (*skandha*), the characteristic of birth is not found, let alone the act of killing.
This is spoken of as a path of karma (*karmapatha*) merely in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); this is not unique to Śākyamuni.
It is said: "In the three sections of our scriptural text, first we cite the *Tathāgatagarbha-parivarta* to prove that both types of birth destroy form;

next, we cite the *Brahmacarya-parivarta* to distinguish which forms are destroyed; finally, we again cite the latter section of the *Brahmacarya-parivarta* to clarify the characteristics of the continuity of retribution severed by the aforementioned [means]."

[Commentary: Third, the conditions for the completion of the offense consist of five factors: first, the victim must be a human being, as offenses against other realms of existence do not constitute grave sins;

second, one must perceive the victim as a human; third, one must possess the intent to kill; fourth, one must initiate the preparatory means; and fifth, it must be made clear that life has been severed.
Regarding the conditions for the completion of an offense, the analysis and explanation of the deficiency of the first condition can be understood [as follows].
[Commentary: Fourth, the meaning of the deficiency of conditions. [Commentary:

If the first condition is deficient and a minor thought of negligence (*pramāda-citta*) arises, one incurs only three *dukkaṭa* offenses, because the objects—the non-human, the animal, and the stump—are not [the primary objects of the full offense].

If a substitute for the original object arises from a general mental state (*mahā-manas*), one incurs only a *pārājika* offense; since the three realms of rebirth follow regardless of the specific transgression, there is no difference.

If, however, a specific mental state (*viśeṣa-manas*) is directed toward a particular object, and another object replaces the designated location, there are four permutations, which may be inferred by analogy with the above considerations.

Regarding the first deficiency among the deficiencies of conditions (*pratyaya*), there are three specific types: the two general [deficiencies] of the Great and Small Vehicles, and the deficiency of the focused mind. As for the single *thullaccaya* (grave offense) of the general [deficiency]:

because the three realms of existence (*gati*) are equally harmed, even though the object is a stump, the intention is not directed toward it; yet, although the expectation is general, since one regards it as a human, one incurs a grave offense due to its gravity.

This must necessarily arise in relation to a wooden stump; if one perceives it as an animal rather than a stump, one should logically incur a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), which is not what is being discussed here.

The *Mingzaiwen* (Text on Clarifying Transgressions) omits the concluding sentence here; it states: "A large transgression consists of one phrase: perceiving a stump as a person. A small transgression consists of three phrases:
first, perceiving a non-human as a human; second, perceiving an animal as a human; third, perceiving a wooden stump as a human.

If one adds only one phrase to the mind—such as killing Wang while perceiving him as Zhang—the offense is equal to a grave [transgression]. The remaining three cases are the same as before; hence it is so stated.
The four phrases apply to the preceding two types of *pramāda* (negligence), totaling eight phrases in all.

[Commentary]: In the second case, where both the perception (*saṃjñā*) and the object (*ālambana*) are absent, there are likewise two types of *pramāda*—small and great—as well as one instance of focused attention (*citta-krta*).

Regarding the absence of the second condition (the object), the first [section] generally enumerates three positions; within each of these positions, there are respectively the single or combined occurrences of perception and doubt.
The distinctions between these are as set forth in the *Jīlüe* (Brief Summary). [Commentary:

Furthermore, regarding the generation of intentional thoughts (*citta-vitarka*), there are four permutations: one offense of *pārājika* and three of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Regarding the generation of intentional doubt (*citta-vicikitsā*), there are ten permutations:
one *pārājika* and nine *saṃghāvaśeṣas*. That is to say, there are four cases of direct doubt and six cases of mutual doubt; these may also be understood by analogy.
Furthermore, when the methods of mental analysis (*citta-vicaya*) become confused, one must construct diagrams of the three distinct positions. [Commentary]:

When both conditions are absent during mental analysis, there are forty permutations; as with the variations in a king’s domain, there are ten permutations for the mind facing [objects], and so forth.
The analogy of the wooden stump can be understood accordingly.
Including the preceding three types of minds, there are fifty-four phrases in total; these can be seen within the *Tri-vidha-vinaya* and the *Pañca-citta-lakṣaṇa*.

One should know that while the first two types of mind differ in their objects but are fixed in their nature, the last one further adds the difference in objects; therefore, it is designated as "doubly deficient."

[Commentary: Regarding the remaining cases of *mahā-saṃvara* (grave) and *an-avadya-saṃvara* (light) offenses, their mental states and objective spheres (*ālambana*) lack specific characteristics and can be inferred accordingly; because such instances are rare, they cannot be listed in full. To provide a brief indication:

for *an-avadya-saṃvara* offenses, if one excludes the "royal person" (*rājapuruṣa*), there are three permutations regarding the mental state (*saṃjñā*). For *saṃśaya-saṃvara* (doubtful) offenses, there are nine permutations.

When both [mental state and object] are excluded—excluding the royal person and when the object is mistaken—only three objects remain, each also having nine permutations. Taken together, these three positions comprise a total of... [the full number].
The thirty-nine phrases are roughly the same as those in the preceding diagram; the only difference is that from each of the "doubt" categories, the first phrase is excluded.
Furthermore, the character *zhāng* (張) is universally changed to the character *rén* (人) for reading. Following the previous method, this is easily understood and need not be repeated here.
Regarding the three objects of the "general harm" (*tōnghài*), there is only the stump (*yù*) as the distinct object (*yìjìng*), resulting in only thirteen phrases in total.
Furthermore, fearing that this may be difficult to understand, it is necessary to set it forth clearly.
Within the text, there are two meanings; thus, one [case] is omitted, which may be inferred from the preceding two, as such instances are rare. [Commentary]:

Third, if the intent to kill is absent, there may be no offense, as in the section on "permissible conditions" (*kṣānti-pratyaya*); or one may incur a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), as in the case of striking a member of the assembly.
Even though there is no intent to kill, one may incur an offense if, for example, one strikes and completely breaks a monk;

or one may gain merit if, for example, one nurses a poor person through illness without receiving a reward; or one may obtain robes and a bowl if, for example, one nurses a wealthy person through illness and is rewarded for the labor;
or one may incur a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) if, for example, one administers medicine to a person in distress as a means to bring them close to death, even though there was no intention to kill.

The six specific cases for the omission of the *citta* (intention) are each interspersed with the character "or" (*vā*). First, regarding the precept text, the subsequent commentary lists two or three divisions based on whether the death resulted from striking once or repeatedly;
this clarifies that there was no intention. The phrase "completely broken" means the full possession of the precepts is lost, while "broken" means the precepts are impaired.
Fourth and fifth, the division of nursing the sick is based on wealth or poverty; this refers specifically to nursing performed according to the Dharma.
Because death occurs, it is not an act of malice; yet among these six [cases], there are two instances where the treatment of suffering involves a fault:
dying from punishment, and administering medicine for illness with an unwholesome mind, which instead causes the disease to increase.

[Commentary]: Fourth, because the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) has not yet been initiated, a single thought-moment is not subject to formal restraint; one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) even if the mind is directed toward killing, because the body has not yet moved and one immediately repents.

Alternatively, one may incur either a light or heavy *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, where if a patient possesses many robes and one expects their death and takes them, or if one, out of weariness or negligence, fails to attend to them and they die, one is only charged with a *sthūlātyaya*.
Because of the absence of skillful means (*upāya*).

Within the deficiency of skillful means, there are three [stages]: first, regarding non-offense, it clarifies the deficiency by stating that "it has not yet arisen," meaning one has not yet encountered a grave condition (*gurutara-pratyaya*);

second, regarding the offense of *duṣkṛta*, it clarifies the deficiency by referring to a grave condition, which pertains to the distant preparatory transgression (*pūrvaprayoga-āpatti*); third, regarding the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.

The Ming [commentary] cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong) to demonstrate that when comparing the gravity of offenses, if the assessment of the robe’s value is too light, the principle fails to reach the middle;

thus, failing to examine it closely constitutes an offense of *sthūlātyaya* (near-slaughter), which should be classified as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (upper *sthūlātyaya*). Therefore, it is marked as "light and heavy. As for those without preparatory effort (*anupakrama*), the opposite—having preparatory effort—is subsumed under the grave offense of *pārājika*.

[Commentary]: Lacking the fifth condition—that the life has not yet been severed—the aforementioned seven preparatory stages (saptaprayoga) constitute seven *sthūlātyaya* offenses. As the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If one kills a person who has not yet died, but [the victim] goes insane, the precept is relinquished; however, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
[The text] omits the [first] precept; it severs the middle finger, with seven conditions above and ten cited below, briefly citing the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* as proof for the first condition.

[Commentary: The above clarifies that whether the victim belongs to the human realm, the non-human realm, or the animal realm, the infliction of harm is equal; the distinction lies only in the relative lightness of the offense.
The examples cited—such as killing non-animals, the two types of killing, and the five conditions for an offense—are all treated identically regarding their completeness or deficiency.
[Commentary] Second, those who are not fields of merit are those who provide nurturance.

[Commentary] Regarding the original intent of the precept: humans are not of miraculous birth; their karma is deposited in a womb, and they take up the residual elements of others to form their own bodies.

Furthermore, since one has personally nurtured and raised [the victim], the debt of gratitude is profound; in principle, one ought to honor, support, and repay this kindness by planting roots of merit.

To instead respond with anger and resentment is equivalent to committing an act of rebellion or injury, which violates the duty of filial care. Because such an offense is extremely grave, it is established as a crime of parricide (*ānantarya*), further augmented by the severity of the *pārājika* offense.
Other cases where the relationship is not one of nurturing do not rank as high as this and are therefore not classified as parricide.

Second, regarding non-merit (*apuṇya*), this is the first section of the introductory text concerning the intention of the "Enlightened Restriction" (*en-zhi*). First, it describes the appropriateness of showing respect.

If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, humans are said to pass through all four modes of birth; however, here, based on the majority case, it says "not born by transformation," which refers to those born from the union of semen and vital energy (*ojas*).

The above clarifies two kinds of kindness: first, the formation of the body, and second, its nurturing. Because both of these types are fully present, they are described as "profound and heavy. Next...

The first clarification addresses violations; the subsequent clarification of the offenses for inflicting harm explains the faults incurred. The term "ingratitude" (*kṛtaghna*) refers to the opposite of the two aforementioned types [of kindness].
Furthermore, "increasing the *pārājika* offense" refers to the crime of harming others. The remaining terms below serve to distinguish these from one another.

[Commentary] Question: When one kills one’s parents, is it because they know [them to be their parents] that they commit the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), or is it because they do not know? Answer:

If the mind is indiscriminate (*mānasa*), even if one does not specifically recognize them as one's parents, since the act accords with the original intention, why would there be no offense of immediate retribution?

As stated in the *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā* (Shan-jian lun): "First, there was a goat beneath a tree; later, one intended to harm it, but the mind indiscriminately took as its object anyone who happened to be there—whether a father, a human, or a ghost."

If one raises livestock to substitute for a sheep, because the mind is distracted, one still incurs the offense of a *ānantarya* (immediate) transgression and so forth; however, if it is a domestic animal and one kills it without knowing it is such, there is no offense.
Thus, the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states: "If one kills without the perception that they are one's parents, even if the victim is an ordained person, one does not commit a *ānantarya* offense."

The initial question arises because various treatises present differing views; therefore, it is asked in order to resolve them. The response to the text’s opening section concerns the commission of an offense through a general state of mind (*mānasa-citta*), meaning that one does not distinguish between kin and strangers, as the intent to harm applies universally.
Next, regarding the subsequent section, it concerns the non-commission of an offense through a specific intention (*kṣaṇika-citta*).

Each of these points is supported by scriptural citations, making the two segments clearly evident. Since the treatise clarifies the obstacles to the precepts (*śīlāvaraṇa*), this discussion is framed specifically for those who have left the household life (*pravrajita*).
[Commentary] Question: If one kills a parent who has left the household life and attained the path of an Arhat, how many *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses does one incur?
Furthermore, since the teachings contain both singular, multiple, and indeterminate cases, this must be examined with careful scrutiny.

[Commentary] The answer is as follows: In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is stated that one may incur one *pārājika* offense and two *ānantarya* offenses; furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that there are two grave offenses: first, killing one's father, the king;

second, killing a *srotāpanna*. These two offenses are combined because the act of severing the father’s life involves two mental objects—the father who provided sustenance and the field of merit—and thus causes harm to both.
In the initial response, first the sūtras and vinaya are cited below; next, the meaning of the gravity [of the offense] is revealed. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 33, states:
"King Bimbisāra of Rājagṛha had a crown prince named Ajātaśatru. Due to karmic causes and conditions, he gave rise to a mind of perversity and rebellion;
he confined his father outside the city walls and even cut off his food, clothing, and medicine for more than seven days."
When the King’s life had come to an end, the Crown Prince felt remorse. The wicked and perverse ministers claimed he was without fault.
Jīvaka further said, "Great King, you should know that such karma carries a double burden of guilt.

Because Bimbisāra had already realized the first fruit [of the path], he is called a *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer). (If one follows the *Amitābha-sūtra*, he had progressed to the third fruit; this account refers to the period prior to that, hence he is called a Stream-enterer.)
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, committing patricide against an Arhat constitutes a single *ānantarya* (immediate) offense because it relies upon a single basis. [Commentary]:
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, killing one's father who is an Arhat results in a single *ānantarya* offense because the basis is one.
Next, in the response, the *Abhidharmakośa* explains that the five heinous acts (*pañcānantarya*) are termed "immediate karmas" (*ānantarya-karma*), as will be explained below.
Regarding the first basis [for counting them as one], because there is no separate life-force [in the father], it is established as a single heinous act solely on the basis of killing the father.

[Commentary] Question: How can the aforementioned *nirvāṇa* be reconciled with this? Answer: It is to manifest that while two immediate causes (*ānantarya-kāraṇa*) are established, since life is a single entity, how could there be two offenses?
It is simply by using the name "immediate" (*ānantarya*) to mark the gravity of this karma that one speaks of "two immediacies";
in reality, they do not exist.

The response in the *Huìtōng* is divided into two parts: first, it demonstrates the intent behind the teaching on *nirvāṇa*; second, it reveals the principle that there is no repetition [of retribution].
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, if one commits multiple distinct transgressions (*ānantarya*), one undergoes the retribution for each according to their respective karma.

However, within the context of *nirvāṇa*, if one commits even a single transgression, one must fully experience the retribution for that one sin; this remains the case even if two transgressions are committed.
Thus, for one who possesses twice as many of the five heinous offenses (*ānantarya*), the retribution is likewise fivefold.
[Commentary] By this, it is clarified that the determination of the quantity of offenses according to the Vinaya depends on four distinct factors: the conditions, the karma, and the four stages.
In the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), there are superior examples of "illumination" (*prakāśa*) and "obscuration" (*andhakāra*), and in the Vinaya, such instances are frequently encountered;

therefore, by means of these, the text clarifies that both conditions (*pratyaya*) and karma (*karman*) each possess four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), with each permutation further containing two positions: "one" and "many.
Here, "conditions" refers to objective circumstances (*vastu-pratyaya*), while "karma" refers to bodily and vocal actions.

[Commentary]: Regarding the first point, "a single object for an initial act resulting in multiple offenses through different combinations," this refers to cases such as two separate rooms, swallowing food, and so forth.

That is to say, factors such as obstruction, difficulty, excess, not begging, leftovers, overnight storage, and improper contact collectively serve as the conditions. As for the two types of action—bodily and vocal—one incurs many offenses with each instance of performing the act or swallowing the food.

As for those that result in the formation of only a single offense, examples include slandering based on a false pretext or digging the earth; in these cases, there is no distinct *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) for each individual act.
From the ultimate perspective:

the first phrase previously clarified many offenses; first clarifying the differences in conditions, it cites the four conditions for room-food and room-utensils, noting that food may involve multiple transgressions.

The *Chao* states: "Each swallow constitutes seven offenses: eating at the improper time, eating what was not received, eating leftovers, storing overnight, storing within the monastery, and cooking within the monastery."
Regarding the act of boiling [meat] oneself and the resulting unpleasant touch, it is explained that these belong to the body;

however, while eating from an upper room is strictly a bodily action, the mention here of "two actions" intends to extend this principle by analogy, as in the cases of slandering a pure person or wishing to deceive the Sangha.
The killing of one's father or an Arhat is included in this category. Next, the *Śāriputrābhidharma* clarifies that this constitutes a single offense.

Slandering that which is merely conventional (prajñapti) constitutes a separate offense of falsehood; however, the preparatory act for digging the earth constitutes the offense of *ānantarya* (grave transgression). If one follows the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, digging the earth also constitutes a *pātayantika*. [Commentary:

Second, regarding the formation of multiple offenses through a single action based on different conditions: it is like a person who strikes another repeatedly over time; with each successive blow, a new offense is incurred.
Taking [the property] also constitutes one offense, just as theft is established through the mutual dependence of preceding and succeeding acts.

Regarding the second phrase, although there are many offenses at the outset, a single person is the objective condition (*ālambana*); each blow constitutes a distinct karma. Furthermore, it clarifies that there is one offense:
the preceding object is the condition, while the preceding and succeeding acts of theft constitute the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) that ultimately leads to a single result.
[Commentary]: Third, regarding the formation of multiple offenses when the conditions, actions, and occasions differ: this is like the distinct offenses for killing or stealing at different times.
Regarding the formation of a single offense: this is like the eight cases for nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), where the preceding and succeeding acts together constitute a grave offense.
The third phrase concerns those who commit many transgressions: when life, another person, or their property serves as the condition, the karma is produced accordingly;
within a single transgression, when a man serves as the condition, there are eight distinct matters through which that karma is differentiated.

[Commentary: Regarding the four conditions where karma and the fetters coincide—namely, when a single act results in multiple offenses—it is as when uttering a single word that simultaneously possesses the four verbal transgressions;
yet only one offense is incurred. Since this is straightforward, there is no need to elaborate further.

Regarding the fourth phrase, "one with many offenses," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "To transmit these words of one person to another because they are untrue constitutes false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*);
because it creates a desire for separation, it constitutes divisive speech (*paiśunya*); and because it is not gentle speech, it constitutes harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).

The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states that the single category of frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*) is necessarily inseparable from these; this text merely cites the case where all [four] are present."

The same applies to three, two, or even one offense; because each precept within a single offense is distinct and each constitutes a separate transgression, they are said to be "simultaneously different" (or "alternately different," which is also acceptable).
[Commentary] Other cases concerning the presence or absence of conditions may all be inferred from what precedes.
The summary [of the precepts] also requires five conditions, as established by the preceding [analysis]: first, the presence of one's parents; second, the perception that they are one's parents;
third, the intent to kill; fourth, the undertaking of the means; and fifth, the severing of life. If any condition is lacking, the offense is likewise determined by comparing it to the above.

[Commentary: Third, regarding the killing of an Arhat: this is rare in the final age, so why must it be mentioned? Nevertheless, there are many instances of such acts of parricide recorded in the Sūtras and Vinaya;

one should recognize these matters in order to serve as a warning against future practice. Since clear awareness and enlightenment ultimately arise from these very conditions, they are briefly explained here.
In the third sentence, the intention for why one must emerge [from ignorance] is first shown.

Although such cases are rare within the teachings, it is necessary to recognize that those who practice later do so because they take what they have learned now as the seeds of cognition (*vijñāna-bīja*); subsequently, when encountering superior conditions, their former wisdom is awakened.
Therefore, it is called "clear awakening" (*vidyā-avabodha*), and these conditions are precisely those being demonstrated here.
[Commentary]: Regarding the intent behind the prohibition: because he is one worthy of offerings, he is called a "field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*);

it is not because he harbors and nurtures [beings] that he is called a field of grace. To clarify: this person has severed the fetters and become a noble member of the Sangha Jewel, the foremost field of merit.

Because he compassionately rescues all beings, he humbly accepts offerings; logically, one must plant causes to reap the holy fruits. Yet, by harboring thoughts of hostility and harm, one damages and destroys the holy body.
Since the obstacle to one's own benefit and the obstruction of others' expansive merit involve such grave emotional transgressions, they are established as *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses.

As for the remaining seven classes of monastics, because their path is not ultimate, the merit they inspire is slight; thus, killing them constitutes an offense equivalent to that of an ordinary person, and even though it is a noble practice, in terms of karmic weight, it is not light.

In the introductory section of the *Zhìyì* (Exposition of the Meaning), the first phrase indicates the intent to proceed with the formal exposition. First, it describes the excellence of the objective realm (*viṣaya*), which warrants reverence;

the four fruits and four stages of approach constitute the eight classes of noble ones (*aṣṭau puruṣapudgalāḥ*). The term "looking down" (*fǔ*) means to look downward; the character "down" (*xià*) is used in contrast to the subsequent section.

Next, it clarifies that those who commit transgressions involving harm (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) do not offer such reverence, thereby losing their own benefit (*svārtha*) and severing the field of victory for others (*parārtha*), thus forfeiting the benefit of others. The remaining portion below serves to exclude other noble beings.

The first four lines constitute the primary distinction; the final two lines resolve doubts. The preceding statement that [the offense] is "equal to that of an ordinary person" refers specifically to *prajñapti*-offenses (*śikṣāpada-āpatti*), for there is a distinction between the stages of ordinary persons and sages, and their karmic retribution must necessarily differ in weight.
[Commentary]: Question: According to the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, killing a *pratyekabuddha* is not the same as killing an arhat. Answer: This is because [the sūtra] refers to a *śrāvaka*.

Regarding entering the Path through sound, there are three capacities: first, the ability to preach the Dharma; second, the ability to manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*); and third, the ability to cause others to attain the Path, thereby bringing profound benefit and vast utility.

This is why [the Buddha] is distinguished from the *śrāvaka*, the *pratyekabuddha*, and others; for the latter do not possess these qualities. Thus, killing a human being is a grave offense. As it says in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"The person who is a *pratyekabuddha* aspires to dwell in solitude. If they transform sentient beings, they merely manifest supernatural powers and remain silent all day long, proclaiming nothing."
It is said that teaching the Dharma to those incapable of receiving it prevents them from attaining the fruit; this passage serves as proof that such a field of merit is narrow.

In the initial question, it was clarified that killing a Pratyekabuddha does not obstruct the precepts; now, because the act of severing [the roots of goodness] and the resulting realization are identical, the fields of merit are likewise equal, and thus the question must be resolved.
In the answer, it first clarifies that the Śrāvaka possesses the three capacities, and subsequently explains this in detail.

Because Pratyekabuddhas do not possess [these qualities], they are slighted; subsequently, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* is cited as evidence that they lack two capacities. Now, there are two types of Pratyekabuddhas:

first, those who appear in a world without a Buddha and are thus called *Pratyekabuddha* (Solitary Realizers); second, those who attain the Way by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination and are thus called *Pratyayabuddha* (Condition-Realizers).
The explanation provided above follows the general trend, yet it does not preclude that *Pratyayabuddhas* are well capable of transforming others.
Some sentient beings, by their very nature, are incapable of hearing the Dharma being preached. [Commentary] Question:

[He] left the household life.

otherwise, as that text states, "An icchantika does not fall under the three types of killing"—would it then follow that there is no sin? According to the Vinaya, one commits a *pārājika* offense regarding an icchantika person as the object;

Regarding the first response to the three difficulties based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the scripture clarifies that both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas fully understand the nature of killing;

thus it says, "knowing the killing [of an Arhat]. Above, according to the scripture, there are the two characters for "parents," but here, as the question specifically concerns Pratyekabuddhas, they are omitted.

Regarding the knowledge that the offenses of Pratyekabuddhas do not differ in degree, the initial section of the response presents the meaning of the sutra. By this standard, even if one kills a Pratyekabuddha, although it is not a heinous crime (*ānantarya*), because the object is so exalted and the karma is extraordinary, it is nonetheless grave.
If one does not concede this, the sutra counters with a rhetorical question. First, it cites the scriptural passage: in Sanskrit, this is called *icchantika*.

[Commentary] Question: If one kills an Arhat, does one incur the immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) because one knows it is an Arhat, or because one does not know? Answer:

Fourth, regarding the question of what can be answered: first, the treatise is cited to clarify that with a specific intent (*niyata-citta*), the offense is not established;

[Commentary]: Fourth, regarding the shedding of the Buddha’s blood with an evil mind:

[The Buddha] was about to descend to take birth for the sake of producing goodness as a field of merit for the world, compassionately aiding all sentient beings; this was also an act of nurturing through grace.

As the Dharma King, he opened the way through the Four Great Vows to transform and benefit the multitudes; his grace is boundless, and one ought to honor and support him to plant the seeds of merit and purify the mind.

If one’s mind instead gives rise to further anger and resentment, and incites an attempt to harm life—though the life itself cannot be severed—it nonetheless causes the shedding of blood from the body, which damages the vessel of the Dharma-body;
because this transgression is particularly grave, it is established as a preparatory act that constitutes a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).

The fourth phrase, "Restraining the Mind," is divided into two sections. The first section is further divided into two parts: first, showing the phrase; second, the main exposition beginning with "The Buddha" below.

The first part clarifies that the depth of his grace merits reverence. "Four Vows" refers to the aforementioned four immeasurables; "Vows" (弘) means to instruct, and they are termed "Great" (弘) because they are universal.
Grace has no exterior because there is nothing left unreached. Following this, the second part reveals the transgressions to clarify the necessity of the regulation.

Regarding those who damage the vessel of the Dharma-body, the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* states that because the physical body (rūpakāya) is the support for the Dharma-body, the application of the disciplinary rule constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
Since the Buddha cannot be killed, the meaning is not ultimate; thus, the distinction between the light nature of the offense and its heavy result can be understood.

[Commentary]: However, although the physical act of shedding blood is the same, its underlying conditions differ. One who harbors a virtuous mind shares the same karmic retribution as one who harbors evil.
When Jīvaka shed blood with a virtuous mind to treat a disease, he enjoyed the retribution of pleasure within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) for an eon; Devadatta, conversely, fell into hell.
Fearing that this might be confused with those who act out of virtue, the text specifies "with an evil mind."

In the first section of the following analysis, it clarifies that those with similar karmic retributions may appear to be confused; this is discussed in terms of time, as they both belong to the same kalpa.
Regarding the next section on the Elder [Jīvaka], it cites the circumstances to explain why Jīvaka is also called "Gīva" (the Good Physician);

the World-Honored One suffered a foot ailment from which blood was drawn by needle, and his complexion immediately became like that of Brahmā—this illustrates a virtuous mind. Devadatta, however, used a mountain to crush the Buddha.

[The text] states that by injuring the Buddha’s finger or foot with a stone fragment, one falls into Avīci; this clarifies the nature of an evil mind. Fearing that [the reader] might later misunderstand, the following is shown to clarify the intended meaning.

[Commentary: Question: If one does not know it is the Buddha, one cannot commit an offense against him; likewise, if one makes an offering without knowing it is the Buddha, one should not obtain merit. Answer: One obtains merit through the act of offering.

If one originally gives rise to a casual thought of merit and respects [the object] even while perceiving it as a tree spirit before the Buddha’s body, one still obtains merit from the Buddha because of the penetration of the mind;
however, if one originally resolves the mind to perceive it as a spirit before the Buddha, then there is no merit.

Regarding the question, following the previous pattern, one ought first to inquire whether [the subject] knows or does not know; alternatively, since the sense of the preceding discussion on Arhats is consistent with this, the question is raised directly.

[Commentary: The remaining conditions for the presence of factors (*sāmagrī*) and so forth are to be explained by analogy with what precedes.
