[Commentary: Regarding the deficiency of conditions, there are cases where they are the same and cases where they are different. When the first object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is deficient, all four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are identical; when other objects are involved, they are all different.

To replace the original [offense] of the Buddha, the two gates are likewise treated thus. If one omits the two phrases concerning "conception" and "doubt," they differ because the Buddha’s right livelihood must never be interrupted.

Since it is clarified that shedding blood constitutes the fundamental offense, even though the object (*ālambana*)—the field—is of the utmost reverence, the rule is established based on the person (*pudgala*);
for the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is determined by the strength of the object.

Regarding the section on "Deficiencies in Conditions" (*pratyaya-vaidhurya*), the first part provides a general heading, while the subsequent section offers a detailed explanation. First, it clarifies the two cases where there is a commonality:

(1) a discrepancy in the object where one perceives a human as a Buddha, and (2) the perception of a non-human as a Buddha; (3) an animal, and (4) a wooden stump—these four permutations all constitute the *thullaccaya* offense. Second, it demonstrates the commonality of being deficient in both [conditions].

Following this, the next section distinguishes the deficiencies regarding perception into four permutations and the deficiencies regarding doubt into ten permutations; these two categories [are explained here].

Regarding the first phrase, whereas previously [such acts] were all classified as *pārājika* (defeats), they are now considered *thullaccaya* (grave offenses). The following explains the reasons for this difference. [Commentary:

Based on this, the meaning of the five *ānantarya* (immediate) transgressions is analyzed through four sections: first, enumerating them and manifesting their characteristics; second, explaining their names and their relative gravity; third, determining their essential nature and manifestations;
fourth, regarding the first two, whether they can be expiated or not; fifth, relating them to the three types of action (*trikarma*); and sixth, clarifying their pervasiveness or restriction.
[Commentary: Regarding the initial enumeration of the five [offenses], they are: matricide, patricide, killing an Arhat, drawing blood from a Tathāgata, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
Among these five heinous crimes (ānantarya), the first passage is easily understood. [Commentary:

To clarify their characteristics, one must consider that they are committed toward those who gave birth and raised one on their lap; thus, the debt of gratitude is at its maximum. This is as stated in the worldly legal codes regarding the gravity of offenses.

Those who commit offenses against their ancestors, grandparents, paternal uncles, and other such close relatives already constitute *pārājika* (grave offenses); how much more so for those against foster fathers, stepmothers, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, and the like, which are not considered *pārājika* at all?
Therefore, the Sūtras and Vinaya rely solely on these two categories of kinship.

Within the second section, "Manifesting the Characteristics," there are two parts. First, the preliminary clarification and determination: for now, this concerns the two grave offenses (*ānantarya*), while the others are described as before.

Alternatively, it may be that the other three [offenses] do not require such clarification because they lack ambiguity. Regarding the phrase "beneath the knees": this expression originates from the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety) and refers to the time of infancy.
As cited below, common usage shows how these terms can be conflated; "grandparents" refers specifically to the parents of one's father, and "uncles" refers to paternal uncles.

The term "elder brother" (*bó*) refers to paternal uncles; stepfathers and stepmothers, though originally not biological kin, are termed "reversals" (*nì*) because they look upward toward one's ancestors.
Since these two [categories] are also kin, how much more so [the case of] paternal aunts and maternal aunts? They are not "reversals" because their clan lineages differ.
This concludes the preceding section by summarizing its essential meaning.
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the names: why is it called "rebellion" (*ānantarya*)?

It is so named because it violates the ultimate field of merit that provides nurturing and kindness, and because it also opposes the dual kingship of the Buddha and the Worldly King. As stated in the treatise, the five *ānantarya* are so called because they constantly continue without any interval.
In the first section of the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names), there are two meanings for "contrary" (*ni*). First, it refers to violating kindness and merit: violating the kindness of one's parents;

violating the merit of an Arhat by causing a schism in the Saṃgha; and violating both [kindness and merit] by drawing blood from a Tathāgata. Second, it refers to violating the transformation of the King: the Buddha is the Dharma-King, while the world has its human kings;
both teachings prohibit [such acts], and thus to commit them is to violate both. Although the Chinese and Sanskrit names differ, the legal code (*vinaya*) is no different. Nevertheless, regarding...
Among the five [ānantarya offenses], only those involving the killing of one's father or mother are considered equally grave by both monastics and laypeople;

the remaining three differ. [The Commentary] states that according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, they are so called because: first, regarding the fruit of rebirth, there is no interval, as one is reborn immediately after casting off the body; second, regarding the experience of suffering, there is no interval, as there is no pleasure within it;
third, regarding time, there is no interval, as it is fixed for exactly one kalpa; and fourth, regarding life, there is no interval, as it is not severed.

The five forms exist without interval, as in the characteristics of Avīci; though eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, they are completely filled by one person or many people, yet they do not obstruct one another—such is the inconceivability of karma.

The subsequent section discusses how the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*’s explanation of meaning still accords with the five meanings of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. The manifestation of these characteristics is very clear;

they are condensed into three points: first, "intermediate separation" (*antara-avakāśa*); second, third, and fourth, "intermediate interruption" (*vicchinna*); and fifth, "intermediate deficiency" (*vighāta*).
However, because form is without interval and its unity or multiplicity does not obstruct one another, ordinary minds find this difficult to believe; hence it is called "karma."

[Commentary] Question: Since all Three Jewels are fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), one may discuss the gravity of offenses such as harming the Buddha or causing a schism in the Saṃgha as being *ānantarya* (immediate) sins; why, then, is causing a schism in the Dharma not mentioned as an *ānantarya* sin?
The initial question concerns how the Three Jewels are identical as fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), yet differ when it comes to constituting a transgression; therefore, the commentary explains this.

[Commentary] The answer is that because slandering the Dharma is so grave, it is not included among the [five] immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*). Just as the five current immediate transgressions are not included among the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*), the details are as found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
In the response, the first part explains this based on the gravity of karma as follows. To provide an illustration, it refers extensively to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states:

"If one commits the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) while on the path of the Śrāvaka, one will suffer in hell for one kalpa. If one does so while on the path of the Bodhisattva, one will destroy the Buddha-dharma;
when this kalpa ends, one will again go to other hells (*niraya*) to undergo immeasurable suffering. This continues in this manner until it pervades all ten directions."

In the "Parable" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, following the section on the hells, the signs of the transgressions incurred by those who slander the sutra are explained in detail, even stating:
"When such a person's life ends, they shall enter the Avīci hell for a full kalpa; when that kalpa is exhausted, they are reborn again.
Thus it continues in succession for countless kalpas. Upon emerging from the hells, they shall fall among the animals, and so forth."

[Commentary: Some say that the gravity of slandering the Dharma refers to the Mahāyāna; in contrast to the field [of merit], this is discussed as an act of parricide—namely, the parricide of destroying the Wheel of Dharma and subverting the Dharma.

In the first section of the subsequent alternative interpretation, there are again two parts: first, it reiterates the previous meaning, and second, it demonstrates the correct interpretation by contrasting it with the Hīnayāna.
The treatise states that regarding the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha, it extends to all Three Jewels.

[Commentary] Question: If this is so, why is it that reviling the Sūtras incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense)? Answer: The previous mention of "reversal" (*ānantarya*) referred to the total destruction [of the Dharma];
the present mention of incurring a *duṣkṛta* refers merely to the act of reviling.

In the subsequent objection, it is stated that violating the Vinaya precepts and violating the other two Piṭakas both constitute a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). This contradicts the previous statement regarding the meaning of "forming a *ānantarya* (immediate retribution).
The answer and explanation can be understood as follows:

[The *Sūtra*] states: "If one merely causes a schism in the Saṃgha, it is not termed an *ānantarya*, because causing a schism in a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) inflicts only minor harm; whereas if one kills an *arhat*..."
Han [the Emperor] incurred this transgression because he harmed true monks and thereby violated the ultimate limit of merit; thus he obtained this retribution.

Among the three [categories], the first concerns the breaking of the Saṃgha by way of contrast: if merely breaking the Saṃgha does not constitute a transgression of immediate retribution (ānantarya), it demonstrates that the karma of immediate retribution arises entirely from the destruction of the Dharma.
As for the second [point], it cites the analogy of killing a noble one (ārya); by the same logic, even killing an Arhat is considered [an ānantarya].

Because it harms the Sangha, which is a true field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), it constitutes a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense; thus, one should know that the "schism of the Sangha" (*saṃghabheda*) is included within the category of these immediate offenses, and for this reason it is not listed separately.

[Commentary: Next, regarding the gravity or lightness of the offenses as previously enumerated, since they are arranged from light to heavy, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The schism of the Sangha is the greatest."
Because they cause the separation from the Three Jewels—by alienating the Saṃgha, destroying the Buddha, and corrupting the Dharma Jewel;

furthermore, because they give rise to envy toward the Buddha, oppose and turn back the True Dharma, and harass the great assembly, such that even within a radius of thirty *yojanas*, meditation and recitation cannot be practiced.

Regarding the gravity of the offenses listed above for the middle finger, this is based on a coarse classification; when distinguished in detail, the three intermediate [offenses] are considered "heavy" when viewed in relation to the preceding [category], and "light" when viewed in relation to the succeeding one.

The reason that harming one's mother is heavier than harming one's father is that within Buddhism, the mother’s grace of conception and nourishment is particularly emphasized, and thus she is held in special reverence;
furthermore, for an Arhat to transcend the mundane world, it is essential to honor one's parents and shed blood [in their service].
The meaning of "supremely venerable" surpasses that of the lesser sages. The following citation from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* provides a unique proof regarding the schism of the Saṃgha;

this passage contains two meanings. First, it clarifies the gravity [of the offense] by way of the object to be destroyed or damaged. Second, it clarifies the gravity by way of the arising of a mind that causes violation and distress.

Regarding "meditation and recitation," these refer to various methods of contemplation (*dhyāna* and *svādhyāya*). Because one either regresses from the path of practice within the sphere of transformation or fails to progress therein, it is said "not."
Regarding the practice of the higher [stages], this is discussed according to the principles of karma and does not concern the formal regulations of the Vinaya.
[Commentary: Regarding the second point, the essential nature and characteristics of the two concentrations and the aspects of repentance:

within the essential nature of the concentrations, three categories are listed; subsequently, it says "the first two," which clarifies that the first refers to the very beginning of the grave offenses (*ānantarya-karma*) and the second refers to the second [category].

[Commentary] Regarding the term "nature and form" (*tǐzhuàng*): for example, the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are not established by the Buddha; because they violate kindness and merit, their karmic principle is inherently grave.
As for those that constitute a *pārājika* offense, these are indeed established by the Buddha. However, this is determined based on the violation of human relations;

it does not depend on kindness or merit. One incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense if the conditions are incomplete. If one considers the schism of the Saṃgha, it should be regulated as extremely grave, for such an act cannot be accomplished alone.
This is because it comprehensively includes three types of persons.

In the first section, since there is a risk of confusion regarding the characteristics established by karma, it is necessary to distinguish and determine them; first, the essence of the karma is shown:

the offenses of the five heinous acts merely violate the path of karma, as such ancient laws have always existed and were not specifically instituted by the Buddha. Next, the essence of the offense is determined. That is to say:
Regarding the initial general presentation of the two categories of *pārājika* (defeats) and *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses) within the Vinaya of Precepts, which collectively subsume the five crimes:
there are three *pārājikas* and two *sthūlātyayas*. This section consists of two parts: first, the explanation of the three *pārājikas*, and second, the explanation of the two *sthūlātyayas*.

Regarding the inclusion of the "three persons" in the offense of schism (*saṃghabheda*), the old commentary cites the *Yìcǎo* (Excerpts on Meaning), which states: "There are three types of schism: first, schism by a king; second, schism by an associate; and third, schism by an assistant."

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that there is "no beginning," this refers to the fact that the characteristics of a transgression through defiance cannot be disregarded. While the killing of one's father by non-Buddhists is mentioned by the Buddha as being subject to expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), this constitutes a violation of the teachings; other cases are explained later.
In the first section of the following analysis, the meaning is established; subsequently, examples are cited to explain and substantiate the text.

Since this passage appears within the *Upasampadā-vidhi* (the Method for Receiving Ordination), it indicates that for a layperson, the initial transgression necessarily violates the abbreviated teaching (*saṃkṣipta-śikṣā*). Even for a layperson who has not received the abbreviated precepts, such an act still warrants expulsion.

Thus, we know that regarding conduct, the gravity of the offense is determined by its specific nature: the moment the act is committed, the ultimate transgression (*atyaya*) is established. This is analogous to the subsequent rule concerning the schism of the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that [certain offenses] are "capable of repentance," it is as in the Mahāyāna, where even the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are permitted to be repented of.
If this is so, why does the sutra state that the king’s grave sins become light? The answer is that there is no fixed nature to sin.

For instance, as in that same sutra, there may be shame (*hrī*) rather than a lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*), or perhaps because the original gravity was transformed, they become light. This applies to the other three *pārājika* offenses and the two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses as well.

Because the *Śaikṣa-vinaya* explains that [offenses] are eliminated through confession, it is self-evident from the text on confessing before the Saṃgha for the *sthūlātyaya* offense of causing a schism among the nine types of pure persons (*pariśuddha-pudgala*) in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Among the three [sections], the first indicates the act of confession; the first two phrases determine that in the Mahāyāna, specifically the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*, [such offenses] are indeed confessable.

This equally applies to the repentance for the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) of the three periods of time; it is also like Aṅgulimāla, who committed the causes for the five heinous crimes but attained their extinction upon encountering the Buddha.
If one cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* below as a challenge, since the thesis established above relies on the Mahāyāna, one must likewise cite the Mahāyāna to pose the challenge:
King Ajātaśatru killed his father and was destined for one kalpa in the Avīci hell, yet the Buddha had him perform repentance.
The Kālasūtra Hell is exhausted in seven days; since it is merely shifted from heavy to light, this demonstrates that a grave offense cannot be expiated.
In the response, there are two points: first, citing that sutra, it shows that existence or non-existence [of the fruit] is not fixed, clarifying that karma is defined by the mind;

thus, although one may repent, one still receives the retribution, leaving no room for doubt. Alternatively, the second point indicates that since the retribution is shifted to become lighter, it clarifies that repentance is permitted.

Next, the remaining sections clarify the confession and regulation. First, the determination of the training in repentance (*śikṣādattaka*); second, the citation of scriptural evidence. First, the proof for the confession of a *pārājika* offense:

the Vinaya mandates that one undergo training in repentance, opening the way for confession without doubt. Next, the proof for the repentance of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense: both the heterodox and the orthodox each consist of five factors; only when these are complete does one constitute a schism of the Saṃgha.

Because the true Buddha’s status is distinct and he is not included within the count of the Saṃgha, it is said that there are nine persons. All those who are heretical followers who cause a schism in the Saṃgha... [text ends]... all [are included].

Since those who have committed the *thullaccaya* (grave offense) are now designated as "pure" regardless of whether they were formerly heterodox or orthodox, we know that the opening for repentance before the Sangha applies specifically to offenses of the highest grade (*uttamāpatti*).
[Commentary] Third, the characteristics of karma:

[Commentary]: Schism (*saṃghabheda*) is a vocal action; the other four [unwholesome courses of action] are bodily actions. If they are performed in conjunction with one another, speech assists in their completion.

Regarding schism, it cannot be accomplished through bodily manifestation alone; it necessarily requires verbal expression to transform the person before one. That which can effect the schism is an unwholesome vocal action;
that which is split is the nature of disharmony (*asaṃvāsa*).
Within the first section on the characteristics of karma, there are two parts. First, it clarifies that each [of the five] is committed individually; the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"Among these five immediate [offenses], four are bodily and one is vocal karma: three are killing, one is false speech, and one is the preliminary stage (the preliminary stage is synonymous with the means) of killing.

Next, it clarifies that they may be committed mutually. The preceding [passage] clarified that the vocal [karma] is combined with the four types of bodily [karma]; next, it clarifies that the bodily [karma] is not [so combined].

Furthermore, within the text, the subject and object are clarified as being without separate entities; that is to say, because the two—phenomena (事) and principle (理)—are not in harmony, they are designated as "nature" (性), and "nature" is precisely the "entity" (體). [Commentary]:
Regarding the schism of the Saṃgha, it arises from the mind of hatred and jealousy; the remaining four factors are common to all three moral natures (trividha-svabhāva).

Of these two [sections], the first clarifies the schism of the Saṃgha by Devadatta: having seen the Buddha honored and revered by gods and humans, and King Bimbisāra providing him with a thousand chariots daily, he subsequently gave rise to a jealous mind. He conspired with King Ajātaśatru to plot the Buddha’s harm;

furthermore, when he requested the Buddha to allow him to lead the assembly, he was rebuked by the Buddha, which led him to harbor resentment. This clarifies that the schism of the Saṃgha is restricted to unwholesome [states].
The remaining nature is shown below; the other four killings are common to all three natures, and the four immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are the same.

However, since their fundamental nature is unwholesome (*akuśala*), they are incidentally associated with the wholesome and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); thus, they are shown to be "partially common."
[Commentary]: Although one may verbally declare the schism of the Saṃgha, the offense is not yet established; it is only when the other party consents that the breaking of the Wheel is accomplished.

Among the three [types of verbal action], this is distinguished and set apart because the act of uttering words constitutes the specific offense of schism, which is uniquely different from the others.

Since blood does not reach the fruit [of the act], the remaining three cases are identical to the case of killing where life is severed; because they constitute an offense, there is no need for further discussion.
[Commentary] Fourth, regarding the explanation of what is permeable and what is obstructed, one must distinguish them according to time, place, and person.
Regarding the three categories within "penetration and obstruction," that which exists is termed "penetration" (tong), while that which is absent is designated as "obstruction" (sai).
[Commentary]: When the Buddha was present, all five [Dharmacakrapravartana] were extant; after his passing, only the three wheels of the Dharma remain, for he is no longer their presiding master.

At the beginning, when the Buddha was present, there were three [conditions] for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; after his parinirvāṇa, there were three [conditions] for its cessation and two [conditions] for its obstruction. Although the Wheel of Dharma remains, because there is no master to compete in its propagation, both [the turning and the cessation] are lacking.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "two places," Jambudvīpa possesses all five [conditions]; the eastern and western continents both possess three. Shedding blood and causing a schism in the Saṃgha require the presence of the Buddha’s body.
Therefore, in the northern continent (Uttarakuru), there is no mixed state of mind at all; it is said that because their lifespan is fixed, there is no mutual killing.

Regarding the next section, if one discusses presence or absence, the three continents possess it while the northern continent lacks it; however, if one considers completeness versus deficiency, the southern continent is complete while the eastern and western continents are deficient.
The following citation from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* provides scriptural proof for the statement that the lifespan in the northern continent is fixed, citing the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
By practicing the ten virtuous actions with moderate intensity, one is born in Uttarakuru with a lifespan of a thousand years, which is neither subject to decay nor extinction;
therefore, the lifespan of those people is fixed.

[Commentary] Regarding the third point, "people" refers to laypeople and the fourfold assembly of monastics; however, because only the four pārājika offenses—specifically the schism of the Saṃgha—apply to bhikṣus, they alone are fully included.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) and other realms, there are no immediate retributive karmas (*ānantarya-karma*), let alone in other world-systems.
The commentary explains: only human beings, specifically men and women, are capable of committing these karmas; eunuchs and the like are not permitted [to do so].

This is because they lack the causal conditions for precepts, their parents’ kindness toward them is slight, and because they lack complete physical faculties, which would otherwise serve as a basis for increasing [merit], and because they receive little affection. Furthermore...
Because they do not give rise to profound shame toward their parents, animals and spirits are not permitted to commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*);
however, if their intelligence is clear and lucid—like that of a wise horse—they may possess the five deeds of immediate retribution.

Among the three [sections], the first correctly clarifies that there is no confusion regarding laypeople; since those who have not yet received full ordination lack the capacity to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, there are only four [categories].
Furthermore, these also include companions and assistants, as will be explained later. Both [the preceding and following sections] cite a treatise:

the first citation presents a verse from the treatise stating that "other realms" refers to the form and formless heavens; the subsequent citation provides an explanation of the preceding passage, specifically distinguishing the human realm and excluding the *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs).
The three meanings are listed as follows: First, regarding the absence of the cause for precepts, one who possesses the full precepts is alone capable of possessing them;

those such as eunuchs constitute an obstacle to the precepts by their very nature. Next, from the passage on "parents" downward, it clarifies that parental kindness is remote and lacks the quality of being a superior condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), because their physical form and retribution are not excellent.
Furthermore, below this, it reveals that filial respect is thin; thus, even if there is killing, it does not constitute a heinous crime (*ānantarya-karma*).

However, since the text only clarifies that the two offenses against one's parents cannot be committed by others, the meaning of this can be understood. The phrase "beasts and below" (*chù xià*) excludes other realms;

the text distinguishes between existence and non-existence based on the foolish and the wise. According to the treatise, those who can commit these [offenses] may be contrasted with the three immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).

How could there be anyone who is not a beast capable of causing a schism in the Saṃgha or drawing blood from a Tathāgata? The five characters stating that the treatise does not include them must surely be a corruption of the transmission.
[Note] The Buddha was at Vaiśālī, teaching the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to the bhikṣus.
[Commentary] Within the context of the conditions for the precepts, he explains the method for practicing the contemplation of impurity.
In the section on the conditions for the precepts, the initial indication of the locus of the condition refers to the Dharma itself.

[Commentary] Regarding "the contemplation of impurity" (*aśubha-bhāvanā*): the Tathāgata established medicinal remedies to counteract mental illnesses; for excessive greed, he prescribed impurity; for hatred, compassion;

and for delusion—the failure to discern the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*)—he prescribed analytical discrimination. Since this first remedy is directed toward greed, it is called "impurity."

Next, in the general exposition of the section, first there is a comprehensive indication of the three types of medicines and illnesses. "Skandhas" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and "dhātus" refers to the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*);

the text is abbreviated regarding the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). Their correspondence to the three delusions has already been shown as before. If these are correlated with the five cessations (*pañca-nivaraṇa*): the first two are the same as here;

third, for those with much ignorance (*moha*), one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*); fourth, for those with much pride (*māna*), one contemplates the ten [types of pride].

The eight elements (these two may be contrasted with the third), the five types of distracted perceptions, and the numerous inhalations and exhalations (which correspond to the subsequent contemplation); the initial section below specifically points to the present text.
[Commentary]: As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are five kinds [of impurity].
First is the impurity of the seed (*bīja-aśubha*): because one appropriates the forms of the father and mother as one's own, the verse says:
"This body’s seed is impure; it is not some other exquisite treasure. It does not arise from purity, but emerges solely from a foul path."
In the initial section on impurity within the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, it is said:
"Because of the winds of deluded and false recollections and the fire of lustful desire, the blood, marrow, and fat of the parents flow and transform through heat into semen;

the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*), conditioned by past karma, dwells within this red and white semen—this is called the 'seed of the body'. In the verse, the first line indicates the subject, while the following three lines provide the explanation.

The first line establishes that the body itself is impure; the following two lines demonstrate the origin of its impurity—the "foul passage" refers to the place where the parents' excrement was discharged.
[Commentary] Second, regarding the impurity of the locus:
because it exists between the stomach (the receptacle for raw food) and the large intestine (the receptacle for digested food), the verse says: "This body is..."
Foul odors do not arise from among flowers, nor from *campaka* blossoms, nor from precious mountains.
The second locus of reliance is also called the place of birth; humans have two internal repositories, the raw and the cooked.

When food remains in the raw repository and has not yet been transformed, it flows into the cooked repository where it becomes excrement. Because the fetal abode is situated therein, it is said to be impure.
In the verse, the first line introduces the subject, while the following three lines exclude non-pure locations to manifest impurity.
Although the *campaka* is also a flower, it is mentioned separately because it is an exceptionally fine flower, highly prized in that country, and frequently cited in the sūtras and śāstras;
this is the underlying intent. It is translated here as "yellow flower."
[Commentary: Third, impurity in terms of its essential nature refers to the body being composed of thirty-six substances, consisting of twelve internal and twelve external aspects respectively.

Thus, the verse says: "The qualities of earth, water, fire, and wind can transform other things into impurity; even if one were to wash this body by emptying the ocean, it could not be made fragrant or clean."

Regarding the third point, the "substantial entities" (*tattva*), also referred to as the "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), the *Ṣaṭtriṃśat-tattva-śāstra* (Treatise on the Thirty-six Entities) enumerates them in full and categorizes them collectively into three groups;
however, they are somewhat out of order there. Now, for the sake of clarity, I shall divide them according to their meaning:

hair, body hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, muscle, sinew, bone, marrow, blood, heart (these twelve constitute the "body-forming" elements, as the treatise states that there are twelve which pertain to both the internal and external), spleen, kidneys, gallbladder, liver, lungs, small [intestine]...

The small intestine, large intestine, stomach, and bladder (*pāu*; "piao" with the *piao* radical added; the reservoir of water); the fat (*fang*; intestinal grease); the *mēng* (*shan*; stomach grease);

the brain and its membranes—these twelve internal constituents are called "impure by nature. Excrement, urine, filth, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, pus, yellow phlegm, white phlegm, and rheum—these twelve external constituents are called "impure in appearance.
In the verse, the first line indicates their substance, while the second line clarifies their flow.
Regarding the transformation of other impure things, the final two lines of the preceding passage collectively demonstrate impurity.
[Commentary]: Fourth, as for external impurity, because the nine orifices constantly discharge fluids that are all unfit for use, the verse says:
"Various kinds of impure substances fill the interior of the body, constantly overflowing and never ceasing, like a leaking bag filled with goods."
Among the four [types of impurity], the nine orifices—the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, as well as the large and small passages—are explained in the verse:
the first two lines clarify internal filth, while the latter two lines indicate external appearances.
[Commentary: Fifth, ultimate impurity, because it ultimately results in death, bloating, and becomes unbearable to behold; thus the verse says: "Examine and contemplate with precision."
This body ultimately returns to the place of certain death; it is difficult to restrain, devoid of reciprocity, and ungrateful like a small child.
The fifth treatise states: "If the body is cast into fire, it becomes ash; if eaten by insects, it becomes excrement; on the ground, it rots; in water, it swells.
In this verse, the first half indicates the subject and the second half provides the explanation. At that time—
Because they do not remain until evening, they are said to be "difficult to restrain"; because they suddenly depart for eternity, there is no returning;
because they abandon their lifelong sustenance all at once, they are said to be "ungrateful"; and because they resemble small children, this is the nature of their dharma.
[Commentary] Having practiced meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he became weary of his body and life, and thus lamented death and urged others toward it.

[Sub-commentary] The note states that because his cultivation was contrary to the proper method and lacked the means to dispel obstructions, he practiced this contemplation while remaining attached and unable to relinquish it;
consequently, he brought about the destruction of his own body. This is not the mark of one possessed of wisdom.
Among the three [sections], the first part states that while wisdom can dispel stagnation, to cultivate non-wisdom is to deviate from the correct path.

[Commentary]: The *Sujāta-sūtra* asks: "The Buddha is an omniscient person; for what reason did he teach contemplation that caused him to die? The answer is: He clearly perceived his past karmic conditions.
Having once been a hunter who killed many deer, he had already fallen into hell; this was the residual retribution for which he left the household life. If...
It was not said that by observing a person killing and seeing that their malicious mind had ceased, one would rejoice in that act of killing and thereby attain rebirth in heaven;
thus there is no fault. Furthermore, after he had spoken, five hundred people died while he was inside his quiet chamber.
The world did not know of this, but [the Buddha] knew it for certain and established the precepts to pacify worldly conditions.
In the introductory section, it was shown that the Tathāgata’s great wisdom discerns the capacities [of beings] and bestows the medicine of the Dharma;

yet when the illness is not cured, this present occasion of "killing" completely contradicts the aforementioned principle. This treatise sets forth the Buddha’s intention to resolve the doubts of the multitude. While the superficial appearance seems to miss the capacity, in reality, it truly corresponds to the illness.
In the response, first the knowledge of capacities and the resulting benefits are described; subsequently, it is explicitly clarified that the Buddha himself does not lack such knowledge.
He manifests as being the same as ordinary people, which is why it is said he is "of the same world" (*saha-loka*). If he were not thus, he would inevitably provoke external slander;
therefore, it is said he "silences criticism. [Note: The bhikṣu Nandika was hired to kill a lay devotee and terrified him.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that Nanda was hired as a laborer, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* says he was a śramaṇa of a non-Buddhist sect who kept a small amount of hair on his head, lived in dependence upon the bhikṣus, and sustained himself by gathering leftover food.
The *Zhongzhu* (Commentary on the Essentials) regarding the hiring of a killer states that the term "bhikṣu" is glossed as "śramaṇa.

Because these two names apply to both the heterodox and the orthodox, those who retain a small amount of hair distinguish themselves from the internal community [of the Buddha’s disciples], while also wearing robes of dyed color (*kāsāya*). One serves to cover the body, and one is placed upon the shoulder. Question:
What kind of person constitutes the conditions for violating this precept? Answer: According to the subsequent censure, it refers to one who possesses the outward appearance [of a monk].
The remark concerning the bhikṣus of the inner assembly and the outsiders being hired is not the *nidāna* (introductory narrative).
[Note] The Buddha, knowing this matter, then expounded the dharma of *dhyāna*.
[Commentary] When it says "the Buddha, knowing this matter, then expounded the dharma of *dhyāna*," it refers to the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

In the first section of the "Explanation of the Revised Contemplation," the methods of *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) are also termed gates of contemplation; thus, they are explained by means of "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
While "stopping the mind" is called *dhyāna* and "illuminating the object" is called "contemplation," both the contemplation of impurity and the counting of breaths possess these two gates.

As for why the explanatory notes differ between the preceding and following sections, it is because the contemplation of impurity primarily takes illuminating the object as its focus, whereas the counting of breaths is predominantly situated in stopping the mind.
[Commentary: The reason for changing the perspective is that previously one was confronted with excessive greed, so the contemplation of impurity was taught;

however, for those whose thoughts are not primarily governed by that [greed], it is not the primary remedy, and thus counting the breaths was taught. Alternatively, while the previous observation of form was coarse, the present observation of the mind is subtle.

The explanation of the "intention" (*manas*) has two parts. First, regarding the suitability of the practitioner, it is like prescribing medicine according to the illness; alternatively, second, it is distinguished as coarse or subtle based on the object of observation.
By seeking the mind within form, one proceeds from the coarse to the subtle and from the shallow to the deep; therefore, it is appropriate to revise [the sequence].

[Commentary: Regarding the explanation of counting the breaths, as detailed extensively in the treatise—namely, first counting, second following, third stopping, fourth contemplating, fifth returning, and sixth purifying—these are all methods for calming distraction to gradually harmonize the mind.

Since the treatises of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna within the *Śāstrasaṃdarśana* (Demonstration of the Dharma) all contain methods of contemplation, I shall here refer to them collectively by simply saying "according to the treatise.
Now, following the explanation in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it says: "Counting" (*gaṇanā*) refers to counting the inhalations and exhalations from one to ten. There are three ways of counting:

if [the count] is equal (counting ten as ten), if it exceeds, or if it falls short (all of which deviate from the method of counting). "Following" (*anugama*) means the mind follows the inhalations and exhalations. "Fixing" (*sthāpanā*) means...
This means causing the mind to abide in the inhalation and exhalation. "Contemplation" (vipaśyanā) refers to seeing the breath bound to the body like a thread through a pearl;
it is also called "turning," which means turning the body's focus toward the mind so that the mind becomes manifest.
"Purity" (viśuddhi) refers to being free from all afflictions and difficulties, whereby the mind attains purification. This concludes the explanation of the intent of contemplation.
[Commentary] A bhikṣu, having cultivated and realized the higher fruits [of the path], formulated this precept because he censured the faults of those above him.
[Sub-commentary] "Cultivating and attaining the higher fruits" refers to the noble, untainted [attainments] that transcend the stage of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the phrase "attaining the fruit of the noble ones who are free from outflows" (*anāsrava*), this refers to those among the four types of noble ones (*ārya*).
[Commentary] Question: When the Tathāgata taught the Dharma and a bhikṣu, relying on that teaching, deeply contemplated impurity (*aśubha*), this was precisely practicing according to what was said.

What fault was there, such that he was further rebuked? Answer: The Buddha taught the contemplation of impurity to cause one to weary of the root of suffering; if one wishes to cultivate its abandonment, one must... [text continues].
If the cause of the aggregates of consciousness is not severed, how can the cause of their accumulation be eliminated? This does not merely mean that the fruit cannot be exhausted;
it causes the causes of delusion to deepen further. Thus, practicing a path that is not the Way is greatly to be censured. As the Sūtra says:
"The body has suffering," yet it does not say to feel weary of and seek detachment from the body—this is a fine proof [of the point].

Within the section on "Reproach" (*garhaṇā*), there is an inquiry that follows the sequence without contradiction; however, as the meaning of the reproach seems inappropriate, it is resolved by means of a question and answer.

This answer is divided into four parts: first, clarifying the intent of the teaching; second, [explaining] how below this, even monks today do not know the reason why they cast themselves into fire or water, hoping for transcendence;
third, showing that while the causes of suffering have not been eliminated, how could one expect to escape the three [realms]? Fourth, [the conclusion].

To face death with no regrets is truly the mark of a man of singular courage; yet, while one might think that existence ends forever and rebirth never occurs, how could one know that as this life perishes, another emerges?

Therefore, one must diligently cultivate the Three Studies, widely apply the Four Great Vows, recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sutras, and keep in mind the auspicious names of the Buddhas, hoping to attain deliverance at the Dragon Flower Assembly and pointing toward the Land of Peaceful Nurturing as one's destination.
Those who take refuge [in the Dharma] deeply loathe birth and death, clearly understand cause and effect, and desire to eliminate the root of suffering; the essential point lies herein.

Therefore, the following clarifies the combined reprimand as in the Sūtra, and the subsequent citation of evidence generally indicates the Sūtra, for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna clarify this and it cannot be pointed to specifically.
The *Śāsanāntara-sūtra* says: "This is that which one should abandon, the substance of evil," and so on, up to: "There is only..."
When the Wise One had received the five hundred questions concerning the extinction [of the deceased] and so forth, he answered: "Who would rebuke those who have already died?

He replied that it is those who receive and practice the method of contemplation and are encouraged by praise who are many; the discourse clarifies that the five hundred were cited as having already died, and it is precisely for their sake that one reforms their contemplation—that they are the ones to be rebuked.

[Commentary] Second, regarding the text within the *Prātimokṣa*, there are six phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, "with one's own hand," clarifying that it is one's own karma;
third, "human life," clarifying the object to be killed; fourth, "holding a knife," etc., clarifying the karma of inciting others;
fifth, "this bhikṣu," etc., which brings the person under the charge of the offense; sixth, the characteristics of the formal act of *pravāsanīya* (banishment).
[Vinaya]: "If a bhikṣu intentionally cuts [a living being] with his own hand.
[Commentary]: The first phrase is easily understood.

Regarding the second point, within the context of taking one's own life, the inclusion of the word "intentionally" (hugu) excludes cases where it was done by mistake; such instances do not constitute a violation of the Dharma.
Next, the second phrase of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is explained. [Note:

This refers to what is called "committing killing. Whether one kills oneself, or instructs another to kill, or dispatches a messenger to kill, or uses a messenger who travels back and forth to kill, or uses a secondary messenger to kill, or acts through a succession of intermediaries to kill, or seeks out a man to kill, or instructs another to seek out such a man.
Whether one kills oneself; or seeks out a wielder of a blade to kill; or instructs another to seek out a wielder of a blade to kill;
or manifests signs with the body; or speaks with the voice; or manifests signs with both body and voice; or instructs another to utter praise [of death];

or sends a letter; or instructs another to send a letter; or causes a pitfall; or uses a lever; or administers poison; or provides the means for killing and other such expedients—this constitutes killing.
[Sūtra] Furthermore.
[Commentary] In the commentary, the characteristics of the various acts of killing are extensively listed and divided into two parts. First, killing by oneself, which has eight aspects:
(1) killing by oneself; (2) physical gestures; (3) verbal speech; (4) both body and speech together; (5) using pits and traps; (6) using weapons or forceful means; (7) administering poison.
Regarding the eight ways of providing the means for killing and the eleven ways of instructing others to do so: first, dispatching a messenger; second, sending a messenger back and forth;

third, using a triple messenger; fourth, using a successive messenger; fifth, seeking out the person; sixth, instructing someone to seek out the person; seventh, seeking out the one who wields the blade; eighth, instructing someone to seek out the one who wields the blade;
ninth, dispatching a letter; tenth, instructing someone to dispatch a letter; eleventh, dispatching a messenger to praise [the act].
In the general classification of the commentary, the items are grouped by category rather than following the sequential order of the text.
[The Sub-commentary] states: "To kill oneself" means to personally carry out the act of killing; whether by one's own body or by a staff, whatever causes death constitutes this offense.
"Suicide can resolve it.
[Commentary] "To teach killing" means either to instruct another to kill, or merely to instruct another in the means for dying.
"To dispatch an agent to kill" means to point out the location where the victim is and go there to harm them. "The messenger who goes and returns" refers to one who receives [the order].
This refers to one who sends [a messenger] to kill, and upon that person's arrival at the destination, returns again to send another; this is what is meant by "repeatedly.

Regarding "successive" messengers: it means that after the first messenger has been sent to kill, that messenger does not go himself but instead sends another, and so on in succession until a hundred thousand people have been dispatched, with the very last person among them actually severing the victim's life.

In these cases, depending on the preceding circumstances, all instances of sending a messenger once, or even up to multiple successive rounds of messengers going and returning, are treated according to the same rule regarding the offense.

Other matters involving formal agreements where the intentions do not coincide or where things are not as desired are all explained as previously stated in the section on "Establishing the Principles.
Furthermore, the four types of seeking mentioned below all involve instructing others in mutual conduct.

Regarding the eight types of instructing others, according to the text, there appear to be nine; since "instructing to kill" was not listed among the previous general classifications, we know that this phrase in the commentary serves as a general heading for the specific characteristics listed below.
In the section on indirect action (*pāramparyeṇa*), the phrase "even down to" definitively establishes that the two preceding cases are likewise offenses;
thus, it should be understood that "sending a messenger" is included by implication and therefore not explicitly mentioned. The remainder refers to other cases that differ.
As previously stated, within the section on "acting oneself or instructing others," there may be differences in the intention of the instructor toward those they employ;

or, at times, due to discrepancies in timing—such as being too early or late—or in posture—such as sitting or standing—due to insanity, the relinquishing of precepts, and so forth, the instructor incurs no offense.

However, if the mind is frivolous or lacks focus, one incurs an offense for every action performed. Below, a brief indication of the four types of seeking is given. Regarding "seeking a man," this refers to desire.
When a brave warrior goes to harm another who is holding a sword, such as those among the *caṇḍālas*, it is because both parties seek it for themselves and both cause others to seek it;
since neither commits the act alone, it is said that "both instruct others."
[Commentary: Regarding "the manifestation of signs through the body," this refers to causing [others] to fall into ravines or abysses out of fear, or showing signs such as death.
Regarding "the manifestation of signs through speech," this refers to using words to praise or encourage death, or using a loud voice to intimidate others into dying;
it is just like those in the world who loathe their own bodies and either throw themselves into fire, leap from cliffs, or commit suicide by dismemberment with a blade or by hanging with a rope.
Those who do not know how to instruct [the practitioner] may join their palms and chant "Excellent," or assist them in ascending the mountain, or provide them with ropes and equipment;
these are those who praise the instruction while simultaneously manifesting both body and speech in violation of the Dharma. This is precisely such a class of people.
Within the manifestation of signs, the body manifests two meanings: first, displaying a terrifying countenance; second, assuming the posture of one about to die.

The mouth also manifests two aspects as per the text. Regarding "one's own part" (*jibun*), this refers to the subsequent explanation. "Manifesting both" means: first, citing the actual occurrence to resolve the transgression; "hanging" (*e*) is read as *kei* (to calculate/plan);
"assisting those who climb the mountain" means helping them to throw themselves from the cliff. This concludes the combination of the sections below.

The teaching on the characteristics of the text (*vyañjana-lakṣaṇa*) consists of providing assistance and preparation, corresponding to the manifestation of body below; the teaching on praise (*praśaṃsā*) consists of joining the palms and chanting "Excellent" (*sādhu*), corresponding to the manifestation of speech below.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "the teaching causes one to praise," it means sending someone to speak to another person, causing that person to speak to the victim who was killed, so as to generate a great multitude of people.

The phrase "the sin is not as grave as dying early" is an expression of praise from within the introductory section of the teaching; it is precisely the two lines from the *Prātimokṣa* (Sūtra of Precepts) stating,
"Better death than a wicked life."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "sending a letter of death," this refers to manifesting signs through one's person upon paper and ink to cause a person to die.

As stated in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Duo-lun), if a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a monk (*bhikṣu*) knows the signs of good or bad fortune and causes another country to be destroyed, thereby gaining wealth or life for themselves, it constitutes the same grave offense as killing or stealing.
If one composes a letter of death and instructs someone to send it to that person, or directs a messenger to speak of it to their relatives, [the same applies].

The Way of Heaven accords with the correctness of humanity; therefore, it is said that it "sustains and nurtures," and so forth. The following section clarifies the meaning of this reiterated expression. [Commentary]:

That which is called "life-force" (*jīvitendriya*) refers to the maintenance of this provisional retribution-body until the end of its single physical lifespan. Because it is the fundamental cause [of existence], it is termed the "life-faculty.

It is called the life-faculty because it sustains consciousness, causing it to abide and dwell [within the body]. This is as described in the *Prakaraṇapāda* regarding the essence of the life-faculty.

This is neither form nor mind; it is simply because the past karma of sentient beings has determined that its timing lies here, and thus the physical form is maintained and held together without interruption.

Therefore, although the breath of one who has died has ceased, wherever there is warmth, consciousness remains therein; this abode of consciousness is what is subsumed under the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

In the first section of the "Explanation of Life" (*āyus*), there are three parts. First, the explanation of the name: life (*jīvita*) has no separate substance; it is the length or brevity of life that constitutes a person's lifespan.

Therefore, it is said that the fundamental capacity (*indriya*) is able to sustain consciousness (*vijñāna*); because it is the basis of life, it receives the name of a "faculty" (*indriya*). As shown below regarding its essence:
because it lacks physical form and is distinct from consciousness, it is not subsumed under either of those two [categories]. Below this, the manifestation is revealed.
Since the preceding section has already described the karmic causes and conditions for rebirth, the following portion correctly demonstrates the characteristics of life (*jīvita*).

Because life exists through the mutual dependence of these three factors—warmth (*uṣman*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*)—as long as warmth and the functions of breath and consciousness have not been abandoned, and the constituent elements of birth have not been severed, this constitutes life.
