In this Vinaya, the dragon is cited as the primary example while others are not mentioned. If one harms [a being] knowing its true nature, the offense is determined according to the rules (*vinaya*);
if one harms it without knowing, the offense is likewise concluded according to the rules. Both cases are explained in detail as listed in the "Conditions" (*paccaya*) section above.

In the section on animals within the *Śīla-skandha*, the first sentence divides the sūtra into two judgments: the wise and the foolish. Under "the wise," there is a detailed explanation of the transformation of wisdom, which is divided into four parts:
first, clarifying the intent of the offense; second, as below, distinguishing and eliminating confusion; third, as below, indicating the characteristics to mark differences;

and fourth, citing the *Ji-zhi-guai-lu* (Records of the Strange), which is a secular work chronicling marvelous events—wherein the Vinaya specifically cites dragons because they frequently possess the power of transformation.

Although this is brief, the meaning of the remaining cases can be understood by analogy. If one determines an offense according to the Vinaya based on whether it was committed intentionally or unknowingly, then for intentional acts, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);
for those committed unknowingly, one follows the standard rule of the Vinaya and incurs a *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession).

As for the subsequent references to "abbreviations" (*saṃkṣepa*), these are already explained within the "Three Approaches" (*tri-yāna*) section of the aforementioned meaning; therefore, it says "as above. Furthermore, regarding the omission of conditions, the latter refers to non-human animals (*tiryagyoni*).
Because the conditions (*pratyaya*) are identical while the gravity of the offense differs, it is said that "the conditions are fully enumerated.
[Commentary: Regarding the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*), the textual analysis is extremely clear. As for the reason why there is no offense, it is as the text says:
"In all cases, there is no harm."

The commentary on "no offense" briefly indicates the general meaning; divided according to the sub-commentary, there are two parts. First, throwing objects or performing tasks—these all constitute accidental contact.
This "accident," however, arises from other matters and is entirely devoid of a harmful intent, which differs from the "error" explained previously.
Students should understand this. Second, returning and going forth [of objects] constitutes unintentional action.
[Vinaya] Not to live in communion.
[Vinaya] The fourth precept on great falsehood.
[Commentary] The fourth precept on great falsehood.
[Commentary: Next, the dharmas violated through verbal karma are explained.

Regarding the precept against great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*), the initial heading distinguishes [the three types of karma]; among these, the first three are bodily karmas. Since the body is the basis of karma, they are listed first.
Verbal karma depends upon the body, and thus it follows next. Since these two types of karma differ, it is pointed out first [here].
[Commentary]: Since ancient times, translators of the scriptures have generally manifested the characteristics [of karma] by means of action (*karman*), often referring to them as "body and speech.

In the present time of formal translation, however, we carefully determine the names and essences so that they do not confuse the object with the mind. Therefore, whatever originates from sound is collectively designated as vocal karma;

this is what the Sūtra refers to when it speaks of "right speech" (*samyag-vāc*). The reason for this is that the opening of a person's face is called the "mouth" (*mukha*); the mouth is merely a dull material form (*rūpa*) that only knows...

Regarding exhalation and inhalation, their detrimental effects are largely subsumed under the *Śarīra-saṃgraha-śāstra*. Although the four types of false speech emerge from the mouth, they must be distinguished as courses of action (*karmapatha*) by means of vocal characteristics.
However, how could the production of sound be limited to the mouth alone? Only when there is no obstruction in seven locations does speech come to be formed;
the rest may be omitted for now.
The title is translated here for the first time; it is shown that all translations from the Han, Wei, Qin, and Jin dynasties onward were like this.
Next, the translation from the Tang dynasty is clarified, hence it says "nowadays. The text consists of two sections:

the first reveals that the current [translation] achieves both [requirements], such that the term and its essence correspond, and the term accords with the faculty of hearing, so that the object and the mind do not become confused. The following section cites a sutra.
The ancient masters established that the three karmas are collectively designated as "speech," and when listing the Eightfold Path, they referred to it as "right speech.
Therefore, they cited the Eightfold Path to prove that what is attained now is the reality. Next, the two errors of the ancients are set forth; first, it clarifies to which category speech belongs.
In the treatise below, the characteristics of these errors are correctly presented: since speech arises from sound and is perceived by the ear, the mouth belongs to the physical form of the body.

If one were to claim that it is seen by the eye, then the realms of mind and objects would become confused. Furthermore, speech is produced based on sound, which subsequently constitutes karmic action;

yet the mouth is a dull material form (rūpa) that is inherently neither good nor evil, and thus the name and its substance would be discordant. However, [the author] has secretly anticipated an external objection here, fearing that one might say:

"Since sound issues from the mouth and names and meanings are manifested through the vocal organs, what fault is there in this? Why then is it pointed out and refuted? This is why [the following passage] was written.
Regarding the clarification that this does not comprehensively encompass the seven locations, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is like a person who wishes to speak;
the wind from within the mouth enters and reaches the navel, where it strikes the navel and produces a resonance. When the resonance emerges, it touches the seven locations before receding.
This is what is called speech. A verse says: "The wind named *udāna* touches the navel and ascends; this wind touches the seven locations, including the neck and..."
The gums, teeth, shoulders, tongue, throat, and chest—speech arises from these. One should discern the essential nature and characteristics of vocal action (*vākkarman*):

phonemes (*akṣara*), phrases (*pada*), and names (*nāman*) depend upon sound; thus, sound itself constitutes their substance, which only then manifests. The translations of the names and meanings in ancient versions are entirely inconsistent;
since this has not been explained in detail here, it is said to be "briefly summarized."

[Commentary: As for why verbal karma is fully enumerated as four with false speech placed at the head: it is because this transgression arises frequently, following along with fundamental afflictions and karmic actions.
Since beginningless ignorance has never failed to involve deception and falsehood—such as claiming what does not exist to exist—there are many such examples.

Now that you have left the household life, you ought to realize the falsity [of these delusions], clarify and purify yourself to achieve purity, and return to the source to realize the True. Why do you not contemplate this so as to increase [your merit] rather than further increasing [your faults]?
Deception is deeply blameworthy; therefore, it is listed first among the grave offenses. As for the remaining instances of abuse and praise, they are minor and thus listed later.

Regarding the sequence—prior, posterior, and intermediate—the first section raises the inquiry, which is then resolved by the following explanation. This is divided into two parts: first, describing how false speech is grave and how delusion is formed through unreality;
second, showing that based on delusion, karma arises, which becomes increasingly unreal. Thus, this false speech accords with these two [factors]: ignorance and... [the rest of the sentence follows].
The phrases "that which is delusive, deceptive, and false" and "that which is karma, not being existent," etc., demonstrate the characteristics of false speech;
because the various types enumerated later are manifold, it is said that they are "not one. Below this, the faults are revealed.

Above, it clarifies what ought to be done but was not done—*t'ai* (汰) means to wash away—as clarified below. Below this, it clarifies doing what should not be done. Therefore, the following provides the conclusion.

The first phrase clarifies the gravity of false speech; the subsequent lines reveal the relative gravity of the remaining offenses. This means that at the end of the four pārājikas, this is the first of the four karmas;
alternatively, it may be "heavy" because it is the first of the great falsehoods, as the preceding text discusses both major and minor offenses together.
As for "flattery," since it is inseparable from slander and frivolous speech, it is not mentioned separately.

[Commentary]: However, many people revile these false appearances because once words are spoken, they cannot be retracted. Therefore, one uses meaning to expand upon consciousness in order to recognize their non-substantiality through four gates:
first, [showing] that the capacity for falsehood resides in ordinary beings and not in the Sage’s intent; second, clarifying the five distinct types of false speech among ordinary beings;

third, establishing falsehood as speech by dividing its characteristics into two parts; fourth, [showing that] the original deception is intended to bring about realization and does not depend on [external validation].
Faith. Within the "Manifestation of Delusion," one reversal refers to the sudden contradiction [of reality]. "Unable to be pursued" describes its swiftness;

as the *Analects* says, "Four horses cannot overtake the tongue. This first presents the four gates: first, distinguishing the sage from the ordinary person; second, distinguishing the heavy from the light.
Three points clarify the distinction between falsehood and reality; four points clarify knowledge and faith.
[Commentary] In the first section, it is explained that the person capable of delusion exists among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and not among the noble ones (*ārya*).

[Commentary] This is because those noble ones possess two kinds of truthful speech: first, realization through the body (*kāyaprativedha*); second, realization through thought and mind (*saṃjñā-citta*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the term "bodily realization" (kāyasākṣin): when one has perfected the cultivation of the Way and its virtue, and realized the Truth to its ultimate limit; when delusions and falsehoods have been severed and eliminated to their end;

when upon emerging from contemplation one speaks with words that necessarily accord with reality and whose meaning is free from deception or betrayal; and when the faults of deceit and falsehood no longer arise—this is what constitutes bodily realization.

In the first section of the "Realization through the Body" (*kāyasākṣin*) within the initial gate, the first four lines—beginning with the description of the body-realizer’s cultivation—correspond to the Four Truths.
Following this, the "utterance of truth" clarifies that this realization is based on mental verification; yet, this noble path cannot be accomplished without the body.

While the mental path is profound and subtle, it is manifested through its formal characteristics. Thus, the *Vinaya-vastu* states: "Among those who are body-realizers, both the Sūtras and the Vinaya declare them to be the foremost."

Question: "In a future life, one shall obtain this. When asked about the explanation given upon emerging from meditation, [the response was: "If one has truly attained the Way, will there not be an offense?
Answer: "The prohibitions of the precepts are not yet complete;

therefore, it does not obstruct those of like intent. [Commentary: However, that sage, through the preparatory means (*prayoga*) prior to meditative concentration, naturally engaged in both principle-contemplation (*li-guan*) and phenomenon-observation (*shi-cha*), and heard of the wonders of other realms.

After [Maudgalyāyana] emerged from his meditative absorption, he related what he had seen to me as follows: "While I was in the concentration of the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna-samādhi*), I beheld these signs.
Others, not understanding this, gave rise to doubt and wonder, asking: "How can one attain the vision of such extraordinary signs through the wisdom of emptiness?

This is merely Maudgalyāyana falsely claiming a superior dharma. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there were indeed such instances; the Buddha said that while it was true, the concentration was not pure. This refers to the former case.
"Expedient means" refers to speech, concentration, the essence [of the practice], such phenomena, signs, thought, mind, and truthful words.

Regarding the thought and mind within the reality of these, we shall provisionally rely on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* to clarify their characteristics by citing the case of Maudgalyāyana entering the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
The text is divided into four parts: first, it shows the thought and mind as he is about to enter concentration; he gathers his mind and forms a correct visualization, when suddenly he sees...

Because it is a distinct matter and not the ultimate fixed concentration, it is said that the principle-observation of skillful means (*upāya*) is precisely the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), while the factual investigation is precisely skillful means.
Furthermore, the following citation from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* records Maudgalyāyana’s own account:

Maudgalyāyana told the bhikṣus, "When I entered the concentration of the wisdom of emptiness, I heard the sound of the elephant Airāvaṇa entering the waters of Lake Nanda. (The Vinaya text lists many such instances; those required...)

Investigating the remainder: the three citations below address the bhikṣus’ doubts; having seen these signs, they realized it was not the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*). The *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] agrees with this, hence the reference below;
the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is likewise. The four citations from the Buddha below resolve their doubts: "In the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), there is nothing;

in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it is neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); the sphere of [neither-perception-nor-]non-perception is also thus. The final two lines conclude and demonstrate the point: if one speaks according to what is perceived, why is it called "perception" (*saṃjñā*) alone?

If one answers truthfully regarding the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) prior to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), while claiming that the essence of the absorption itself is identical to false speech, there is no offense; this is simply because one does not recognize [the distinction] and forms the perception that it is a "correct absorption.
[Commentary: Question: If, as cited above, both types are truthful, then when citing those Great Sages (the Buddhas), would they also have these two types? Answer: As follows...
When one comes to illuminate the objects of perception, they are entirely exhausted; there is only the realization of the body. This is why it is called "true speech. As for the reason for this:

the Śrāvakas perceive objects as having obstructions, and their two types of inferior functions differ. When entering [samādhi], they penetrate beyond sight and hearing; when emerging, they are like ordinary people in their perceptions and views.
Because this principle exists, they still possess conceptual thought and mind. The Buddha is not like this; the opposite of the former can be understood. Therefore, Vimalakīrti—
The *Cloud of the Constant Samādhi* states that one perceives all Buddha-lands; furthermore, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* says:
"Because one has forever severed the delusions of dreams and conceptual thoughts, the mind of non-conceptualization is true speech.
In response to the question, the preceding two statements merely refer to the limited sages (śrāvakas), whereas this answer clarifies how the ultimate sage differs from them.

In the first part of the middle section, it is marked that the ocean of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is fathomed only by the Buddha; because he has realized the ultimate principle and speaks in accordance with reality, there is no divergent thought.

Below, the text investigates and explains this: first, it describes that the Lesser Sages possess conceptual thought (*saṃjñā*), stating they are "obstructed," which refers to their being equal to ordinary people as explained below;
it calls their function "inferior," which refers to the inequality of their entry and exit as explained below. This is due to...
The realization of the wisdom of partial emptiness is not the ultimate perfection, for while it eliminates coarse afflictions, one still remains deluded regarding phenomena.

The Buddha next clarifies that the Tathāgata is without conceptual thought (*asaṃjñin*), which contrasts with the former [state], as his illumination of objects is unimpeded and his entering and emerging from meditation are equal.
The following passage cites scriptural evidence; first, to prove this equality, that sutra records the various brahmins asking: "Who in the world possesses the divine eye?"

Vimalakīrti replied: "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, constantly abides in samādhi; his meditative resolve is never deficient. He perceives all buddha-fields without ever speaking of them as being equal.
Furthermore, this serves as proof for the non-obstruction [of the dharmadhātu], for it arises from the conceptualizing mind due to a failure to understand the objective realm.
Since the Buddha has attained unimpeded penetration, how could he have any such conceptualization? This passage cites various bodhisattvas praising the Buddha.

The verse reads: "How great! The Greatly Awakened, the Great Holy Lord" (this line offers a general praise of the three bodies; the following lines offer specific praise of each). Stainless, undefiled, and unattached (the Dharma-body);
Teacher who tames gods and men like an elephant or horse, whose fragrance of the Way and virtue perfumes all (the Response-body);
Wisdom is serene, emotions stilled, anxieties dissolved, and the mind tranquil; consciousness ceases and the mind is also silent, forever severing dreams and delusions.

Thoughts and perceptions no longer possess the various elements (dhātus), aggregates (skandhas), or sense bases (āyatanas) [because the retributive body is false and lacks reality, and thus thoughts are likened to dreams].
[Commentary]: Because those ordinary beings below lack the two kinds of truthful speech of the sages, their words deceive others and cause them to have false understandings;
therefore, they incur the fault of falsehood.
This can be clearly understood through the explanation regarding ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

[Commentary] Question: The bodies and minds of ordinary persons also possess "real speech within phenomena" that realizes the truth, such as when one says to another, "I have personally realized suffering and pleasure.

This does not hinder their delusion or forgetfulness; yet, even while their perceptions contradict the actual state of the object, they speak words of truth. Why is it that the Vinaya does not establish an offense for them, as it does for others?

Question: What is the difference between the conceptualization of reality by a sage and that of others? Answer: Although there may be instances where [others] do not commit an offense, their conceptualizations based on recollective mindfulness are not derived from correct understanding.

Because they have not yet severed the fundamental mind of falsehood and delusion, they may later speak in contradiction to their own minds and contrary to their thoughts, thereby resulting in false speech once again.
Since such a distinction exists, they are not the same as sages.

In the question, he first describes the "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*) to distinguish it from intellectual understanding; thus he says, "In the matter [of practice], one does not descend. This directly challenges the notion of "conceptual mind.

Above, he designates "bodily realization," where principle and phenomenon are distinct. When discussing how deluded concepts involve both the holy and the ordinary as common objects, since confusion and intermixture are permitted, the meaning must necessarily be distinguished.
Regarding why the Vinaya does not establish [a formal offense] for this: great falsehoods permit overweening pride (*abhimāna*), whereas minor falsehoods are only...
Regarding the initial demonstration of the difference from "the thought of understanding" (*prativedha-saṃjñā*) within the response to the objection concerning "bondage":

because one realizes through wisdom that the mind is illusory and gives rise to conceptualization based on this realization, it is called the "thought of understanding. Since ordinary sentiment calculates things as real, this is the reason for their difference. As for the subsequent inference of the cause of this difference:

it is truly because the fundamental delusion of ordinary beings has not yet been eliminated; even if they were to dispel their confusion, they would still subsequently harbor thoughts of contradiction.
As stated above, because the noble ones have already eliminated the fetters and afflictions, even if their thoughts should occasionally deviate, they will certainly never speak falsely.

[Commentary] Next, it is explained that the false speech of ordinary beings is immeasurable according to its conditions; however, as for the definitive naming of the offenses, they do not exceed five categories:
*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, *pāyattika*, and *duṣkṛta*.
Next, the five specific categories are explained.
[Commentary]: Regarding these five stages, they are divided into two groups. [Commentary]:

As for why the two types of falsehood—those of the *īryāpatha* (postures) and the *lābha* (gains)—are equally grave deceptions when compared to supramundane dharmas, it is because ordinary people, in relation to the supramundane...

When the Dharma has not yet been truly realized, to falsely claim to have attained realization and thereby deceive others for the sake of seeking fame and profit constitutes a grave offense of profound harm;
thus, one incurs an extremely heavy penalty. If, however, one uses such words to deceive non-humans (amanuṣya), the harm is somewhat lighter, and thus one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
These distinctions in the degree of severity are unique to the case of the "non-ordinary Dharma" (i.e., the claim of spiritual attainment).

Regarding the first two [categories], the former indicates the general principle while the latter provides the detailed explanation. First, it describes deceiving humans; next, it describes deceiving non-humans.

These two cases are distinguished by the difference in their objects despite the similarity of the speech, and thus they are categorized as light and heavy respectively. "Jiao" (交) means "to meet"; "shao" (稍) means "slightly less.
The final section concludes the discussion.
[Commentary: Regarding the fact that while the other three types of false speech are identical in using worldly conventions to deceive others, their offenses differ:

it is because slander arises easily from ordinary emotions; one falsely constructs empty appearances without the three roots [of greed, hatred, or delusion], deceiving the Saṃgha with a more serious offense.

Seeing that the person has committed an offense, one intends for them to be disciplined and expelled, so that they remain forever outside the community; because the circumstances are particularly grave, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṃghāvaśeṣa). Furthermore, there are two...
Regarding the offenses committed in this chapter: since the act of deceiving the Sangha by slandering what was seen or heard is minor, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;

because the act of speaking untruths in jest violates dignified decorum (*vīrya-īryāpatha*) only slightly, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, the third stage establishes the worldly custom of not wearing mourning garments.

Regarding the remaining three [categories], the first provides a general indication while the subsequent sections provide detailed explanations. First, the great slander is clarified; next, the minor slander is explained.
It should be understood that the minor falsehood is not treated as a *pārājika* offense because its nature is self-evident. Below, the frivolous falsehood is clarified.

These three types of speech differ in their verbal expression but are identical in their objective referents (*ālambana*), thereby demonstrating their distinctions. Third, the concluding indication: the character "fu" (服) is an error and should be read as "fei" (非).

[Commentary: Above, the distinction between ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*) was established based on a general summary of their respective meanings; now, by examining this through the lens of the teachings, there are specific paths and precedents:
some say that an ordinary person may receive a heavy [karmic retribution], while others say that a sage may receive a light one.
Next, in citing the scriptures to investigate the arising [of phenomena], one should further establish a distinct path, namely that there are many specific characteristics.
As for the phrase "it possesses its own," the various characteristics cited subsequently are all categorized according to these two [aspects] as they appear in the text.
[Commentary]: Why is this so? As the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one says, 'I have not yet attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin,' or says that one has lost it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one says that one has attained it, it is a grave offense (*guru*).
The first passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra* concerns the gravity or lightness of great falsehood as asked by Upāli of the Buddha; this continues through the subsequent text.

Regarding the Buddha’s response concerning those who have attained the stage of *anāgāmin* but not yet [the higher fruits], he has enumerated all four fruits in detail; in this present text, they are abbreviated.

Below, the text proceeds by means of questions and answers involving specific individuals to clarify the terminology, often omitting the introductory phrases of the questions with the word "乃至" (*naiti*, meaning "up to" or "and so forth").
As for the term "偷蘭" (*sthūla*), this refers to the light offense incurred by claiming to have attained the state of an *ārya*.

[Commentary]: Some say that today [the monk] did not enter the meditative absorption of the world (*lokasamādhi*), while those before him asked, "What was it like yesterday? He replied, "It was the same; I did not enter.

All these cases are considered *pācittiya* (offenses involving confession) because they are deemed to be near to the characteristics of a noble one (*ārya*). Therefore, they are classified as *pācittiya*.
Next, regarding the statement that the meditative absorptions of the form and formless realms are called "worldly concentrations" (laukika-samādhi) and do not constitute an offense:

by saying they do not constitute an offense here, it is implied that they do constitute an offense at other times. Furthermore, the text states that if one says the dhyāna-methods result in a *pārājika* offense, this refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) incurring a grave offense.

[Commentary]: Or, if one says, "I am a learner," and when asked what constitutes being a learner, one replies, "I am one who is learned, possesses sharp faculties, and is proficient in meditation, recitation, and wisdom," one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
To claim to be a person who has attained the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) training is a grave offense.
The relative gravity among these three cases can be understood.

[Commentary]: Alternatively, it may be said that from "I am one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) down to answering "I am indolent and do not study," claiming to be a noble one beyond training constitutes a grave offense.
Among the four [offenses], the one involving indolence (*kausīdya*) is also classified as a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) because its characteristics overlap with those of a *pācittiya*.

[Commentary]: If one says, "I have nothing," "I have no fear of lacking a livelihood," or "I have no fear of the great assembly," and even replies, "I have no robes or bowl," this is called "having nothing.
A *thullaccaya* for claiming freedom from greed and delusion while severing the five fears is grave.

Among the five [fears], "having nothing" (*akiñcana*) is excluded because it would overlap with the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); "lack of livelihood" (*ājīva-śaṅkā*) and the others are excluded because they would overlap with the virtues of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
The Noble Ones are free from the five kinds of fear. The text cites the first and the last;

the second is the fear of ill repute (*aśloka-śaṅkā*), the third is the fear of death (*maraṇa-śaṅkā*)—the former being the fear of not surviving, while this refers to the fear of dying—and the fourth is the fear of the evil destinies (*durgati-śaṅkā*). The answer is that even for one who lacks robes and bowl, these are excluded because the terminology overlaps with other meanings. Thus it is concluded.
Lan’s answer—that he is free from greed and so forth—is a usurpation of the virtues of a Sage; therefore, it is categorized as a grave offense.

[Commentary: Or, when he claimed, "I am one who has exhausted all fetters and latent tendencies (āsrava-anuśaya)," and even went so far as to say, "I am now a Buddha," Lan replied, "Because these did not exist in the past, they have been exhausted.
One who awakens to all unwholesome dharmas is called a Buddha; thus, Lan stated that he had severed the fetters and latent tendencies.
The title "Buddha" is emphasized.

Among the six [sections], the first provides a general heading, while the subsequent parts reveal the characteristics of delusion. First, regarding the light offenses: the term "past" refers to the fact that from the very beginning there have been no fetters;
"awakened to the unwholesome" means that the Buddha is called an "Awakened One" (Buddha) because his mind is capable of awakening.
Since "realizing [it]" is itself Buddhahood, the concluding phrase "the gravity [of the offense] is established" is easily understood.
[Commentary: To say "I am a Buddha" or "I am a Teacher of Gods and Humans" constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), because people do not believe it.
If one says, "I have fallen back from the four fruits of the śramaṇa," it involves the same category as what was previously mentioned regarding a *pārājika* (defeat).

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that those who do not believe in the two titles of the Buddha do so because they lack confusion [regarding his status]. This passage serves to resolve the preceding text on the gravity of transgressions;

as for the subsequent statement that even the regression of one from the four fruits is grave, it is because once one says "I have regressed," it clearly manifests that one had previously attained them.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duolun), if one says that practices such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) are merely mundane dharmas, one incurs a grave offense.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states that "impurity" is one of the five cessations (*pañca-nivaraṇa-pratipakṣa*); another treatise says it is the initial gateway to the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), through which all noble ones (*ārya*) enter the Path.

[Commentary]: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a person writes a letter stating for himself that he has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), and shows this letter to others, even though the letter says he has attained the fruit, he has not actually attained it;
he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The intent of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is that by relying on a written document to deceive, one avoids the offense committed through speech.

[Commentary] The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one says, 'If it is claimed that all those in such-and-such a place are not ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), I am also among them,' this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense because the reference is not definitive.
However, if one says, 'I too have attained this Dharma,' one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*)."
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are three cases: first, "transgressing" (越) refers generally to others; second, "committing a *sthūlātyaya*" (犯蘭) refers to involving one's own portion;

Third, regarding the arising of delusion in the sacred Dharma, it must involve a discrepancy between both mind and object; whereas in ordinary phenomena, delusion arises through the mind alone.

within the two aspects of the dual division, it is generally indicated that there are two parts, which correspond to the five previously mentioned categories of offenses.
[Commentary]: Generally, when discussing false speech, it is divided into four propositions: first, both the mind and the object are false; second, both the mind and the object are real; third...

Therefore, the citation of evidence below can be understood. The character "na" (那) is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùhū*).

[Commentary: Regarding the fourth point, false speech was originally intended to deceive others so that they would develop faith; however, at the time of the formal conclusion (*niḥsargika-pācittika*), one simply states the conclusion without waiting for their faith.

This is because, among the other precepts where the formal conclusion generally involves taking the deluded mind as the basis, this specific precept regarding falsehood is unique; therefore, it must be distinguished.
[The Master] shows:
[The *Shu* (Commentary) says: As the ancients explained, "knowing the coarse and believing the subtle," and so forth—how could this be ultimate?

To refute the meaning of the ancients, the *Zhongyanyi Chao* (Excerpts on the Meaning of the Middle) cites them as saying: "Knowing the coarse and believing the subtle only allows for faith to arise subsequent to knowledge."

Establishing the present middle section, this is the first master’s interpretation. First, it generally indicates the title; below that, it provides the formal explanation.

The first two phrases explain the aforementioned "destruction of requisites," while the latter two phrases explain "not depending on faith. Next, it clarifies mutual commission. Regarding verbal commission, as for bodily commission, it is as taught in the case of killing.

It is lamentable that those who deceive the shallow by means of the deep are slain; furthermore, because the matters of bodily and vocal karma may be confused or ambiguous—where doubt arises regarding what is light and what is heavy—and these are not explicitly detailed in the text, it refers back to what was stated previously, namely the gateway of the three types of action (trikarma).
[Commentary]: Regarding the explanation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, there are also four points.
[Commentary]: As for the reason for establishing these prohibitions: it is because the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) is not realized by ordinary beings;

since they have not yet attained it, they recklessly engage in empty talk, claiming for themselves that they have realized it. Thus, they delude the minds of the multitude and deceive the world in their quest for fame and profit.
The obscuration of the Dharma is most extreme when it exceeds the proper time; therefore, it must be strictly regulated.

Within the explanation of the intent behind these regulations, four types of transgressions are enumerated: first, the transgression of secretly appropriating the Dharma by claiming to have realized it for oneself;

second, the transgression of deceiving others; third, the transgression of seeking [gain] through improper means; and fourth, the transgression of extinguishing the Dharma. "Obscuring" (*yì*) refers to covering over and concealing it. Its...

To claim that what does not exist already exists is "yì" (obscuration), meaning darkness; to claim what is not so is so is "wǎng" (deception), meaning falsehood. Below, the conclusion summarizes the inquiry regarding which of the four precepts is most serious.

Question: In explaining the intent of each of the four precepts, it is stated that they are each grave. Upon ultimate examination of the first category [of offenses], which precept is the most serious?

Answer: All four precepts are grave; how could there be a hierarchy of superiority or inferiority? However, each focuses on a specific aspect, and in relation to one another, they may appear inferior. For example, sexual misconduct obstructs the Path.
The remaining three are minor: stealing violates and distresses others; killing damages the vessel of the Path; and lying involves taking what is not one's due and deceiving at the opportune moment.
By analogy with the above, the meaning can also be understood.

[Commentary] Second, explaining the names of the precepts: when the substance deviates from the true record, it is called "falsehood" (mṛṣā); because the transgression is grave and the deception is profound, it is named as such.

To accomplish the great work, that which resides in the mouth is termed "vocal restraint" (*vāg-śīla*); because it is a practice capable of counteracting [transgressions], it is called the "precept against great false speech.
In the first section of the "Explanation of Terms" (*Shiming*), the text provides a word-by-word commentary on the root text of the precepts.

[Commentary]: As the ancient interpretation states: that which does not accord with reality is called "false. To falsely proclaim the virtues of a sage is to claim a state that transcends the realm of ordinary beings;

hence it is called "exceeding the human law" (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*). There are two ways in which one "exceeds": either from the stage of an ordinary person reaching that of a sage, or from the realm of desire reaching that of the form realm.
Because these two types of claims alike deceive people, it is termed the "precept against falsely claiming to have exceeded the human law."

In citing the ancient sources, that [text] establishes the name of the precept as "the precept of falsely claiming superhuman attainments" (uttarimanussadhamma), and thus provides this explanation with two meanings.

The first meaning refers to the stages (*bhūmi*), such as the first and second fruits of the path (*phala*) and so forth; the latter refers to the realms (*dhātu*), such as the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and so forth.
[Commentary] Question: Why is it said only that he "surpassed the human dharma" (over-man-dharma) and not that he "surpassed the heavens"? Answer:

As explained in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*, because the Buddha established the precepts among humans, humans possess the *prātimokṣa*; they cultivate wholesome dharmas extensively and enter the Path more excellently than the devas.

Therefore, it is simply said that he "surpassed humans. Furthermore, because the offenses of humans are grave, whereas those of the devas are not, there is no need for further discussion regarding the latter.

In the questions and answers, three meanings are primarily discussed in the interpretation: first, the explanation based on the establishment of the precepts; second, the explanation based on the superiority of the person; and third, the explanation based on analogy.

Regarding the first, it is explained in terms of the formulation of the prohibitions. Regarding the second, it is explained by way of the person’s excellence: because the gods are mostly attached to pleasure and do not cultivate wholesome qualities, they are inferior to humans;

thus, it is said that [the offense] "surpasses that of humans. Furthermore, the third explanation is by way of analogy: having already surpassed humans, how much more so would one surpass the gods? This principle is necessarily evident.
Therefore, it is said that there is nothing to be discussed.
[Commentary] Third, the explanation establishing the conditions for the offense consists of nine factors: (1) the object before one is a person; (2) the perception that the object is a person;

(3) the deception regarding the object is false; (4) knowing that the object is false; (5) the intention to deceive another; (6) proclaiming superhuman dharmas; (7) having already spoken of them oneself.
The realization of the eight words clarifies the nine preceding objects known through understanding.
Within the conditions (*pratyaya*), the first and last are the objective realm (*viṣaya*); the second and fifth are both mind; the rest are all false dharmas.
[Commentary: The fourth explanation concerns the deficiency of conditions.

[Commentary: If the first condition is missing, there are three cases of general (non-specific) intention and four cases of specific (definitive) intention regarding a different object that replaces the original one;
these are identical to the previous precept. If the second condition is missing, there are three cases of shifting general intention and four cases of shifting specific intention;

adding the case of perceiving a king as a person, there are six cases of general intention involving doubt and ten cases of specific intention involving doubt. When both conditions are missing, there are four cases.
The ten formulations may be understood as above. Regarding the third formulation, "the object is unreal but one perceives it as real": there is no offense;

however, one may incur a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) or a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing), as in the case of the precept regarding the attainment of the Path. Regarding the fourth formulation, "the object is unreal and one knows it to be so, yet one increases pride": there is no offense.
Regarding the fifth formulation, "there is a deceptive intent, but one does not intend to carry it through to completion, acting instead out of sport": this incurs a *dukkaṭa*.

The sixth *āpatti* of the *sthūlātyaya* (偷蘭闕) concerns falsely claiming superhuman attainments (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). Now, regarding the claim of human dharmas, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*:

"To say of oneself, 'I maintain pure precepts,' 'lust does not arise in me,' 'I do not recite the four Āgamas or the Vinaya,' or 'I do not practice seated meditation or dwell in a forest hermitage (*arañña*),' yet to say, 'I recite them'—these are all *sthūlātyaya*.
The seventh *āpatti* of the *sthūlātyaya* concerns claiming for oneself that one has already realized [the fruits of the path], whereas now one does not speak of it for oneself.

Regarding the realization [of offenses]: if one praises the Triple Gem out of a sense of personal merit, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); if one’s teacher is involved, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If one falsely claims that another has attained [realization] for the sake of scheming for fame and profit, living by a wrong livelihood, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

If the eighth condition—clarity of speech—is lacking, it is a light *sthūlātyaya*. If the ninth condition—the person addressed not hearing or not understanding—is lacking, it is merely a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the initial stage of the "unclear" (*avyakta*) within the "deficient conditions" (*vaikalya-pratyaya*), there are three propositions concerning a tree stump:
first, perceiving a tree stump as a person; second, perceiving a tree stump as a non-human; and third, perceiving a tree stump as an animal. Within the second [category], there are likewise three:

the first clarifies the transformation of perception (*vikalpa-parāvṛtti*) through a "slight negligence" (*paritta-vimati*), consisting of three propositions; that is, regarding a single individual, one perceives them as a non-human, or two as animals.
One should form the perception of three things as being a tree stump, and by applying the four phrases of mental discipline, one develops the perception of them as kings.

Next, the explanation of the distracted mind of doubt has six aspects, which are also categorized according to the minor distractions; the direct doubts are threefold: first, doubt regarding non-humans;

second, doubt regarding animals; and third, doubt regarding tree stumps. The mutual doubts are also threefold: first, [doubting whether it is] a non-human or an animal; second, [doubting whether it is] a non-human or a... [text fragment].

Regarding the omission of the third [factor], the precept on truly attaining the Way: if one speaks to those who are not yet fully ordained, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense); if one speaks jokingly or with a smile, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). Regarding the omission of the sixth [factor], speaking of human dharmas:

this refers to minor false speech (*sappāṇaka-uttarimanussa-dhamma*), whereas merely falsely claiming spiritual accomplishments constitutes major false speech (*musāvāda*). This is because the conditions for the latter are absent.
Regarding the seventh *sthūlātyaya* offense, the first part indicates the meaning of the deficiency, while the subsequent section clarifies the characteristics of that deficiency.

To praise the Triple Gem—that is, to speak of the *saṃgha-ratna*—is to include both the noble ones (*ārya*) and the virtuous; thus, to address them as "Teacher" (*śāstr*) is [permissible]. However, to merely offer empty praise for the sake of gain constitutes an offense.
If one intentionally plots for profit and fame, it is equivalent to the following case and constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.

[Note] When the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, the price of grain was high and alms were difficult to obtain. There were those observing the rains retreat on the banks of the Vāku River who praised one another for having attained the qualities of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).
Lay devotees with faith reduced their own portions to give as offerings. Subsequently, [the monks] went to the Buddha's presence;
because they questioned him about this, he rebuked them and established this precept.
[Commentary]: Regarding the conditions for the precepts, the first point clarifies how one might resort to wrong livelihood due to the high price of grain. The *Analects* states:

"The gentleman remains steadfast even in poverty, whereas the petty person, when impoverished, oversteps the bounds. These words have their basis; they serve as a worldly admonition for those of dull capacity who harbor such thoughts.
Regarding the citation from the *Analects* within the section on the conditions for ethical discipline (*śīla*), this is because the circumstances are analogous.
That passage records that when Confucius was in Chen and his provisions were exhausted, Zilu asked, "Does even a gentleman experience such destitution?

The commentary cites his reply, stating that a gentleman, even when dwelling in hardship and poverty, remains firm in maintaining his will without wavering; thus it is said he is "resolute" (*gu*). A petty person, however, when faced with distress, lacks this steadfastness.
The phrase "it is not for this reason" refers to the charge of being indiscriminate; this section below demonstrates the intent of the citation.
