that is to say, the relative gravity of the offense when facing a nun differs from the above cases. Regarding robes: it refers to the five robes, including the addition of receiving [them], being separated from them, and losing them.

"Because they are not different. [Commentary] Furthermore, it is argued: "If the establishment of offenses were based on convenience such that the precepts were not differentiated, then consider the following case:

Because those in the household have severed desire and possess pure faith free from doubt, why would they laugh or revile? This should be understood as follows: first, because there is a presence or absence of even slight desire;

Now, when "attachment" (*tṛṣṇā*) is mentioned here, it refers to the attachment that defiles through lustful desire, for it is not a pure mind.

**[Commentary]:** Regarding the phrase "mutual contact," the Vinaya clarifies that there are ten types of tactile characteristics (*sparśa-lakṣaṇa*), which are easy to understand. As for "grasping the hand or the hair":

fifth, it cites "upholding the Vinaya" (*vinayadhara*) to clarify the dharma of practice; sixth, it cites "sitting in meditation" (*dhyāyin*) to clarify the dharma of realizing the Path.

In the first section of the commentary on the cultivation of goodness, the six stages encompass all wholesome dharmas; these six are condensed into two, which are not outside of the stages of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*), or alternatively, they are three, namely the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).

[The Sub-commentary] states that regarding the aforementioned *dhūta* practices, when categorized by their characteristics there are twelve, but when condensed by way of substance, there are only four items, namely: clothing, food, [shelter, and medicine].

five are established for contentment with place, namely, staying in a quiet place, a cemetery (*śmāśānika*), at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*), in the open air (*ābhyavakāśika*), and sitting wherever one happens to be (*yathāsaṃstarika*). Among these four modes of deportment, the one [pertaining to sitting] is precisely sitting while binding the mind to mindfulness (*smṛti*).
This refers to the observation arising from present wisdom; the rest is as explained in the *Śāstra*.

There is no offense if a bhikṣu says to a woman: "This place is wondrous, supreme, and most excellent;

If one offers equal worship to her, and if a woman thinks, "He is praising my body," or if, in the course of reciting the Vinaya,
he mentions this [praise] and she thinks he is praising her body, or if he speaks erroneously— none of these constitute an offense.

[Commentary] Within the section on defining the characteristics: if one merely speaks of desire as previously described in the precepts, or if one merely praises the body and incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense, or if one praises the body while soliciting desire, only then does one commit the full offense of this precept; other aspects and conditions can be understood accordingly.
In the commentary on the sixth [precept], the *Bianxiang* (Discernment of Characteristics) states: "The rest can be understood. This note refers back to the preceding precepts;

it means that [the offenses] regarding sending letters, manifesting signs, reporting [one's intentions], and seeking out different destinations are all the same. Regarding the section on non-offenses, the first point concerns praising others as they truly are and preaching the Dharma, etc.;

[Vinaya] The Fifth Precept on Acting as a Matchmaker.
[Commentary] The fifth precept concerns acting as a matchmaker for marriage.
[Commentary] Regarding the intent behind the formulation of this precept: these rites of marriage and betrothal are indeed fetters of birth and death that obstruct the Path.
Since those who have left the household life must distance themselves from attachments, it is all the more necessary to avoid such [laypeople].
Yet, they repeatedly come and go, their speech and discourse are contrary to the rules, and their demeanor is deeply base and shameful. It is logically necessary to prohibit this;

however, because their affairs are so numerous and excessive that they hinder the practice of the Path, and because their conduct incurs ridicule and cannot escape worldly reproach—possessing all these faults—it was therefore established as a regulation.

Regarding the precept against acting as a matchmaker for marriage, the exposition of its faults within the intent of the regulation has four parts: first, it clarifies how this obstructs the Noble Path;
second, it clarifies how it violates monastic decorum; third, it clarifies how it neglects spiritual progress and is vulgar and base;
fourth, it clarifies how it invites worldly censure. The following section provides a summary.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the name: it is called "mediator" (*méi*) because men and women consult with one another back and forth to bring about marriage; "mediator" (*méi*) means "to deliberate.
It refers to the planning and deliberation regarding two clans in order to effect a harmonious union.

In the *Shiming* (Explanation of Terms), the first part indicates the meaning of the name, while the subsequent part reveals the characteristics of the act. "Calculation" (*jiàduò*) refers to weighing its acceptability or otherwise;
the character for "good" (*hào*) is pronounced with a departing tone.

[Commentary] There are eight conditions for committing this offense: first, the person (male or female); second, the perception (real or mistaken); third, acting as a matchmaker; fourth, knowing it is a matchmaking activity.
Five words clarify the six types of speech regarding the precepts; seven concern going to speak of an offense, and eight concern returning to report the violation.
[Commentary] The deficiency of conditions can be understood.
[Note] When the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, the Kāla bhikṣu had formerly been a great minister who was well-versed in worldly laws within the city.

When people went to inquire freely about marriages, those engaged in marriage would encounter various circumstances—good or bad—and immediately wish that Kāla might experience such suffering or pleasure.
Laypeople criticized this, and the bhikṣus reported the matter as a transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established a precept.

[Commentary]: Regarding the conditions for the precepts, Kāla originally knew the signs of marriage and the fortunes or misfortunes of others; thus, although he had left the household life, he returned to pursue his former profession.

Because such habitual practice gives rise to a constant state of mind, one does not speak of it as being a transgression—just as those who currently engage in butchery or trade do not consider their ways wrong because they are deluded by profit.
Is it not therefore the case that the conduct [of Kāla] was likewise permissible? Thus, in the Vinaya, it is stated that a guest who has arrived first must not keep a writing brush.
A guest tailor must not keep needles; one who arrives before the wood for construction may not keep axes and the like. These rules are all intended to restrain evil habits.

Furthermore, regarding those who claim that their marriage was determined by good or bad fortune and that they must experience suffering or joy as a result, such ignorant worldly people do not realize that these are the consequences of past conditions.
Once the circumstances have been met, they simply blame the matchmaker for bringing them suffering or joy; this is a sign of transgression, and therefore it is proscribed.
Here, because the bhikṣus and Kāla were involved, his words are relevant.
In the initial clarification of the causal conditions for the precepts, "kāla" refers to the original circumstances of marriage; "yin-gou" (姻媾) are all names for wedding ceremonies.

"Xi-lu" (祿) refers to one’s allotted lot of life, including fortune and misfortune—that is, good and bad luck—as illustrated by the examples provided below. Therefore, the teachings are cited below to provide proof.

This is intended to make known that those who have left the household life must certainly eliminate worldly habits. Furthermore, the following explains the *Vinaya* rules concerning disparagement and praise:

"If someone obtains a marriage that is to their liking, they will joyfully provide offerings and offer praise, saying, 'May Kāla always experience such happiness,' and may other bhikṣus also receive such offerings.
If, however, one does not obtain what is to their liking, they will then say: "One should cause..."
Kāla constantly suffered affliction, as did the other bhikṣus who likewise suffered affliction and failed to receive offerings and so forth.
However, because that [text] spoke of "defamation" and stated that others must also be excluded from it, it says: "Due to the various bhikṣus," etc.;
since they are of the same category, they likewise encounter derision and defamation. Based on this, the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states that Kāla and the others below should be combined.
The phrase "and other bhikṣus" likely contains a scribal omission.

[Commentary] This refers to one who causes those who ought to be united to reconcile.
[Commentary]: Regarding the first of the four phrases of the Prātimokṣa, it is clear that the "go-between" who facilitates coming and going is precisely the root of the karma.

The section beginning with "holding the man's intention" explains the preceding established characteristics; the section beginning with "for the sake of establishing a wife" constitutes the offense itself.
The phrases in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Jieben) can be understood through their literal meaning.

[Commentary: Regarding the explanation of the act of matchmaking (*dūtīkarma*), the phrase "going back and forth between this and that" refers to the specific characteristics of the act to clarify the nature of matchmaking.

[Commentary: Third, regarding "maintaining the male's intention," the following is a reverse explanation of the second characteristic, the mutual coming and going. The intentions of both male and female refer to families suitable for marriage;

Therefore, the Vinaya speaks generally of this as being "nothing other than males and females."
Third, in the commentary on the text: First, "male" (*nán*) is pointed out; below, the passage cites and explains "to betroth" (*píng*), which is equivalent to "to marry.

Since this necessarily depends on both parents, the subsequent text specifically cites them to establish the rule, thereby comprehensively including the two preceding cases.

[Note: There are twenty kinds of women protected by a mother, protected by a father, protected by both parents, protected by a brother, protected by a sister, protected by a brother and sister, protected by oneself, protected by the Dharma, protected by one's clan, protected by one's kinsmen, protected by one’s own pleasure, a female slave given as clothing, and a female slave given for wealth.

These are: the female slave of the same trade, the female slave drifted by water, the female slave who does not pay taxes, the female slave set free, the female slave working for hire, the female slave protected by another, and the female slave obtained from border regions. [Commentary: Among the twenty types of female and male characteristics explained in the commentary, the female traits are clarified first.
This is because men generally seek women when coming together for union; thus, they are explained first according to the point of their being sought.

The commentary on the first section states that, according to the seeker (the male), the man should logically come first; therefore, it refers to the sought-after (the female) to clarify the intent of the Vinaya.
[The Sub-commentary] explains that the discussion regarding the status of women—such as noble or low-born—is also intended to dispel doubts, provided that they are permitted to marry.
Both noble and base individuals alike commit the offense of *kṣudrāvaśeṣa* (residual).

Next, in the general division that clarifies the main point, the first part indicates the meaning of the text; the subsequent section [addresses] the resolution of doubts, as there may be apprehension that the act is not established for a base person, or doubt that it is not established when the noble and the base act as intermediaries for one another.
[Commentary]: Some say that if a man protected by his mother takes a girl protected by her mother, then a union may be possible;

however, there is no such principle if a man protected by his mother takes even a slave-girl from a frontier region. Therefore, the text says: "Regarding those who ought to be united," the current interpretation is as stated above.
As we see in the world today, how could one possibly arrange a marriage [in such cases]? Even a slave-girl became Lady Zhao, and a fisherman’s daughter [became a queen].
"Would it not be possible for the King’s daughter and the celestial being to unite?
To reject the ancient precedent is to first produce that [opposing] view; the ancients held that when a man and woman reach twenty years of age, they may be matched through a matchmaker.
Yet, taking the preceding text as evidence, what is said regarding 'those who ought to be harmonized' merely refers to the auspicious union of two families."
How could it be that [the distinction] between noble and lowly classes is so different that one would know [the truth] otherwise?
Now, the "lower scale" (xiàjīn) is not a mere summary; these three matters serve to examine their false attachments. The *Hanshu* states:

Empress Zhao of Emperor Xiaocheng was originally a palace attendant from Chang’an (referring to an official maidservant in the inner chambers, not one from the imperial harem). She was skilled at singing and dancing and was called Feiyan. When Emperor Cheng saw her...
Yue invited him into the palace, where he became a highly favored counselor. The King of China had a daughter named Kumuda;
upon seeing the fisherman, she became infatuated with him and could no longer eat or drink. She confided her feelings to her mother, who sent plump fish as a gift to the princess.
The princess would not accept them without payment, so the mother explained the situation to her. The princess then consented.
On the fifteenth day of the month, he stayed behind a statue in a certain temple; when the time came, he went there.

The princess arrived at the shrine and entered alone, whereupon the deity immediately grew weary of her and caused her to fall asleep. The woman then removed her jeweled necklace, left it behind, and departed.
Only after she had gone did she awaken, and she died, consumed by the fires of lust. According to the Vinaya, this was a case of a bhikṣu engaging in sexual conduct with a celestial maiden.
Regarding the repeated offenses of sexual misconduct, it is known through many evidentiary circumstances that they are not to be distinguished [from one another].

[Commentary: As for "protected by the mother," this refers to cases where, after the father has passed away, the mother raises the child; fearing instability or peril, she constantly supervises and guards them, hence the term "protected.

This is like the story of Mencius’s mother, who moved three times for the sake of her son, thereby enabling him to achieve the Way and become a patriarch of Confucianism. As for "protected by the father," it refers to...
This is as previously stated: it is like the case of the world’s Cengcan, who did not marry as a son because both his parents were still alive and he was under their protection;
this principle is clearly evident and applies equally to elder brothers and sisters.

First, regarding the protection provided by the mother, the initial explanation of the meaning of "protection" is as indicated below in the citation. As for the phrase "the father passed away," the Son of Heaven is said to "pass away" (*beng*);
this is because the ancient language used this term interchangeably. As for Mencius, the *Shiji* states that his courtesy name was Ziyu and that he was a native of Zou.
When Mencius was young and lived with his widowed mother near a cemetery, he would frequently play at being a tomb-digger. His mother said:

"This is not a place to live; let us move to the side of the marketplace. Mencius again jokingly acted as a merchant, and his mother said, "This is not a place to live either. They then moved to the side of an academy;
there, [Mencius] practiced the rituals of bowing and yielding, advancing and retreating with propriety. His mother said, "This is truly a place where one can live.
Mencius subsequently became a great Confucian scholar. The Preface to the *Mengzi* states: "He was raised by a compassionate mother who moved him three times."
This is what the teaching says regarding protection by one's father, as explained previously; it refers to cases such as when a mother dies and the father raises [the child].
As for Zeng Shen, a disciple of Confucius, because he was raised by a stepmother, his wife once offered steamed pears that were not ripe;

consequently, she was sent away, and he remained unmarried for the rest of his life. His son Yuan requested permission on his behalf, and [Zeng Shen] told his son: "Gaozong put his stepmother to death."
Xiaoyi was exiled by Yi Jifu because of his stepmother;
how could I know that I would escape blame? Wen cited this from the *Jia Yu* to clarify the father’s protection of his son.
[Commentary: Regarding "protecting oneself," it means that from the beginning there is no teacher or friend; one's nature is formed by Heaven.
Thus, even when encountering the defilement of the mundane world, one is not stained, like Mahākāśyapa or Liu Hui.

Regarding "spontaneously protecting oneself" and "attaining centrality": this refers to natural self-establishment. The *Analects* says: "Is it not said that what is hard cannot be worn thin by grinding?

Is it not said that what is white cannot be stained black by dyeing? (This metaphor illustrates how a gentleman remains unstained while in a turbid world; though sharing the same environment as others, he remains inwardly upright.
According to the *Dharmatrāta-dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (*Fufa zang zhuan*), when Mahākāśyapa was fifteen years old, his parents wished to betroth him to a wife. Upon hearing this, [he...]
Filled with sorrow and distress, he said to his parents, "My aspiration is pure; I have no need for a wife. Later, his parents arranged a marriage for him and obtained a golden-hued maiden.
They made a pact between them: "When you sleep, I shall practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*); when you walk, I shall sleep.
In this way, they remained pure and took no pleasure in worldly defilement. Subsequently, he informed his parents of his desire to leave the household life (*pravrajyā*) and so forth.
Mencius said: "Liu Xia Hui (whose surname was Zhǎn and given name Qín; 'Liu Xia Hui' is his courtesy name) did not feel shame in serving corrupt rulers nor did he decline minor offices.

When advancing, he did not conceal his worth but insisted on following the Way. Even when neglected and cast aside, he did not resent it; even when beset by hardship and poverty, he did not lament it.
He lived among commoners with an air of ease and composure, unable to bear leaving them. Whether you were 'you' or I were 'I,' even if one were to expose one's shoulders and chest..."
"Exposed as you are at my side, how could you defile me? [In this context, *mǐnmǎn* means distress; *tì* and *chén* both refer to garments; *měi* means to soil.
[Commentary] As for those called "Dharma-protectors" (*fǎhù*), some protect themselves according to worldly laws and do not permit reckless abandon;

thus, there is a common saying that a man of thirty and a woman of twenty must wait for the proper rites before acting. Beyond these ages, there are those who run after one another without restraint, and so forth. Furthermore—
According to worldly law, since marriage through a matchmaker is a crime punishable by imprisonment, one fears that [the former practice] would violate this law;

therefore, it is called "Dharmapāla" (Protector of the Dharma), which the Vinaya explains as "practicing the pure life" (*brahmacarya*). Now, explaining this according to worldly law, it is said "or," first clarifying the observance of ritual propriety and worldly laws.
The phrase "what is called the royal instruction for the laity" refers to the *Neize* (Inner Regulations) chapter of the *Liji* (Book of Rites). Regarding the man:

In selecting women, one takes an odd number (a yang number) while for men one takes an even number (an yin number). If the numbers are reduced, it is not permitted; if they exceed them, it is allowed.

Therefore, it is said that there is no prohibition against "running" to each other [to elope]. Furthermore, the subsequent passage stipulates that out of fear of punishment, one must not dare to engage in illicit or excessive unions.

[Commentary: Regarding what is called "protection by clan" (*gotra-rakṣā*), it refers to those whose family lineage is highly esteemed and who are renowned throughout the land. If one were to defile such a person through improper conduct, it would be unacceptable;
it is essential that there be a formal matchmaker, for it cannot be done otherwise.

Regarding "protected by one's clan" (*gotra-rakṣita*): because those who fear bringing disgrace upon their noble lineage dare not commit transgressions, the term "within the seas" (*hai-nei*) refers to the entire world situated within the four oceans.
[Commentary]: As for "protected by kinsmen," even if one’s clan is of high status, if a close relative passes away and one were to falsely fabricate misconduct, the kinsmen would not permit it.
It is called "protected" because it is guarded.
Among the protections provided by kinsmen, the closest relatives are one's parents; their passing is referred to as "death," which is like the withering of a tree’s branches.

[Commentary: The ten preceding points are excellent, and their characteristics are self-evident; below, the ten types of female slaves are clarified according to the Vinaya, where the text is directly interpreted and the characteristics are manifest.

1. Money as the price; 2. A fellow practitioner performing the same work together; 3. One who has not yet become husband and wife; 4. One rescued from being swept away by water; 5.
One who does not pay taxes, provided one does not take their tax dues; 6. One set free, whether purchased or born in the household; 7. A hired laborer, employed for wages like a domestic servant. 8.

A guest worker, hired for wages to perform labor like a domestic servant. 9. [Note: The numbering here follows the sequence of the original list. 9. [The ninth item corresponds to the final category listed above.]

[Commentary]: There are twenty types of men who are identical to women; their names are changed and they are thus permitted [to receive offerings]. To avoid further prolixity, the Vinaya provides only a brief indication.

Among males, twenty are divided into the categories of "free" (liáng) and "servile" (jiàn). Regarding those who are free, they are termed "males"; those who are servile are termed "slaves" (nú), their specific characteristics being the same as mentioned above.
[Commentary] When male and female categories are interlaced to form various permutations, the resulting combinations are numerous; for instance, take the case of a male protected by his mother.
From daughters protected by their mothers down to lowly female slaves, one man may marry twenty women; with twenty men, this results in four hundred permutations.
Following this principle, examples such as signets, writing, and the manifestation of signs are likewise immeasurable.

Within the sequence of verses, the first part demonstrates the multiplicity of reciprocal phrases; subsequently, it briefly cites direct phrases, mentioning "four hundred" as a mere illustration of the medium of speech.
Following this, the same principle applies to the remaining four or five types, totaling two thousand phrases.

When these are combined and cross-referenced, they become incalculable; therefore, it is said to be "immeasurable. One need only recognize the three [aspects of] receiving and expounding the teaching mentioned below.
This clarifies that there is no transgression of the boundaries of propriety that is not encompassed [by this rule].
[Vinaya]: If one acts for the sake of consummating marriage, or for the sake of illicit intercourse—even for a mere moment—it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

[Commentary]: The four phrases beginning with "If for the sake of accomplishing the duties of a wife" serve to eliminate doubts. The world says that a "matchmaker" (méi) exists for the sake of exhausting one's life;

"wife" (fù) is a term for submissive service. While the broom and dustpan represent the ultimate fulfillment of one’s karmic retribution, there may be cases of severe violation through illicit intimacy for a brief moment that do not necessarily constitute a transgression.
To remove such false notions, the text concludes that from the very beginning of marriage down to even a momentary lapse, there is no [exemption].
It is not because of a desire for worldly affairs that one simultaneously commits a grave offense; this is to gather in the main lines and collect the nets.
Regarding the first part of the fourth phrase, the preceding text provides a general indication of the meaning, while the subsequent section raises a point of doubt.

"Broom" refers to the implements used for sweeping and sprinkling water; it clarifies the ritual of humble service. In secular books, it is commonly said that sweeping and sprinkling are the duties of women.

The duties of this position are to adjudicate matters below; it begins with the wife’s affairs and concludes with a momentary private liaison while residing in the secondary quarters—hence the text says, "As for [the case where]...
[Commentary]: "Momentary" (*xūyú*) is a synonym for time. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Twenty moments (*nāḍī*) constitute a blink (*akṣi-nimeṣa*); twenty..."
A *kṣaṇa* (instant) is equal to twenty finger-snap (*tatkṣaṇa*). Twenty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*. Twenty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta* (a brief moment).

At the time of the longest day, the daytime consists of eighteen *muhūrtas* and the night consists of twelve *muhūrtas*; if the night is long and the day is short, the reverse should be understood accordingly.

This is the method of calculating the duration of day and night according to the Western Brahmans. As for the water-clocks (*ghaṭikā*) of this region [China]: [The remainder of the text follows the same pattern of numerical conversion.]

In the sūtras, there is no inquiry into the division of the hundred *kṣaṇas* according to the two solstices of winter and summer, nor the method of approximating time by means of arrows floating in water;
thus, the so-called study of seasonal divisions has not yet been elaborately described.
The subsequent section is divided into three parts. First, the general indication: because these are the specific characteristics of time, they are called "alternative names" (*paryāya*).

Next, the citation of the commentary: *kṣaṇa* refers to the single opening and closing of the eyes; *lava* is also a name for time in the Western [Sanskrit] tradition, though its etymological explanation is not detailed [in this text].

(In the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is called *tatkṣaṇa*, and it states that thirty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*; this differs entirely from the present text and cannot be reconciled. Regarding the maximum length of the day:
Furthermore, taking the summer solstice as an example, when the night is long and the day is short, it is said that at the winter solstice the day is twelve [units] and the night is eighteen;

thus it is called the "reversal of the above. At the spring and autumn equinoxes, day and night are divided equally. Below this, three points clarify that the two regions differ in their methods of timekeeping;
the *Lèikè jīng* (Sūtra on Water Clocks) was produced during the Liang dynasty to clearly establish the method for setting up the water clock.
Question: At the winter solstice, there are forty *ke* (dials) by day and sixty *ke* by night; at the summer solstice, it is the reverse.

During the two equinoxes of spring and autumn, the days and nights are each equal, consisting of fifty *ke*. Regarding the "arrow" (*jian*) placed in the water, the regulations for the clepsydra state:
the arrow is four feet five inches long and is divided into four sides, with three periods of twenty-five *ke* on each side, totaling one hundred *ke* across the four sides. As for that arrow—
Within the water jar, a wooden lotus is placed upon it, with a wooden figure seven inches high seated in a kneeling posture at the center of the flower.
With both hands, the figure holds a tray from which a floating arrow emerges from the center of the tray to verify the number of time intervals.
As the water leaks, the arrow rises one interval per *kṣaṇa*; each arrow on the tray corresponds to twenty-five *kṣaṇas*.
Because water was released once, four such cycles constitute a day and night; I have not yet had the leisure to provide a detailed explanation here.
As for the study of time and seasons, it is said that knowing the specific hours constitutes a specialized field of learning that cannot be fully discussed in this context.

[Note]: If one first receives the words [of a proposal], it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); if one goes to deliver the message and does not report it back, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);

if one returns and reports it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring formal meeting of the Saṃgha). If one sends a messenger, or uses a letter, a finger-seal, or gestures, for every instance of matchmaking that is clearly understood, there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for each round-trip.
If it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. This excludes matchmaking regarding the two [sexual] organs; matchmaking regarding other parts of the body is also a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one acts as a matchmaker for a married woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if for a non-human, a *paṇḍaka*, or a person with both sexual organs, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one acts as a matchmaker for an animal or a male human, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one carries another’s letter and does not read it, or performs other errands for a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
A *bhikṣuṇī* commits the same offense. There is no offense if a man and a woman had previously been intimate but later separated and subsequently reunite.
If one carries books while visiting parents who are ill or imprisoned, provided one maintains faith and diligence, the same applies to laypeople;
likewise, it is the same for a bhikṣu when acting on behalf of the Buddha-dharma.

[Commentary]: Regarding the analysis of the characteristics in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), within the section on the gravity of offenses committed by oneself, there are five types of intermediaries (*dūta*). First, the intermediary through speech is presented;
the latter four are then concluded by analogy.
[Commentary]: Within the intermediary through speech, there are three types.

[Commentary: Regarding "receiving the speech [of another] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅)," it should be understood as the preliminary stage (*prayoga*) of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (僧殘) offense that is classified as a *sthūlātyaya* (蘭). The reason it is designated as a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) despite the intent to go and speak is that one did not actually go in person; thus, because one received the instruction but failed to go, the resulting offense is a minor *duṣkṛta*.

As for the commentary on "receiving the speech," the phrase "minor compared to going in person" means that because one accepted the command but did not proceed, the formal conclusion of the offense is a light *duṣkṛta*.
[Commentary: Second, regarding going to another to speak [of the offense] without returning a report—since a report would constitute a grave offense, it is merely a *sthūlātyaya*.
To go [to speak] constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*, which is the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for a *pārājika* offense.

[Commentary] Regarding the initial intent of the regulation: For those who have left the household life, dwelling together in harmony is of primary importance; they must protect one another so as not to cause mutual distress or offense.
Yet now, harboring internal anger and resentment, they fabricate false appearances and bring grave charges against others to slander them.
Thus they destroy their own mental conduct, increase the cycle of birth and death, and extinguish the True Dharma. Furthermore, they defile the virtuous and distinguish them from the worthy.
When a person extensively afflicts others, it ruins their lifelong cultivation of the right practice; such an act of deception is so grave that it specifically requires a sacred regulation.

As the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "First, to protect one's own practice and ensure the Dharma endures for a long time; second, to stop slander and allow those living the holy life (*brahmacarya*) to cultivate the path in peace, so as not to obstruct their right practice."

Regarding the regulation of the mind, there are three sections. First, it describes what ought to be done, granting permission as if by command. Next, "Now" and below clarify what ought not to be done; this also has three parts. First, it describes the faults.
Second, from "It harms oneself" below, it reveals the damage, which is threefold: first, it harms oneself, and below that, it extinguishes the Dharma; furthermore, it harms others.
Those excluded from the assembly are singled out because one who commits the four grave offenses (caturmahāpatti) should immediately be expelled. Thus, [the text] addresses deception.
The lower three [points] demonstrate the establishment of the teaching; as shown by the citations below, they reverse the upper three harms to establish the three benefits.
[Commentary: Next, regarding the explanation of the names: because there are no three actualities within, it is called "baseless"; to falsely accuse with such weight is termed "slander.

thus, there is no further [category] below. Next, the general indication uses the phrase "that which is prevented" (*suǒ fáng zhě*) to manifest that these are the characteristics of transgressions.
[Commentary] Third, regarding the gravity of the offense according to its magnitude:

[Commentary] Question: If one slanders another by falsely claiming they have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), yet there are no actual three bases (*trīṇi mūlāni*)—namely, having actually seen, heard, or suspected it—and one deceives the Saṃgha with a false understanding, does this constitute the offense of lying (*mṛṣāvāda-pāyattika*)?
Answer: As stated in the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing): There is no separate offense of *pāyattika*, because slander is invariably established through falsehood and deception.

Regarding the intent of the question on the three offenses committed individually (*tān-fàn*): since slander is fundamentally based on falsehood, the principle requires that it be accompanied by deception (*wàng*). In the response, the *Śāstra* clarifies that for an offense committed individually, there is no separate karmic action (*karma*).

[Commentary] Question: Just as when killing an animal, both the life-force and the property of the owner are damaged, resulting in the commission of two offenses, one should likewise [consider the case] in relation to the Saṃgha.

Question: Why is it that false understanding is not classified as the same as slanderous falsehood? Answer: They are not the same. This is because slander is invariably established through mere pretense and falsity;

there is no intention to be truthful when one slanders. Furthermore, while theft causes harm to the owner and injury to the livestock, [slander] does not. Therefore, the two types—those involving both [falsity and harm] and those involving only one—are distinguished separately.
In the initial objection within the "Difficulties in Turning," the seven-character lines serve as the verses. The first two lines cite an analogy:

killing another's livestock constitutes a *pārājika* offense for the hope of harming the owner, while killing the livestock itself constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense; thus, both offenses are contained therein.

The latter two lines present the difficulty, which is resolved in the response by clarifying the distinction between the dual and single [applications], which can be understood as corresponding to theft and slander.

[Commentary]: If this is so, why does the *Śāstra* state that killing grass for the purpose of theft constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), and even when one has received a deposit and, upon the owner’s demand, claims not to have received it, this likewise constitutes only a *duṣkṛta*?
Since these are all preparatory offenses (*prayoga*) for the precept against stealing, how can they be similar [to the full offense] without there being a distinct offense?
Answer: The cited cases establish the principle that no *pārājika* (defeat) offense falls; one should know that this accords with my previous argument.
In the first part of the subsequent objection, two passages are cited: the first states that if one cuts down grass or trees growing upon a treasure-store, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;

the second concerns the passage on receiving deposits, which quotes the *Śīla-skandha-vinaya* regarding killing living beings—namely, that destroying plant life or speaking falsehoods does not constitute a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
These points do not conflict with the meaning established in the preceding text, which concludes that both harming the owner and harming livestock result in a dual offense.

Because they are inconsistent, these are cited as objections. All the following constitute a formal objection based on similarity: that is, being identical to the preceding case with no distinction, meaning there is no distinct resultant offense.
In the response, the first phrase acknowledges the wording of the prior objection, establishing that it constitutes the preparatory stage (*upāya*) for theft;
the second phrase establishes the reverse—that it constitutes a single, standalone offense—which precisely accords with the previous principle.

[Commentary]: Now, according to the *Vibhaṅga*, both single and combined [offenses] are possible. If one's original intention is solely to slander without a deceptive mind, then based on the mind alone, only one offense is incurred.

If it involves both deception and slander—such as when a monk deceives others while slandering—the two offenses are incurred, as in the previous case of killing one’s father while simultaneously engaging in double-tongued speech toward an Arhat. This is the principle of mutual correspondence between the two acts.
Next, regarding the section on the meaning, first there is a general heading; below, it is discussed specifically according to two points, hence it is called a "specific discussion.

Below this, the specific indications explain the single and multiple aspects in relation to the mind, thereby reconciling both interpretations because karma follows the mind and thus offenses may be either dual or single.

One who thoroughly understands the observance and violation of precepts will see this therein. As for the examples provided below, there are two; the first cites the precept against killing, therefore it is pointed out.
As previously stated, if one kills a father who has become an Arhat, if one merely kills the father without knowing he has attained sainthood, one incurs only one *ānantarya* offense;

however, if one knows he is a saint, then both offenses are incurred simultaneously. Next, regarding the precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*), the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Shan-chien-lü-p'i-po-sha*) enumerates the three verbal transgressions in their various permutations as distinct propositions;
therefore, it says that "mutually confronting [others] constitutes one instance of divisive speech. It is not otherwise.
1. False speech and harsh speech, but not divisive speech; 2. Divisive speech and harsh speech, but not false speech;
3. Divisive speech and false speech, but not harsh speech; 4. All three types together. The remaining two cases serve as the heads for alternating permutations in the same manner.

These distinctions between double and single offenses arise because the transgressions involve both mental conditions and individual factors; thus, one must not judge the current case of slander based on a partial assessment.

[Commentary on the Sūtra]: Regarding the fourth point, the limits of the offense: If one asks why it is said that the matter is settled when one originally intended to slander with the expectation of monastic discipline, the answer is as follows: The intention of the slanderer was to have [the person] disciplined;

the disciplinary expulsion depends solely upon the power of the Saṃgha. Consequently, when his anger is vented and he thinks the matter is decided, he utters the words "it is settled," and thus the offense is committed.

Within the fourfold limit, the first two phrases of the response clarify that no disciplinary action (*daṇḍa*) need be undertaken because the verbal expression has already been completed and the intent not yet fulfilled;

this is because the matter was resolved through the power of the Saṃgha rather than by oneself. The latter two phrases reveal that from the completion of the verbal expression, the anger was fully discharged and the intention manifested, whereby the karmic act was finalized.
[Commentary]: The conditions for the offense are eightfold. [Commentary]:

First, this refers to monks and nuns as distinguished from the three lower groups of practitioners; because the intent behind slandering and causing distress is slight, it does not obstruct their spiritual cultivation.

Furthermore, while the name of the offense committed is light, the gravity of the crime of slandering is heavy. This is comparable to striking or robbing: in the case of the two higher groups, the offense is grave, whereas for the three lower groups, it is light. This may be understood accordingly.
[The text] understands. Among the five [points], the first clarifies the two meanings of the primary object: first, it explains that "not abandoning cultivation" means the affliction is slight;
this is because, being at a lower stage, there is no great harm. Furthermore, next, it explains that "light transgression" refers to [the case of] sand.

If one commits a grave offense against the general rule, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one slanders [a monk], it is a *pāyattika*. As for the meaning of committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is not convenient [to treat them as identical].
For example, as will be cited below, striking [a monk] and seizing his robes are regulated identically for both monks and nuns.

[Sūtra]: If that is so, why is it that when a formal accusation (*jñapti*) is made, the monks do not collectively incur the same single *pāyattika*? [Answer]: It is because there is no difference; violating the assembly is the same in both cases.
This is why the same offense applies equally to both the senior and the junior.

Next, regarding the first of the objections raised in the *Nan* (Difficulties): since it is stated that whether one expels a bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera based on the same grounds constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of falling), the response explains that this refers to the legal procedure (*saṃghakarma*) directed toward the community as a whole, rather than being addressed to an individual person.

[Commentary]: If that is so, since the violation of the assembly is one and the same, why do the offenses for monks and nuns fall equally into the category of *pārājika* (defeat), yet when it comes to mutual compliance regarding the assembly’s transgressions, the gravity of the offense is divided?

The answer is: because a nun has the formal instruction (*śikṣāpada*) upon which she can rely, her offense is *pārājika*; whereas for a monk, the situation is the reverse of the former, and thus his offense is merely *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
In the subsequent objection, it is stated that if a nun follows a monk in committing a *pārājika* offense, or a monk follows a nun in committing one, they both incur a *duṣkṛta*;

this is likewise because it would constitute a violation of the community rather than an individual offense. In the response, regarding the nuns' reliance on the teachings, it is because the eight *gurudharma*s enjoin them to show respect; since monks do not have to show deference to those below them, it is said that this is the reverse of the former case.

[Commentary] Question: Why is it that slandering is treated the same as for a *bhikṣu* (Great Monk), while striking is treated the same as for a *śrāmaṇera* (Lesser Learner)? Answer: Striking is based on the inferiority of one's status, whereas slandering concerns a difference in spiritual practice;
according to other Vinayas, the offenses for striking and slandering are equal.

Question: Since the "slander" within "striking and slandering" is the same as [the offense of] the Saṃgha, it should not be treated differently. Answer: In the first part of the response, the distinction is made according to the meaning;

it does not differentiate based on the specific category [of the offender]. [Commentary]: Although they are bhikṣus, their status must be pure, as stated in the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra: "One who has not committed a pārājika offense... and so forth.
To speak of it as real is to open up the position; it is like leaving a village or a room.
Because one who is pure commits an offense, next, based on the second condition of the ancient first master, the initial establishment of the doctrine is as follows.

The citation of evidence from the subsequent text regarding "not committing an offense" excludes those cases where there is no offense; by opening up the investigation of the reality, one must ascertain that the object is pure before entering the formal offense.

Furthermore, below [the text] cites two examples where both [offenses] are seen in the Ninety [Śaikṣas]. According to that, if one’s precepts, views, or deportment are broken, there is no offense [in the case of the latter].
[Commentary: If this is so, why does the Vinaya state that "if a person who is impure slanders another, he commits a Saṃghāvaśeṣa"? The answer is: he commits [an offense].
This refers to the final four chapters.

Regarding the "Resolution of Doubts," the initial objection cites a passage that somewhat contradicts the preceding meaning; the response explains this by referring to the lower chapters to clarify the impurity [of the offense].

[Commentary]: If that is so, then striking [another] constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). The answer is: regarding the aspect of causing distress, it depends on the stage [of the offender]; regarding slander, it concerns disciplinary punishment; thus, there is a distinction between the clear and the turbid.
They must be distinguished.

Next, the objection that the previous [explanation] regarding the failure to establish a formal charge for a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) due to false accusation is incorrect because it is identical to the case of striking [someone in a pure state] is answered by citing the parallel response;
the text is clear.

[Commentary] Furthermore, there is another interpretation: those who slander [the rule regarding] impurity also constitute a slander against the various dharmas of the treatise, because it takes only what has been seen or heard.
Thus, to contradict what was seen as pure and say that one commits an offense is to afflict oneself and others; therefore, whether pure or turbid, the offense is the same.

One cannot follow the conditions [of the specific case], as in the case of the first precept where a *bhikṣuṇī* might be involved. When the root of the precept says "it is not," this is stated according to the origin story (*nidāna*), and it may also be applied accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "slandering one who is pure by claiming they are not in a state of perception," why would one add such slander? The text below states, "The three roots speak of reality; perception is real.

Therefore, the Vinaya says: "That person is not impure; because he did not see the offense, his slander constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, similar to the characteristics of a *sthūlātyaya* offense for striking [someone] when a grave offense has been committed."

Next, regarding the initial establishment of the principle among the masters: they take only those who have seen or heard [of the transgression] through the three external faculties, and do not discuss internal virtues as being "pure.
Second, the explanation of the obstacles has two parts: first, refuting what the previous masters relied upon; second, explaining the main text of the precepts.
Because Dhavapa was pure, he was cited and included in the Prātimokṣa-sūtra; however, when it comes to discussing subsequent offenses, one need not necessarily follow the literal text.

Regarding the first [category], the matter is cited as the basis for the accusation against the bhikṣu Ṭhapaka; it does not originate from a bhikṣuṇī, and since the subsequent rule was established based on this discussion, it applies to the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
This makes it clear that a definite offense is committed regardless of the specific circumstances, and it may also be understood in terms of the intent behind the slander.
That is to say, what is set forth in the root text refers to the mind of the slanderer and does not depend upon the object being slandered. Below...

The next section, "Explanation of Non-offenses," consists of three parts. Regarding the phrase "perceiving the three roots as real": this is also based on the fact that for one who is capable of slandering [the Sangha], there is no obstruction.

Therefore, the following citation of scriptural evidence clarifies that "impurity" refers to the defilement of the object; it specifically addresses the commission of a grave offense (*pārājika*), so how could it apply merely to other categories?

To claim that such an offense is not seen is to say that the three roots are pure. As in the following cases, one should follow this precedent; since the reasoning presented previously contradicts the principle, it is treated as such.
The *Qiangshi* (Strong Exegesis) cites this as a basis because its meaning accords with the present context.

[Commentary: The interpretations above have been presented in succession. However, below, in the section on "Prohibiting according to the Vinaya," it says: "If one prohibits [an act] that is groundless (*amūlaka*) and lacks a remaining offense (*anavaśeṣa*), the prohibition and the disciplinary treatment (*daṇḍakarma*) are not established.
Regarding the sin of slander, 'lacking a remaining offense' refers to a grave act (*gurutara-karman*), while 'remaining' refers to a previously committed offense."
How can you later say this?
Now, regarding the first section of the middle [chapter], the first two phrases conclude the reference; however, when citing and demonstrating below, one adopts the latter interpretation.

Writing the character "ru" (如) as "duo" (多) [is an error]; it refers to the *Kṣepaka-vastu* (遮犍度). This reveals that even if there is an actual offense, provided it lacks a basis (*amūlaka*), it constitutes [an offense].
Regarding the phrase "How can one later claim [otherwise] after having slandered?

[The Commentary] asks: If one slanders another who is actually impure, yet the slanderer perceives them as pure while explaining to others that they are impure and thus incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, then if the object before one is not actually a human being but one forms the perception of a human in one's mind and acts according to that perception by killing, [what would happen]?

If one commits a *pārājika* offense when the person killed is actually not human, or if I have slandered someone who is actually pure while perceiving them as impure in my mind, or if I perceive them as human while they are actually pure—if one speaks of them as impure while maintaining the perception of purity, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Likewise, if one kills a non-human while perceiving them as human, one similarly incurs a *pārājika* offense. If it is said that the mind of one who slanders another is evil...

Because the intent of the mind is what determines the gravity of the offense: the intent to kill is extremely evil, so why would it not be a grave offense? Now, regarding the analysis of the characteristics:

if one perceives something as pure but tells another that it is impure, there is no *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Likewise, if one perceives a human being as a non-human and inflicts harm, this is also not grave.
Since these cases are equivalent, why is it that [only] defaming someone by perceiving them as pure when they are actually impure, or perceiving a non-human as a human, constitutes an offense?

Regarding the offenses of killing and slandering, there are distinctions of gravity; yet, in both cases, the object and the mental state are equally violated. What principle underlies this inequality of cause and effect?

Within these difficult points, the precept against killing is analyzed by combining the object (*ālambana*) and the perception (*saṃjñā*), broadly dividing them into two parts, the first of which concerns discrepancies in the object.

The response to the objection is twofold: first, an objection concerning the reality of the object through a series of successive arguments; second, an objection concerning perception and mind, which is also twofold.
Now, following "If it were to... and so forth, there is an objection based on the discrepancy of perception, which is again twofold:
first, citing two lines of reasoning that are equal, and below this, an objection against the previous claim that they are not equal.
[Commentary] The answer regarding slander takes "the mind being empty" as its meaning, whereas for killing, both the mental state and the object must be real.

In the answer, slander is defined by the emptiness of the mind and does not require the prior existence of the object; however, for killing, both must be real, for if they differ, it is not established [as a transgression].
[Commentary]: 2. Perceiving [the person] as a great bhikṣu; 3. having a mind of anger; 4. being groundless; 5.
even before a single bhikṣu, or before a saṃgha, or before the person being slandered—each word constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, because of anger, slandering someone who is not present regarding a grave matter constitutes a *pāyattika*. 6. Regarding a grave matter; 7. the words being completed; 8. being heard and known.
In the subsequent listing of the seven conditions, the second is again enumerated to show that what was previously established has now been superseded;

it indicates that as long as one is capable of slandering without basis, it does not matter whether the object of the slander is pure or impure. Among the five [conditions], "even down to a single bhikṣu" shows that a formal recitation (pratideśanā) does not necessarily require a *saṃgha*;
the *Mahāsāṃghika* school further adds that prior to the slander, there must have been an act of insult or humiliation.

Regarding the gravity of each instance of violating the monastic regulations: according to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, those who do not appear before [the assembly], or who do not confront their accusers, or who speak privately and offhand rather than in the midst of the community, do not undergo formal disciplinary treatment by the Saṃgha; therefore, their offenses are reduced in severity.
[Commentary]: "The deficiency of conditions can be understood.
Because the deficiency of conditions results in their being fully present, it is said that they "can be understood.
[Note]: When the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, the Venerable Trapusa had attained arhatship and produced fire from his hands for the sake of the Saṃgha.
The administrative official, who was praised by the Buddha as foremost in loving-kindness, subsequently received a poor dwelling and poor food among the assembly.

He then had his sister nun publicly slander him before the Saṃgha; when he was questioned and made to confess his own words, the bhikṣus reported this transgression, and based on this, the Buddha established this precept.
[Commentary]: Regarding the conditions for the precepts. [Commentary]:

First, concerning the matter of Trapuṣa attaining the status of an *āryasaṃgha*, this is cited to show that administrative duties are difficult to perform exhaustively, which gives rise to the conditions for slander.
The *Samantapāsādikā* states that this man was a prince who left the household life.

In the *Śīla-vinaya-vaibhāṣya*, within the section explaining the circumstances of Svāti, it first recounts the conditions for the slander: when those who are unable to provide sufficient support are many and their dispositions differ, there is much that remains insufficient;
even among the Noble Ones this is so, and for ordinary monks, it is only natural that those in charge of affairs are subject to praise and blame based on right and wrong.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* next describes the original account, stating that "Svāti" is the name of a bhikṣu and "Malla" is the name of a king.

Because this prince left the household life, he is called Trapusa-māra-putra; at the age of seven, he left the household life, shaved his head, and immediately attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

[Commentary] Question: For what reason does one who has attained the state of no-more-learning still practice ritual matters? Answer: One who has attained the state of no-more-learning has exhausted the afflictions that serve as the causes for [further] rebirth.
Therefore, since the primary retribution has not yet perished, it does not hinder the cultivation of merit for the purpose of eliminating the karma that constitutes the fruit.
In the initial question, because the afflictions were exhausted and the fruit was perfected, there was nothing further to cultivate;

thus, the answer first explained that for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the causes of suffering are exhausted, meaning the causes of accumulation have already collapsed and they will not undergo further existence. Now, the following passage explains the cultivation of practice to eliminate the fruit.
The practitioner still possesses the bitter fruits [of past karma] and must therefore repay former deeds; thus, in the *Sudarsana-prcchā*, it is asked:

"Among the three types of action—study, meditation, and administrative work—why is it that one cultivates only the lowest type? The answer is: "This is because one is drawn by the latent vows of a previous life.
Once, in a past existence, when one was born into a householder's family during the time of the Buddha Pāṭhadumbara, the people of that country...
Together they held a great assembly, inviting the Buddha and the great multitude into the country to offer them sustenance.
Among the assembly, there was an Arhat who was arranging the seats and the various foods and drinks. When Trapusa saw this, his heart was filled with great joy;

he went to the place where the Buddha was and said to him: "I pray that in my future life I may meet the Buddha, leave the household life, and quickly become an Arhat to distribute [offerings] for the assembly."

The arrangement of rooms, bedding, and food and drink is no different from that of an Arhat today; having now attained the fruit of sainthood to fulfill his past vows, he therefore manages these affairs.
[Commentary] Question: What are the characteristics of one praised by the Buddha as "foremost"? Answer: As stated in the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing): "In managing the monastic community..."
Because they have parted from [unwholesome ways], all those who share the same karma and practice dwell in one place;
even those who engage in indeterminate speech, who do not cultivate the three karmas, who sleep after eating, bathe, become stout, and converse on worldly matters, are made to dwell together.
Because they enter the gateway of the Path and take delight in the Path, they attain rebirth in the heavens.
Next, regarding the previous citation of the Buddha’s praise which merely states "the foremost" without clarifying its characteristics, this is now shown. The answer contains two parts:

first, it clarifies those who can bring peace to those with a sense of shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*), namely those of similar karma and similar practice—specifically, those who study the *Sūtras* together and reside in the same place;
as well as those who study the *Abhidharma*, the *Vinaya*, preach the Dharma, or practice seated meditation.
It is likewise stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*: "Because each has its own points of doubt and obstruction, they consult where there is a place for inquiry;
thus they remain close to one another. Next, the following clarifies those who can encompass all shamelessness, lack of remorse, and indeterminate speech.

This phrase provides a general heading: "not cultivating the three types of action" and so forth refers to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). "Common worldly discourse" and "the aforementioned speech" are to be understood accordingly.
Regarding those who compose treatises and speak words of non-action, some may fear that the current text has been transmitted erroneously;

furthermore, it causes those living together to believe that anyone residing in the same place as one within the Gate of the Way is not to be cast out. It ensures that those who delight in the Way and seek rebirth in heaven do not fall into the evil realms.
Because it possesses these two capacities, it is praised as supreme.
[Commentary] Question: Since one is already engaged in monastic affairs, what is the purpose of displaying supernatural powers? According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are eight reasons:

first, to stop subsequent slander by demonstrating that one is free from the three poisons; for example, when the Buddha was slandered by a woman, he himself spoke of his ten powers and four fearlessnesses.

Second, because those who study or practice meditation may see a person engaged in administrative affairs and feel inclined to treat them with contempt, [the administrator] displays the power of fire to extinguish such competitive pride.

Therefore, there are three reasons: first, to subdue the pride of forest-dwelling bhikṣus; second, because those in cities and market towns are constantly preoccupied with worldly affairs and distractions;
third, to manifest the fruits of diligence so as to encourage those who are lazy; fourth, to increase the roots of merit of the donors;
fifth, to demonstrate that the mind does not waver even when slandered; and sixth, to show that the Saṅgha possesses great majestic power by sharing a bed.

If even those who possess [such qualities] have such supernatural power, how much more so for other great virtuous ones—how could they not be lofty and eminent? Eighth, out of concern for the correct practice (*samyak-karman*), he does not neglect or abandon it;
he is constantly in a state of meditative concentration while simultaneously attending to monastic affairs, thereby accomplishing both.

Regarding the first question among the three: since there is no motive for performing worldly affairs (*kārya*), one should not manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains this through eight conditions;
the first is to stop slander, for it is feared that people might think [the practitioner] possesses attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion.
As for the subsequent citation of the Buddha as an example, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "The Buddha was slandered by a Brahmin woman, so he let out a lion’s roar himself."
First, claiming to possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities to manifest one's purity;

second, relying on learning and intellectual understanding, or relying on meditative practice, because those who manage affairs are considered inferior to oneself, thus harboring a sense of superiority and inferiority—where "inferior" means being less than oneself;
third, regarding the three types of self-reliance on *dhūta* practices, such as being conceited and arrogant due to one's own few desires while neglecting extensive duties; fourth.
Regarding the fruit of diligence in the middle [category], it refers to the fact that practicing diligence can induce its corresponding result.

Among the six types of persons, the "venerable one" (āyuṣmat) is excluded because he has fallen away due to doubt arising from slander. Of these, the first, sixth, and eighth benefit oneself, while the remaining five are for the sake of others;
each of these can be understood by investigating how they respectively eliminate evil and give rise to goodness.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, it was asked: "How is it that one knows through entering meditative concentration (samādhi) regarding the light and spiritual power (ṛddhi) when there is distraction?

Regarding this, the treatise itself explains: First, it is like the Buddhas; second, it is the result of karmic retribution; third, it is the power of dhyāna-concentration; fourth, it is the power of nāgas.

These are all equally inconceivable (*acintya*), so there is no need for further inquiry. Second, as for this person of sharp faculties, one should know that at the time of the event, they may either enter or emerge from concentration.
The rapidity of these shifts is said to be like a single mind; it is as if one person were beating a drum while singing with their mouth—the two minds are always distinct.
Furthermore, what is so difficult about the temporary stability of meditative concentration? It is like a potter’s wheel.

Next, it is asked: "In the common course of affairs, supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) arise from the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*). However, performing worldly tasks while emitting light deviates from this norm.
To explain this, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) is cited below; that text generally explains the four inconceivable things (*catur-acintya*).

Here, we take the first and third [of these] as applicable to the question at hand. Regarding those who emulate the Buddhas, it is because the Buddha is always in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and yet remains unimpeded.
Because they function as actual activities, the operation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) can only be known through direct realization; both are unfathomable.

Second, following the question, there is an explanation which further divides into two parts. In the first part, although they are equally "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), there is no lack of distinction between sharp and dull faculties regarding their entry and emergence.

While the swift [attainment] resembles a single mind, it is only those with sharp faculties who can be illustrated by this analogy; by extension, one should know that for those of dull faculties, it is not so.

It cannot be so swift or rapid. Furthermore, the next passage explains that although one enters meditative absorption and emits light to perform worldly activities, because of the prior power of the heat, the light does not yet cease; thus it is said to "abide for a while.
This is like a potter’s wheel: once set in motion, it continues to spin by its own residual momentum.
[Commentary]: Among the assembly at the Cizhi (Maitrībala) monastery, those who received poor food often said it was due to the power of their past karma;
furthermore, because they lacked a pure mind day and night, devas, nāgas, and spirits created the conditions that caused what they obtained to be unsatisfactory.
In the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, the commentary cites a treatise to demonstrate that the initial condition was a past cause;

furthermore, because the celestial beings and others possess supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that enable them to perceive the minds of others, they caused [the practitioner] to lose his vision of what was wholesome. It says:

"Because he lacked merit, even when he encountered a virtuous donor who invited him to teach, he did not rejoice in the gift of Dharma; instead, he prepared a seat outside the door and provided offerings there."

Taking this as a standard, how could one dare to move recklessly? The dark spirits will inflict secret punishment, merit and virtue will diminish daily, and every movement will fail to achieve its purpose—all such cases are like those of Cīrṇabhūmi.
[Commentary] Dividing the text of the precept itself into seven parts: first, the person who commits the offense; second, harboring a mind of anger within; third, uttering slander.

1. The object (*ālambana*); 2. The purity of the *śīla-sūtra*; 3. Distinguishing the characteristics through an extensive explanation; 4. Clarifying mutual purity and impurity; 5. The four cases where the accusation is groundless; 6.

The five *pārājika* offenses, which are grave when slandered with false intent; 7. "If at another time... and below, the confession of the false characteristics by one's own words; 8. "If a bhikṣu... and below, the formal determination of the offense.
In the general classification of the *Prātimokṣa*, the first two and the sixth belong to the transgressor; the middle three phrases belong to the object of the accusation;
and the seventh indicates the method of offense. Regarding the three points that highlight differences between the two versions:
while the *Prātimokṣa* states that the person is "pure," meaning they are not a *pārājika* bhikṣu, the *Vibhaṅga* (Extensive Explanation) clarifies this by stating, "He is pure, like Ṭhapaka."

This matter is indeed pure; yet it is also said that if a person is not pure and slanders another based on groundless charges—whether through what has been seen, heard, or suspected—they commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and thus fall into defilement.
[Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu...
[Commentary]: The first point is self-evident.
[Vinaya]: "Because they are shrouded by hatred. [Commentary]:
Regarding the second point, "shrouded by hatred" means that because their hatred obscures the arising of kindness and compassion, they further engage in slander.

In the second sentence of the commentary on the text, it describes the cause for the arising of slander due to anger and concealment (*mrakṣa*); the meaning of anger robbing one of a compassionate heart is the same as that of concealment.
[Note: Due to the causal conditions of the ten unwholesome dharmas, anger follows along with ten matters, and among those, anger arises from two specific matters.
[Commentary] Regarding the annotation on the ten unwholesome dharmas:
some say that it is because these ten unwholesome acts can serve as the basis for slander.

[The author] explains the ancient interpretation of the ten unwholesome karmas, noting that they are only capable of giving rise to slander and cannot produce anger; therefore, [they are not included here].

[The text says: "Grasping. [Commentary: The current explanation states that the root from which anger arises does not exceed the categories of sentient and non-sentient beings. Speaking specifically in terms of sentient beings, there are no more than three causes and conditions:
first, those who harm me whom I love; second, those who harm my virtuous friends whom I cherish; and third, one's own person. It is on account of these that [anger arises].
When distributed across the three periods of time, there are nine; therefore, the Sūtra speaks of the nine bases of malice (*āghāta-vastu*) as the seeds.

Because a non-sentient object is added [to these], it is said that anger arises toward each and every one of the ten matters. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, hatred and resentment apply to both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*), whereas if one does not take pleasure [in them], this extends even to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Now, regarding the initial general summary within the explanation of the middle [section], there follows a specific analysis of the three conditions of mental states (*citta*).
First, "I hate him, but love her"; second, "I love him, but hate her"; third, "We both hate each other. All objects of anger are not outside the scope of love and hatred.
Below, it refers to a passage in the sūtra that is not detailed; however, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "This person has already harmed me."
"He harmed me in the past, he is harming me now, and he will harm me in the future" (these three phrases correspond to the past, present, and future);

"He benefited my enemy in the past, he is benefiting them now, and he will benefit them in the future" (this corresponds to the first phrase of the present); "He harmed my friend in the past, he is harming them now, and he will harm them in the future" (this corresponds to the second phrase of the present).

To give rise to resentment toward these is called the nine grounds for resentment (*navāghātasthānāni*). The first [category], which applies universally to all objects, includes both sentient and non-sentient beings.
Regarding all disagreeable events, the *Mahāsāṃghika* Vinaya is cited to distinguish between ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble learners (*śaikṣa*):

since those who have not yet severed their craving may still experience anger or displeasure, these are not considered latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); therefore, they apply universally even to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
[Vinaya] A bhikṣu who is not one guilty of a pārājika offense.

[Commentary] Regarding the three types of bhikṣus who are not guilty of a pārājika offense, these refer precisely to those who were the object of the slander; the explanation is as found in the enumerated clauses.
Regarding the phrase "the three middle fingers are like the enumerated clauses," it is either a brief indication within the preceding enumerated clauses,
or it is likely a scribal error for the character "enumerated" (列) in the phrase "enumerated conditions" (列緣). [Vinaya] To slander [another] with a groundless *pārājika* offense.
[Commentary]: The fourth [category], "slandering with groundless *pārājika* offenses," clarifies its grave characteristics. "Slandering" refers to the fault of violating the root of the precept;
"offense" refers to the previously mentioned grave offense. This is the fifth phrase. "Groundless" means not having seen the commission of the offense.
In the first section of the commentary on the fourth and fifth [offenses], there are two parts: first, a general indication of the two phrases regarding slander; second, a specific explanation.

First, the fifth [offense] regarding groundless [accusations] is explained; next, the fourth [offense] is explained. For now, the case of "not seeing" is cited, while the others are as noted in the annotations.

[Note] This refers to the three bases: seeing, hearing, and suspicion. Regarding the basis of seeing: it means seeing one violate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), seeing one steal five *kārsāpaṇa* coins, or seeing one take the life of a human being;
or if one hears from another that [these acts] were committed, this is called the basis of seeing. Regarding the basis of hearing:

it means hearing that one violated the holy life, heard that one stole five *kārsāpaṇa* coins, heard that one took the life of a human being, or heard them personally claim to have attained a superhuman state (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*); or if one says they heard it from another, this is [the basis of hearing].
This refers to the two types of roots—[the roots] of hearing and doubt—which arise from views. [Examples of those arising from views are:

entering a forest or leaving it with a woman, being naked and bare-bodied, having one's body defiled by impurities, carrying a blood-stained knife, or having evil persons as companions. Those arising from hearing are:
if, in a dark place, one hears the sound of a bed moving, the sound of turning over, the sound of bodily movement, or the sound of conversing together.
If one hears the report that I have committed unchaste conduct, or even hears the report that I have attained the state of a superior person—
apart from these three grounds, to slander me by means of any other matter constitutes groundless slander.

[Commentary] Within the sub-commentary, the section on the cessation of understanding first explains the fourth phrase. Prior to explaining "rootless" (*amūla*), it first explains "having roots" (*samūla*);
because these three roots do not exist there, it is called "rootless.
This explanation of the sub-commentary provides a general interpretation; regarding the initial passage that first explains the fourth [phrase], it explains only the two characters "rootless."
To explain the remainder of the text, one should refer to the following points and indications for comparison.

[Commentary]: Question: What is meant by "root" (*mūla*)? Answer: Regarding the characteristics of false accusation (*ābhyākhyāna*), there is no difference between them and the act of formal charge (*codanā*).

Although in reality there is no hearing or seeing, one falsely employs the pretext of having heard or seen to bring a charge against another; because this very "hearing or seeing" serves as the basis for the charge, it is called a "root."

Regarding the initial question within the "Establishment of Names," it can be answered as follows: although one may lack direct perception or hearing [of an offense], one must rely on false attribution to bring forth the charges against another so as to effect their formal expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) by the Sangha. Because this serves to initiate the formal accusation, it is termed a "root" (*mūla*).
Thus, the phrase "in reality non-existent" (*vastuto 'sat*) and so forth indicates that "false" (*jia*) is synonymous with "erroneous" (*wang*).
[Commentary]: If this is so, why is it that one who slanders based on not having seen or heard is not called a "root of slander"? The treatise answers that hatred (*dveṣa*) is the root of slander.

Regarding the initial objection within the subsequent refutation—asking why, when the name "root" is properly applied to the current precept, one must instead cite and explain the transgression (*atikrama*)—the answer is that since slander itself has its own root, it is not [itself] the root of slander.

[Commentary]: Regarding the objection that "raising a charge" (*ukkhepana*) should also have the mind as its root, the answer is that while the meaning actually applies universally, the roots are distinct.
Why is this so? Because one first perceives through seeing or hearing, and subsequently gives rise to the mind that raises the charge; thus, seeing and hearing function as the roots.
Furthermore, since slander arises from prior anger—first hating someone and then initiating the slander—anger is the root of slander.
